question_html: After a buy-back, KG Limited issues bonus shares ‚Äî 1 share for every 4 equity shares held. 1,200 lakhs original equity – 300 lakhs bought back = 900 lakhs equity remaining. What is the amount of bonus shares to be issued, and from which source?
option_b: ₹300 lakhs from Securities Premium
option_c: ₹225 lakhs (25% of ₹900 lakhs) from Capital Redemption Reserve
option_d: ₹200 lakhs from P&L Account
explanation_html:
After buy-back, remaining equity share capital = ₹1,200 – ₹300 = ₹900 lakhs.

Bonus issue = 1 share for every 4 shares held = 25% of existing equity.
Bonus shares = 25% × ₹900 = ₹225 lakhs.

Source: Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR) ‚Äî As per Section 69(2) of the Companies Act, the CRR may be applied in paying up unissued shares to be issued to members as fully paid-up bonus shares.

Journal entry: CRR Dr. ₹225 ‚Üí Bonus Shares A/c Cr. ₹225; then Bonus Shares Dr. ₹225 ‚Üí Equity Share Capital Cr. ₹225.

The CRR was created at ₹300 lakhs; ₹225 lakhs is utilised for bonus, leaving ₹75 lakhs in CRR.

question_html: What is the amount of net borrowing cost capitalized to the cost of the factory?
explanation_html:
As per AS 16 (Borrowing Costs):

Gross borrowing cost = ‚Çπ28,00,000 x 9% x 9/12 = ‚Çπ1,89,000

Less: Investment income on temporary investment = ‚Çπ25,000

Net borrowing cost capitalised = ‚Çπ1,89,000 - ‚Çπ25,000 = ‚Çπ1,64,000

The question specifies 9-month basis (April 2022 to December 2022). Investment income earned while temporarily investing loan proceeds is deducted before capitalisation.

question_html: Vijay Ltd. borrowed ‚Çπ 30 Iakh at interest rate of 5% per annum and purchased plant and machinery for ‚Çπ 60 Iakh (using borrowed funds) and started production. It took 1 year time for Vijay Ltd. to create optimum market for the goods manufactured and generate revenue. How much borrowing cost can be capitalised with cost of plant and machinery:
option_b: ‚Çπ3 Lakh
option_c: Nil
option_d: ‚Çπ5 Lakh
explanation_html:
As per AS 16 (Borrowing Costs), borrowing costs are capitalised only when they are incurred in connection with a qualifying asset ‚Äî an asset that takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use.

Plant and machinery that is purchased (not constructed) and is immediately ready for use upon purchase is NOT a qualifying asset. The 1 year period taken to create a market and generate revenue is a commercial period ‚Äî not a construction/preparation period for the asset itself.

Since the plant was ready for use immediately upon purchase, no borrowing cost can be capitalised. Capitalisation applies only while the asset is being made ready (e.g., under construction), not while the business is ramping up.

question_html: After completing a buy-back under Section 68, within what time period must the company extinguish and physically destroy the securities bought back?
option_b: Within 7 days of the last date of completion of buy-back
option_c: Within 30 days
option_d: At the end of the financial year
explanation_html:
Section 68(6) of the Companies Act, 2013 states: Where a company buys back its own securities, it shall extinguish and physically destroy the securities so bought back within SEVEN DAYS of the last date of completion of buy-back.

This is important because buy-back leads to reduction of share capital ‚Äî the bought-back shares must be cancelled (not held as treasury shares as in some other jurisdictions). The company cannot re-issue these shares after buy-back.

Additionally, the company must file a return with the Registrar (and SEBI for listed companies) within 30 days of completion of buy-back, and maintain a register of securities bought back.

question_html: Under the Pooling of Interests Method (AS 14), what is the key principle for recording assets and liabilities of the transferor company in the transferee's books?
option_a: Assets and liabilities are recorded at their fair values at the date of amalgamation
option_b: Assets and liabilities are recorded at their existing carrying amounts (book values), except where adjustment is needed for uniform accounting policies
option_c: Assets are recorded at fair value; liabilities at book value
option_d: All assets and liabilities are written off against goodwill
explanation_html:
Under the Pooling of Interests Method (used for merger-type amalgamations), AS 14 prescribes that the assets, liabilities and reserves of the transferor company are recorded by the transferee company at their existing carrying amounts (book values).

The only exception: if the transferor and transferee companies follow different accounting policies (e.g., different inventory valuation methods), adjustments are made to bring consistency. For example, if the transferor uses weighted average and the transferee uses FIFO, the transferor's inventory is restated to FIFO values.

This contrasts with the Purchase Method where assets/liabilities can be recorded at existing carrying amounts OR fair values.

question_html: Dee Limited plans to buy back 20% of its equity capital (50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each) at ₹50 per share. Investments were sold for ₹22 lakhs (cost ₹30 lakhs). Securities Premium = ₹22 lakhs, Revenue Reserve = ₹30 lakhs. Which source is used for the premium on buy-back?
option_b: Securities Premium = ₹20 lakhs for premium (50,000 × ₹40)
option_c: Premium split equally between Securities Premium and Revenue Reserve
option_d: Premium is adjusted from Capital Reserve
explanation_html:
Buy-back details for Dee Limited:
Shares bought back = 20% × 2,50,000 = 50,000 shares
Face value per share = ₹10; Buy-back price = ₹50
Premium per share = ₹40
Total premium = 50,000 × ₹40 = ₹20 lakhs
Total face value = 50,000 × ₹10 = ₹5 lakhs

Securities Premium A/c (balance ₹22 lakhs) Dr. ₹20 lakhs ‚Üí To Premium Payable on Buy-Back A/c ₹20 lakhs. The full premium is charged to Securities Premium as the balance (₹22 lakhs) is sufficient.

CRR creation = ₹5 lakhs (from Revenue Reserve, as the face value of shares bought back out of free resources).
Note: Loss on sale of investments (₹8 lakhs) reduces the Profit & Loss Account.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
question_html: As per Section 2(87) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company shall be a subsidiary if the holding company:
option_a: Holds more than 25% of the equity shares of the subsidiary
option_b: Controls the composition of the Board of Directors OR exercises/controls more than one-half of the total share capital
option_c: Holds more than 75% of equity shares giving it an automatic right to pass special resolutions
option_d: Provides more than 50% of the funding requirements of the subsidiary
explanation_html:
Section 2(87) of the Companies Act, 2013 defines a subsidiary company as one in which the holding company:
(i) Controls the composition of the Board of Directors; OR
(ii) Exercises or controls more than one-half of the total share capital either at its own or together with one or more of its subsidiary companies.

A company is deemed to be a subsidiary even if there is indirect control through subsidiary companies. Control over the Board of Directors means having the power to appoint or remove all or a majority of directors. It does not require holding the shares outright ‚Äî control through subsidiaries also counts. Importantly, Section 19 prohibits a subsidiary from holding shares in its holding company.

chapter_id: Accounting for Branches including foreign branches
question_html: Under the Stock and Debtors Method, when goods are invoiced at cost, which additional account is NOT maintained compared to the Debtors Method?
option_b: Branch Debtors Account
option_c: Branch Adjustment Account
option_d: Branch Profit and Loss Account
explanation_html:
Under the Stock and Debtors Method when goods are invoiced at cost, the following accounts are maintained:
1. Branch Stock Account (for closing balance of stock)
2. Branch Debtors Account
3. Branch Expenses Account
4. Goods Sent to Branch Account
5. Branch Cash/Bank Account
6. Branch Fixed Asset Account
7. Branch Profit and Loss Account

The Branch Adjustment Account is an additional account used ONLY when goods are invoiced at selling price (above cost). It is used to record the 'loading' (profit element) and to eventually arrive at gross profit. When goods are at cost, there is no loading, so no Branch Adjustment Account is needed. The credit balance of Branch Adjustment A/c represents the gross profit earned on branch sales.

question_html: By using the Debt Equity Ratio Test determine the number of shares that can be bought back:
explanation_html:
Debt Equity Ratio Test: Post buy-back, debt cannot exceed twice the equity.

Total debt = ‚Çπ28,75,000 + ‚Çπ16,50,000 = ‚Çπ45,25,000.

Minimum equity required = ‚Çπ45,25,000 / 2 = ‚Çπ22,62,500.

Current equity = ‚Çπ31,25,000. Max usable = ‚Çπ31,25,000 - ‚Çπ22,62,500 = ‚Çπ8,62,500.

Using the simultaneous equation method per ICAI (buy-back reduces both paid-up capital and free reserves): maximum = 28,750 shares.

question_html: At the end of Year 2, the Project should be valued at:
option_b: ‚Çπ 35.50 Crore
option_c: ‚Çπ 35.10 Crore
option_d: ‚Çπ 25 Crore
explanation_html:
When the building is reclassified from Inventory to PPE at the start of Year 2, it is transferred at its carrying amount of ‚Çπ 35 crore (lower of cost and NRV from Year 1).

Under AS 10, subsequent expenditure is added to the carrying amount of PPE only if it increases the future economic benefits beyond the originally assessed standard. The ‚Çπ 50 lacs spent on structural changes are necessary to use the building as a corporate office (without these the office cannot be set up) ‚Äî so they are capital expenditure and are added to PPE.

PPE value at end of Year 2 = ‚Çπ 35 cr + ‚Çπ 0.50 cr = ‚Çπ 35.50 crore.

question_html: As per AS 17, which of the following is excluded from Segment Assets?
option_a: Trade receivables directly attributable to the segment
option_b: Property, plant and equipment used exclusively by the segment
option_c: Income tax assets and assets used for general enterprise/head-office purposes
option_d: Investments in associates where the segment's result includes dividend income from such associates
explanation_html: As per AS 17, Segment Assets do NOT include: (i) Income tax assets (deferred tax assets, advance tax, tax deposits etc.); and (ii) Assets used for general enterprise or head-office purposes. These are unallocated corporate assets presented as reconciling items. Segment assets are those operating assets employed by a segment in its operating activities and either directly attributable or reasonably allocable to the segment. If segment result includes interest/dividend income, the related receivables/loans/investments are included in segment assets. This distinction is tested through numerical problems where deferred tax must be excluded before applying the 10% asset test.

question_html: Sun Ltd. has entered into a sale contract (₹ 5 crore, profit ₹ 1 crore) with delivery due in the first month of the next year. For non-delivery, compensation of ₹ 1.5 crore is payable. As at 31-3-20X2, goods were not manufactured and it is unlikely Sun Ltd. can meet the obligation. As per AS 29, (i) Should provision be made? (ii) Should the provision be ₹ 50 lakhs (₹ 1.5 cr minus ₹ 1 cr profit)?
option_b: (i) Yes, provision of ₹ 50 lakhs (net of profit); (ii) Yes ‚Äî offset is allowed
option_c: (i) Yes, provision of ₹ 1.5 crore (full compensation); (ii) No ‚Äî profit has not yet accrued, so full provision is required
option_d: (i) Disclose as contingent liability; (ii) Not applicable
explanation_html:
(i) Provision: Sun Ltd. has a present obligation arising from the sale contract (past event = entering the contract). It is probable that Sun Ltd. will fail to deliver (goods not manufactured, unlikely to meet obligation). A reliable estimate of compensation (₹1.5 crore) exists. All three conditions met ‚Üí Provision of ₹1.5 crore must be recognised.

(ii) Measurement: The goods were not manufactured by 31-3-20X2 ‚Äî no profit of ₹1 crore has been earned or accrued for FY 20X1-X2. You cannot offset a future expected profit (which hasn't been earned) against a present liability. Provision must be made for the full ₹1.5 crore. As per AS 29, gains on expected disposal/transactions are not taken into account in measuring a provision ‚Äî the provision and the expected profit are separate events.

question_html: AB sells goods to CD on 1st March 20X1. CD has significant cash flow problems but is trying to raise bank funding. On 5th May 20X1, CD secures the funding and is expected to pay. Under AS 9, when should AB recognise revenue?
option_a: 1st March 20X1 ‚Äî on the date of sale when goods are transferred
option_b: 31st March 20X1 ‚Äî at the year-end balance sheet date
option_c: 5th May 20X1 ‚Äî when the uncertainty about collectability is resolved
option_d: When the actual cash is received from CD
explanation_html:
AS 9 states: revenue from sales transactions should be recognised when performance conditions are satisfied, provided that at the time of performance it is not unreasonable to expect ultimate collection. If at the time of raising a claim it is unreasonable to expect ultimate collection, revenue recognition should be postponed.

On 1st March 20X1, due to CD's significant cash flow issues, it is unreasonable to expect ultimate collection. Therefore, AB should not recognise revenue on 1st March. Revenue should be recognised on 5th May 20X1 ‚Äî when the uncertainty about recovery is resolved (CD secures funding).

Until then, inventory transferred to CD remains AB's inventory (shown as inventory lying with customers).

question_html: Under Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013, how should current maturities of long-term debt be classified?
option_b: Under Short Term Borrowings
option_c: Under Non-Current Liabilities
option_d: Disclosed as contingent liabilities only
explanation_html:
As per Schedule III (as amended by MCA notification dated 24th March 2021), current maturities of long-term debt (i.e., instalments of long-term loans due within the next 12 months from the balance sheet date) shall be shown under Short Term Borrowings as part of Current Liabilities. They were previously shown under "Other Current Liabilities" but the amendment specifically categorises them under Short Term Borrowings.

This distinction is critical for Balance Sheet preparation: the long-term portion stays under Long Term Borrowings (Non-Current Liabilities), while the current maturities move to Short Term Borrowings (Current Liabilities).

question_html: Under the Net Assets Method of computing purchase consideration, what is included?
option_b: Value of assets taken over (at agreed/fair values) minus liabilities taken over (at agreed/fair values) = Net assets transferred to the transferee company
option_c: Total assets minus total liabilities including share capital and reserves
option_d: The market capitalisation of the transferor company
explanation_html:
Under the Net Assets Method, Purchase Consideration = Value of Assets taken over minus Outside Liabilities taken over.

The values used are: (i) At the agreed values between the parties; or (ii) If no value is agreed, at book value.

From Illustration 2 (B Ltd. absorbing A Ltd.):
Assets at agreed values: PPE ₹35,75 (₹32.50 × 110%) + Investments ₹6,00 + Current Assets ₹4,50 (₹5,00 × 90%) = ₹46,25
Less: Liabilities: Debentures ₹7,70 (₹7,00 × 110%) + Current Liabilities ₹5,00 = ₹12,70
Net Assets = ₹33,55 lakhs = Purchase Consideration

Note: Share capital and reserves are NOT deducted ‚Äî only outside/third-party liabilities are deducted.

question_html: As per Section 68(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company can buy back its own shares out of which of the following sources?
option_a: Free reserves, Securities premium account, and Proceeds of any shares or other specified securities
option_b: Revaluation reserve, Free reserves, and Share premium account
option_c: Capital reserve, Revenue reserve, and Securities premium account
option_d: Free reserves only
explanation_html:
Section 68(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 permits companies to buy back their own shares out of:
(i) Free reserves; or
(ii) Securities premium account; or
(iii) Proceeds of the issue of any shares or other specified securities.

Important Note: No buy-back shall be made out of the proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of shares. For example, if equity shares are to be bought back, proceeds from preference shares (a different kind) can be used but not proceeds from a fresh issue of equity shares.

Revaluation reserve is specifically excluded ‚Äî it represents unrealised profits and hence cannot be used for buy-back of securities.

question_html: Sumedha Ltd. took a ₹10,00,000 loan to be repaid in 10 equal half-yearly instalments (₹1,00,000 each). As per the amended Schedule III (MCA notification dated 24th March 2021), how should this loan be classified in the Balance Sheet as at 31st March 20X1?
option_b: Entire ₹10,00,000 under Short Term Borrowings
option_c: ₹8,00,000 under Long Term Borrowings; ₹2,00,000 (current maturities ‚Äî 2 instalments due in next 12 months) under Short Term Borrowings
option_d: ₹9,00,000 under Long Term Borrowings; ₹1,00,000 under Short Term Borrowings
explanation_html:
As per the amended Schedule III, instalments due within 12 months from the balance sheet date are classified as current maturities of long-term debt under Short Term Borrowings/Other Current Liabilities.

As at 31st March 20X1, the next two half-yearly instalments are due:
1st instalment: 30th September 20X1 ‚úì (within 12 months)
2nd instalment: 31st March 20X2 ‚úì (within 12 months)

Total current maturities = 2 × ₹1,00,000 = ₹2,00,000 ‚Üí Short Term Borrowings
Remaining 8 instalments = ₹8,00,000 ‚Üí Long Term Borrowings

question_html: B Ltd. had 20,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, ₹8 paid up. In June 20X2, each share is sub-divided into two shares of ₹5 with ₹4 paid up. What journal entry is passed and what is the paid-up capital?
option_c: No entry needed since the amount remains the same
option_d: Equity Share Capital Dr. ₹1,60,000 / To Capital Reserve Cr. ₹1,60,000
explanation_html:
For sub-division of shares, the entry applies only to the paid-up portion, not the uncalled amount:

Original: 20,000 shares × ₹10 face value, ₹8 paid = ₹1,60,000 paid-up capital.
Sub-divided: 40,000 shares × ₹5 face value, ₹4 paid = ₹1,60,000 paid-up capital.

Entry: Equity Share Capital (₹10) A/c Dr. ₹1,60,000 / To Equity Share Capital (₹5) A/c Cr. ₹1,60,000

The paid-up capital remains unchanged at ₹1,60,000. The proportion between paid-up and unpaid amount (8:2 ‚Üí 4:1) must remain the same after sub-division as required by Section 61. Note: the entry is passed only on the paid-up portion (₹8 × 20,000 = ₹1,60,000), not the full face value.

question_html: In the books of M/s Prashant Ltd., closing inventory as at 31.03.20X2 amounts to ₹ 1,63,000 (on FIFO method). The company changes to weighted average method; closing inventory under this method is ₹ 1,47,000. NRV is ₹ 1,95,000. As per AS 1, what is the effect of this change in accounting policy that must be disclosed, and at what value should closing inventory be stated?
option_a: Profit reduced by ₹ 16,000; Inventory stated at ₹ 1,63,000 (FIFO, since NRV is higher)
option_b: Profit reduced by ₹ 16,000; Inventory stated at ₹ 1,47,000 (weighted average)
option_c: Profit reduced by ₹ 48,000; Inventory stated at ₹ 1,47,000
option_d: Profit increased by ₹ 16,000; Inventory stated at ₹ 1,63,000
explanation_html:
Since NRV (₹1,95,000) is higher than both FIFO cost (₹1,63,000) and weighted average cost (₹1,47,000), inventory is valued at cost under lower of cost or NRV. The company has changed its method of cost ascertainment from FIFO to weighted average.

Effect of change = ₹1,63,000 – ₹1,47,000 = ₹16,000 reduction in profit and inventory value.

As per AS 1, the company must disclose: (i) the change in accounting policy (from FIFO to weighted average), (ii) the reason for change (better reflects consumption pattern), and (iii) the financial effect ‚Äî reduction in profit and inventory by ₹16,000. The closing inventory is stated at ₹1,47,000 under the new policy.

question_html: M/s XYZ Ltd. has three segments. Total Assets = ₹ 10 crore. Segment X: ₹ 2 crore (including deferred tax asset ₹ 0.50 crore), Segment Y: ₹ 3 crore (DTA ₹ 0.40 crore), Segment Z: ₹ 5 crore (DTA ₹ 0.30 crore). The accountant says all three are reportable segments based on the asset test. Is this correct?
option_a: Incorrect ‚Äî only Segment Z is reportable since it has the largest assets
option_b: Correct ‚Äî all three segments are reportable since each holds more than 10% of the total segment assets after excluding deferred tax assets
option_c: Incorrect ‚Äî only Segments Y and Z are reportable since Segment X's net assets are below 10%
option_d: Incorrect ‚Äî income tax assets should not be excluded since they are part of total enterprise assets
explanation_html:
As per AS 17, Segment Assets do NOT include income tax assets (including deferred tax assets). Revised figures:
Total Assets = ₹10 cr – (0.50+0.40+0.30) = ₹8.80 crore
Segment X: ₹2.00–₹0.50 = ₹1.50 cr; 1.50/8.80 = 17.05% ≥ 10% ✓
Segment Y: ₹3.00–₹0.40 = ₹2.60 cr; 2.60/8.80 = 29.55% ≥ 10% ✓
Segment Z: ₹5.00–₹0.30 = ₹4.70 cr; 4.70/8.80 = 53.41% ≥ 10% ✓

All three segments hold more than 10% of the total assets. The accountant's contention is correct.

question_html: How much revenue should be recognised by the Company in the financial year 2024-25:
explanation_html:
Installation was completed on 5 April 2024 ‚Äî falling in FY 2024-25.

Installation fee deferred from FY 2023-24 = ‚Çπ1,000 √ó 5 ACs = ‚Çπ5,000.

This ‚Çπ5,000 is recognised in FY 2024-25 when the service obligation is fulfilled (installation completed).

question_html: ABC Ltd. is installing a new plant (not a qualifying asset) with the following costs: (1) Cost of plant: ₹ 25,00,000; (2) Initial delivery: ₹ 2,00,000; (3) Site preparation: ₹ 6,00,000; (4) Consultants' fees: ₹ 7,00,000; (5) Interest charges to supplier for deferred credit: ₹ 2,00,000; (6) Estimated dismantling costs after 7 years: ₹ 3,00,000; (7) Operating losses before commercial production: ₹ 4,00,000. What is the correct capitalised cost of the plant?
explanation_html:
As per AS 10, directly attributable costs and initial decommissioning estimates are capitalised; interest on deferred credit (for non-qualifying assets) and pre-production losses are expensed:

Cost of plant₹ 25,00,000✓
Initial delivery₹ 2,00,000✓
Site preparation₹ 6,00,000✓
Consultants' fees₹ 7,00,000✓
Dismantling costs₹ 3,00,000✓
Total Capitalised₹ 43,00,000

NOT capitalised:
Interest on deferred credit (₹ 2,00,000): Since this is not a qualifying asset under AS 16, interest cannot be capitalised ‚Äî expensed to P&L.
Operating losses before commercial production (₹ 4,00,000): Explicitly excluded under AS 10 ‚Äî expensed as incurred.

question_html: Under AS 14, the Pooling of Interests Method is used for:
option_a: Amalgamation in the nature of purchase, where assets are taken over at fair value
option_b: Amalgamation in the nature of merger
option_c: Both types of amalgamation at the discretion of management
option_d: Amalgamation in the nature of purchase, where assets are taken at book value
explanation_html:
AS 14 prescribes a specific method for each type of amalgamation:

Amalgamation in the nature of Merger ‚Üí Pooling of Interests Method: Assets, liabilities, and reserves of the transferor are recorded at their existing carrying amounts (book values). The identity of reserves is preserved. Minimal changes are made to financial statements to reflect the pooling.

Amalgamation in the nature of Purchase ‚Üí Purchase Method: Assets and liabilities are incorporated either at existing carrying amounts or at fair values. Goodwill or Capital Reserve arises from the difference between consideration and net assets acquired.

There is NO choice ‚Äî the method is determined by the TYPE of amalgamation, not management discretion.

question_html: For AS 18 (Related Party Disclosures) and AS 28 (Impairment of Assets) to be exempt from application to an MSME non-company entity in its entirety, which additional conditions must the MSME satisfy?
option_a: Turnover not exceeding ₹ 250 crore and borrowings not exceeding ₹ 50 crore
option_b: Turnover not exceeding ₹ 100 crore and borrowings not exceeding ₹ 25 crore
option_c: Turnover not exceeding ₹ 50 crore AND borrowings not exceeding ₹ 10 crore AND not a holding or subsidiary of a non-qualifying MSME
option_d: Only condition is that the entity is not a holding or subsidiary of any other entity
explanation_html: AS 18 (Related Party Disclosures) and AS 28 (Impairment of Assets) are not applicable in their entirety to MSMEs which satisfy all three of the following additional conditions: (a) turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed ₹ 50 crore in the immediately preceding accounting year; (b) borrowings do not exceed ₹ 10 crore at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year; and (c) not a holding or subsidiary of an MSME not covered above. Note: These thresholds (₹ 50 crore / ₹ 10 crore) are much lower than the general MSME thresholds (₹ 250 crore / ₹ 50 crore). Students frequently confuse these two sets of limits ‚Äî this is a common exam trap.

question_html: Under the Purchase Method (AS 14), when is Goodwill recognised vs Capital Reserve?
option_a: Goodwill when net assets > purchase consideration; Capital Reserve when purchase consideration > net assets
option_b: Goodwill when purchase consideration > net assets acquired; Capital Reserve when net assets acquired > purchase consideration
option_c: Goodwill is always recognised in purchase amalgamation regardless of amounts
option_d: Capital Reserve is always recognised; goodwill is not recognised
explanation_html:
Under the Purchase Method:

Net Assets acquired = Total assets transferred – Liabilities assumed (at agreed/fair values)

If Purchase Consideration > Net Assets: Excess = Goodwill (intangible asset). The transferee paid more than what the identifiable net assets are worth ‚Äî the excess represents goodwill (brand, customer relationships, etc.). Goodwill should be amortised over a period not exceeding 5 years unless a longer period can be justified.

If Net Assets > Purchase Consideration: Excess = Capital Reserve (a gain ‚Äî the transferee acquired more than it paid for). This represents a bargain purchase.

Goodwill arising on amalgamation represents a payment in anticipation of future income.

question_html: At the end of Year 1, at value Project should be recognised:
option_b: ‚Çπ 35 Crore
option_c: ‚Çπ 35.10 Crore
option_d: ‚Çπ 25 Crore
explanation_html:
As per AS 2, inventories are valued at the lower of cost or NRV.

Cost: Land ‚Çπ 10 cr + Construction ‚Çπ 25 cr = ‚Çπ 35 crore. (Administrative meeting costs of ‚Çπ 10 lacs are not product costs ‚Äî they are period costs charged to P&L.)

NRV: ‚Çπ 40 crore.

Lower of cost (‚Çπ 35 cr) and NRV (‚Çπ 40 cr) = ‚Çπ 35 crore.

Note: Option (c) ‚Çπ 35.10 crore incorrectly includes administrative meeting costs of ‚Çπ 10 lacs as part of inventory cost.

question_html: Accounting Standards (ASs) are written policy documents issued by the Government with the support of other regulatory bodies. Which of the following is NOT an aspect covered by Accounting Standards?
option_b: Measurement of transactions and events
option_c: Taxation treatment of transactions
option_d: Disclosure requirements relating to transactions
explanation_html: As per the ICAI study material, Accounting Standards cover four aspects: Recognition, Measurement, Presentation, and Disclosure of accounting transactions or events in financial statements. Taxation treatment is governed by separate tax laws and is not one of the aspects covered by Accounting Standards.

question_html: As per AS 14, which of the following is the correct definition of Purchase Consideration?
option_a: The total value of all assets taken over from the transferor company
option_b: The aggregate of shares and other securities issued and cash/asset payments made by the transferee company to the shareholders of the transferor company
option_c: The net assets of the transferor company at fair value
option_d: The total amount paid by the transferee to all stakeholders including debenture holders and creditors
explanation_html:
AS 14 Para 3(g) defines purchase consideration as "the aggregate of the shares and other securities issued and the payment made in the form of cash or other assets by the transferee company to the shareholders of the transferor company."

Key points:
‚Ä¢ Only payments to shareholders (equity and preference) are included
‚Ä¢ Payments to debenture holders are NOT part of purchase consideration ‚Äî they represent liability assumption
‚Ä¢ Payments to creditors are also NOT included ‚Äî assumed as liabilities

This distinction is critical and tested consistently in ICAI examinations. In Illustration 1, the amount payable to debenture holders (via issue of 8% Mortgage Debentures) is specifically excluded from purchase consideration.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
question_html: H Ltd. acquires 80% of S Ltd. on 31st March 20X1 for ₹ 2,20,000. S Ltd.'s Share Capital = ₹ 2,50,000; Profit & Loss A/c = ₹ 1,00,000 (all pre-acquisition). What is the Capital Reserve/(Goodwill)?
option_b: Capital Reserve ₹ 60,000
option_c: Nil ‚Äî cost equals net worth
option_d: Capital Reserve ₹ 40,000
explanation_html:
Net worth of S Ltd. = ₹2,50,000 + ₹1,00,000 = ₹3,50,000.
H Ltd.'s 80% share = 80% × ₹3,50,000 = ₹2,80,000.
Cost of Investment = ₹2,20,000.

Since H Ltd.'s share of net worth (₹2,80,000) exceeds the cost paid (₹2,20,000), Capital Reserve = ₹2,80,000 – ₹2,20,000 = ₹60,000.

Rule: Goodwill = when cost > parent's share of equity (paid premium). Capital Reserve = when parent's share of equity > cost (paid less than fair value ‚Äî bargain purchase).

question_html: The amount of Profit/Loss on Sale of Investment is:
option_b: ‚Çπ 1,000 lakhs Profit
option_c: ‚Çπ 2,000 lakhs Loss
option_d: ‚Çπ 1,000 lakhs Loss
explanation_html:
Investments sold: market value ‚Çπ1,000 lakhs sold for ‚Çπ3,000 lakhs.

The scenario says sell investments with market value of ‚Çπ1,000 lakhs but the total investments have a book value of ‚Çπ3,000 lakhs and total market value of ‚Çπ1,500 lakhs.

Proportion sold = ‚Çπ1,000 out of ‚Çπ1,500 market value = 2/3 of investments.

Book value of investments sold = 2/3 √ó ‚Çπ3,000 = ‚Çπ2,000 lakhs.

Sale proceeds = ‚Çπ3,000 lakhs.

Profit = Sale proceeds ‚Äì Book value = ‚Çπ3,000 ‚Äì ‚Çπ2,000 = ‚Çπ1,000 lakhs Profit.

question_html: A trader has purchased 500 units @ ₹ 10 per unit. He sold 400 units @ ₹ 15 per unit. The net realisable value (NRV) per unit of the remaining 100 unsold units is ₹ 8. As per AS 1's principle of prudence, what is the value of closing inventory and the profit for the period?
option_b: Closing inventory: ₹ 800; Profit: ₹ 1,800
option_c: Closing inventory: ₹ 800; Profit: ₹ 2,000
option_d: Closing inventory: ₹ 1,000; Profit: ₹ 1,800
explanation_html:
As per the principle of prudence under AS 1, inventory is valued at lower of cost and net realisable value.

Cost per unit = ₹ 10; NRV per unit = ₹ 8.
Since NRV (₹ 8) < Cost (₹ 10), inventory is valued at NRV = 100 × ₹ 8 = ₹ 800.

Profit = Sales – Cost of goods sold
= (400 × ₹15) – (500 × ₹10 – 100 × ₹8)
= ₹6,000 – (₹5,000 – ₹800)
= ₹6,000 – ₹4,200 = ₹1,800.

The possible future loss of ₹200 (100 units × ₹2) is recognised in the current period by valuing inventory at NRV. This prevents overstatement of profit by ₹200.

question_html: Under AS 7, a construction contract with a fixed contract value of ₹ 600 (in ₹ 000) has the following data for Year 1: Cost incurred to date = ₹ 390; Estimated future costs = ₹ 260. What is the provision for foreseeable loss to be created in Year 1 (in ₹ 000)?
explanation_html:
Total estimated cost = ₹390 + ₹260 = ₹650 (₹ 000).
Contract price = ₹600. Total foreseeable loss = ₹50.

Stage of completion = ₹390 √∑ ₹650 = 60%.
Revenue for Year 1 = 60% × ₹600 = ₹360.

Actual loss (Year 1) = Revenue – Cost = ₹360 – ₹390 = –₹30 (loss of ₹30).

Provision for future loss = Total foreseeable loss – Current year actual loss = ₹50 – ₹30 = ₹20.

Total P&L charge in Year 1 = Cost ₹390 + Provision ₹20 = ₹410; Revenue ₹360; Net Loss = ₹50 (full foreseeable loss).

question_html: Bright Enterprises, an unlisted non-company entity with turnover of ₹ 180 crore and borrowings of ₹ 35 crore, qualifies as an MSME and was availing MSME exemptions. In the immediately preceding accounting year, its turnover jumped to ₹ 270 crore, making it a Large entity. What is the correct treatment for the current accounting period?
option_a: Continue using MSME exemptions since transition period is permitted
option_b: Apply full AS requirements from the current period; revise previous year figures to remove MSME treatment
option_c: Apply full AS requirements from the current period; previous year figures need not be revised; disclose the change and the fact that previous figures are not revised
option_d: Apply full AS requirements only from the next accounting period, giving the entity time to adjust
explanation_html: When an MSME no longer qualifies in the current accounting period, the relevant standards or requirements become applicable from the current period. However, the figures for the corresponding period of the previous accounting period need not be revised merely by reason of having ceased to be an MSME. The entity must disclose: (i) that it was an MSME in the previous period and had availed exemptions/relaxations; and (ii) that the previous period figures have not been revised. These disclosures must appear in the notes to the financial statements. Option (b) is incorrect because it requires revision of prior year figures which is not mandated. Option (a) is incorrect as the entity must comply fully with AS from the current period.

question_html: What is the maximum number of shares that can be bought back according to the Resources Test?
option_b: 42,500 shares
option_c: 37,500 shares
option_d: 54,375 shares
explanation_html:
Resources Test: Buy-back value ‚â§ 25% of (paid-up capital + free reserves).

Free reserves = Revenue Reserve ‚Çπ23,50,000 + Securities Premium ‚Çπ2,50,000 + P&L ‚Çπ2,00,000 = ‚Çπ28,00,000. (Infrastructure Development Reserve is a specific purpose reserve ‚Äî excluded from free reserves.)

Paid-up capital = ‚Çπ17,00,000. Total = ‚Çπ45,00,000.

25% of ‚Çπ45,00,000 = ‚Çπ11,25,000 (maximum buy-back value).

At ‚Çπ30/share: ‚Çπ11,25,000 √∑ ‚Çπ30 = 37,500 shares.

question_html: Which of the following best describes the concept of 'Creative Accounting' as discussed in the context of Accounting Standards?
option_a: Use of creative visual presentation in financial statements to attract investors
option_b: Twisting of accounting policies to produce financial statements favourable to a particular interest group
option_c: Development of innovative accounting standards by the ASB
option_d: Preparing financial statements using internationally accepted creative formats
explanation_html: Creative accounting refers to the twisting of accounting policies to produce financial statements favourable to a particular interest group. For example, overstating profits and assets by capitalising revenue expenditure, or understating them by writing off capital expenditure against revenue. Accounting Standards curb such practices by providing adequate guidance, especially for borderline cases.

question_html: During the implementation period, how the expenditure incurred will be accounted for:
option_a: It will be expensed in profit and loss as and when incurred
option_b: It will be recognised as an asset 'Intangible asset under development'
option_c: It will only be disclosed in notes to accounts and will be recognised when complete
option_d: It will be recognised as an item of Property, Plant and Equipment
explanation_html:
As per AS 26 (Intangible Assets), when an intangible asset is being developed/implemented but is not yet ready for use, the expenditure incurred during the development phase should be recognised as an Intangible Asset Under Development (analogous to capital work-in-progress for tangible assets).

The costs are accumulated until the asset is ready for use, at which point they are reclassified to the intangible assets account and amortisation begins. Expensing during development (option a) would be incorrect if the asset ultimately meets the recognition criteria.

question_html: If expenses of liquidation of the vendor company are paid by the purchasing company then, in purchasing company's book, the account debited is
option_b: Liquidation expense account.
option_c: Vendor company account.
option_d: General reserve.
explanation_html:
Under AS 14 (Accounting for Amalgamations), when the purchasing company pays the liquidation expenses of the vendor company, such expenses are treated as part of the purchase consideration.

Since the liquidation expenses are paid on behalf of the vendor company, they represent an additional cost of acquisition over and above the agreed consideration. This increases the effective purchase price, which in turn increases the Goodwill (or reduces the Capital Reserve) arising on amalgamation.

Therefore, the debit goes to the Goodwill Account in the books of the purchasing company.

Option (b) is incorrect ‚Äî there is no separate "liquidation expense account" in the purchasing company's books. Option (c) is incorrect ‚Äî the vendor company account represents the agreed purchase consideration, not liquidation expenses. Option (d) is incorrect ‚Äî these expenses cannot be charged directly to General Reserve.

question_html: Under AS 14, in an amalgamation in the nature of merger, how are reserves of the transferor company treated by the transferee company?
option_a: All reserves lose their identity and are clubbed into a single General Reserve of the transferee
option_b: Only Revenue Reserves are taken over; Capital Reserves are not carried forward
option_c: The identity of all reserves is preserved ‚Äî General Reserve becomes General Reserve, Capital Reserve becomes Capital Reserve, etc.
option_d: All reserves are credited to Securities Premium Account of the transferee company
explanation_html:
In an amalgamation in the nature of merger (Pooling of Interests Method), AS 14 requires that the identity of the reserves is preserved. The General Reserve of the transferor becomes the General Reserve of the transferee; the Capital Reserve of the transferor becomes the Capital Reserve of the transferee; the Revaluation Reserve of the transferor becomes the Revaluation Reserve of the transferee, and so on.

As a result of preserving identity, reserves available for distribution as dividend before the amalgamation would also be available for distribution as dividend after the amalgamation. The Profit and Loss Account balance is either aggregated or transferred to General Reserve. This is in contrast to purchase amalgamation where the identity of reserves (other than statutory reserves) is NOT preserved.

question_html: Under AS 15, what is the fundamental difference between a Defined Contribution Plan and a Defined Benefit Plan?
option_a: Defined Contribution Plans are mandatory, while Defined Benefit Plans are voluntary
option_b: In Defined Contribution Plans, the employer pays fixed contributions with no further obligation; actuarial and investment risk fall on the employee. In Defined Benefit Plans, the employer bears the actuarial and investment risk
option_c: Defined Contribution Plans require actuarial valuation, while Defined Benefit Plans do not
option_d: Defined Benefit Plans are funded by a separate trust, while Defined Contribution Plans are not
explanation_html:
AS 15 distinguishes the two plans as follows:

Defined Contribution Plans (DCP): The employer pays fixed contributions into a separate fund and has no further obligation. Actuarial risk (benefits less than expected) and investment risk (assets insufficient to meet benefits) fall on the employee. Example: Provident Fund. In DCP, the contribution is directly charged to the income statement ‚Äî no complex actuarial calculation is required.

Defined Benefit Plans: Post-employment plans other than DCPs. The actuarial and investment risk fall on the employer. The employer is obligated to provide the promised benefit regardless of fund performance. Example: Gratuity. Detailed actuarial calculation is required to determine the charge.

question_html: The amount of depreciation to be charged for the year end March 31, 2024
option_d: Nil
explanation_html:
As per AS 10, depreciation begins when the asset is available for use ‚Äî in its intended location and condition.

The plant was NOT yet complete as at 31 March 2024 ‚Äî construction resumed only in February 2024, and the environmental device was installed in March 2024. The plant is still under construction/development as on 31 March 2024.

Therefore, no depreciation is charged for the year ended 31 March 2024. Depreciation commences only when the plant is ready for use (after 31 March 2024).

question_html: Under AS 7, which of the following costs is excluded from contract costs?
option_a: Site labour costs and costs of materials used in construction
option_b: Costs of moving plant and equipment to and from the contract site
option_c: General administration costs for which reimbursement is not specified in the contract
option_d: Insurance costs attributable to the contract
explanation_html:
AS 7 identifies three categories of contract costs: (i) costs directly related to the specific contract; (ii) costs attributable to contract activity in general and allocable to the contract; and (iii) other costs specifically chargeable to the customer under contract terms.

Costs excluded from contract costs include:
‚Ä¢ General administration costs for which reimbursement is not specified in the contract
‚Ä¢ Selling costs
‚Ä¢ Research and development costs (not reimbursable)
‚Ä¢ Depreciation of idle plant not used on the contract

Options (a), (b) and (d) are included: site labour, materials, and equipment movement are direct costs; insurance is an allocable indirect cost.

question_html: The revenue expenditure of ‚Çπ 50 lacs should be recognised as:
option_b: Part of Grant
option_c: Revenue expenditure in the Profit and Loss
option_d: Deducted from loan
explanation_html:
Under AS 10, only costs directly attributable to bringing an asset to its working condition are capitalised. Revenue expenditure (general operating costs, maintenance, etc.) cannot be capitalised as part of PPE.

The ‚Çπ 50 lacs spent on revenue expenditure is by definition a period cost. It is neither part of the cost of the machine, nor related to the grant (which is a capital receipt), nor deductible from the loan. It must be charged to Profit and Loss Account as an expense in the year incurred.

question_html: Sunshine Foundation, a charitable trust, collects donations and distributes them entirely to flood-affected people. It does not engage in any commercial, industrial, or business activity whatsoever. Which of the following correctly states the applicability of Accounting Standards to Sunshine Foundation?
option_a: Accounting Standards apply since the trust handles significant funds and must maintain financial records
option_b: Accounting Standards apply since charitable trusts are governed by the Companies Act, 2013
option_c: Accounting Standards do not apply since the entity is solely carrying on activities which are not commercial, industrial or business in nature
option_d: Accounting Standards apply only to the extent of AS 1 (Disclosure of Accounting Policies) and AS 4 (Contingencies)
explanation_html: Accounting Standards apply to any enterprise engaged in commercial, industrial, or business activities, whether or not profit-oriented and even if established for charitable or religious purposes. However, AS do not apply to enterprises solely carrying on activities which are not of commercial, industrial or business nature. The ICAI material gives the specific example of "an activity of collecting donations and giving them to flood affected people" as an activity that is not commercial/industrial/business in nature. Since Sunshine Foundation solely carries on such activity with no commercial component, Accounting Standards are not applicable to it. If even a small part of its activity were commercial, AS would apply to the entire entity.

question_html: The cost of inventories of items that are not ordinarily interchangeable and goods or services produced and segregated for specific projects should be assigned using the following cost formula
option_a: By specific identification of their individual costs
option_b: First-in, First-out (FIFO) Method
option_c: Weighted average cost formula
option_d: The formula used should reflect the fairest possible approximation to the cost incurred in bringing the items of inventory to their present location and condition.
explanation_html:
As per AS 2 (Valuation of Inventories), the cost of inventories of items that are not ordinarily interchangeable and goods or services produced and segregated for specific projects should be assigned using specific identification of their individual costs.

This method tracks the actual cost of each specific item. It is appropriate when items are distinguishable and individually identifiable (e.g., custom-built machinery, fine jewellery, specific project inventories).

FIFO and Weighted Average are used for ordinary interchangeable inventory items. Option (d) is a general principle, not a specific cost formula.

question_html: Under Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013, Cash and Bank Balances should be presented as:
option_b: Separated into: Cash and cash equivalents (cash at bank with scheduled banks, cash at bank with others, cash in hand) AND Other bank balances
option_c: Only bank balances ‚Äî cash in hand is shown under advances
option_d: Net of bank overdraft and cash in hand
explanation_html:
Schedule III requires Cash and Bank Balances to be presented as two sub-groups:

(i) Cash and Cash Equivalents:
‚Ä¢ Balances with banks ‚Äî with Scheduled Banks (separately)
‚Ä¢ Balances with banks ‚Äî with Others/Non-Scheduled Banks (separately disclosed by bank name)
‚Ä¢ Cash in hand

(ii) Other Bank Balances:
‚Ä¢ Bank deposits for specific periods (e.g., 9-month FD, margin money deposits)
‚Ä¢ Unpaid dividend accounts
‚Ä¢ Other earmarked balances

This distinction is important: balances with non-scheduled banks must be specifically disclosed (as in Pioneer Ltd.'s case where ₹2,000 with Perfect Bank Ltd., a non-scheduled bank, is disclosed separately from the ₹2,45,000 with scheduled banks).

question_html: Mayuri Ltd. acquired Plant and Machinery for ₹ 25 lakhs and sold Furniture and Fixtures for ₹ 4 lakhs during the same year. A junior accountant proposes to show net cash outflow of ₹ 21 lakhs under investing activities. Is this treatment correct under AS 3?
option_a: Correct, because netting is generally permitted for investing activities of an enterprise
option_b: Correct, because both items relate to fixed assets and can be shown on a net basis
option_c: Incorrect; the purchase (₹ 25 lakhs outflow) and sale (₹ 4 lakhs inflow) must be shown separately as gross amounts under investing activities
option_d: Incorrect; both must be shown under operating activities since they relate to assets used in operations
explanation_html: As per AS 3, an enterprise should report separately major classes of gross cash receipts and gross cash payments arising from investing and financing activities. Netting is not permitted except in specific permitted circumstances (e.g., cash flows on behalf of customers, or items with quick turnover, large amounts, and short maturities). Purchase of Plant and Machinery and disposal of Furniture and Fixtures do not fall under these exceptions. Therefore, the correct treatment is: Cash outflow of ₹ 25 lakhs (purchase of Plant and Machinery) and Cash inflow of ₹ 4 lakhs (sale of Furniture and Fixtures) ‚Äî both shown gross under Investing Activities.

question_html: How should subsidy received be accounted in the books of the company?
option_b: Credit it as "Other income" in the statement of profit & Loss A/c in the year of commencement of commercial operation.
option_c: Both A & B are permitted
option_d: Credit it to General Reserve.
explanation_html:
Under AS 12 (Accounting for Government Grants), grants of the nature of promoters' contribution should be credited directly to Capital Reserve and are treated as part of shareholders' funds.

Such grants are not available for distribution as dividends. They are distinguished from grants related to assets (deducted from asset cost or deferred income) and grants related to income (recognised in P&L).

Here, the grant of ‚Çπ500 lakhs is explicitly described as being in the nature of the promoter's contribution ‚Äî therefore it must be credited to Capital Reserve.

Crediting it to P&L (option b) or General Reserve (option d) is incorrect for a promoter's contribution grant. Option (c) is incorrect because only option (a) is the correct treatment under AS 12.

question_html: At what amount the SAP ERP should be initially recognised as 'intangible asset:
explanation_html:
Initial cost of SAP ERP = ‚Çπ25,00,000 (contract price).

Less: Refund received due to delay = ‚Çπ20,00,000? No ‚Äî the refund is ‚Çπ2,000,000 = ‚Çπ20,00,000.

Net cost recognised = ‚Çπ2,50,00,000 ‚Äì ‚Çπ20,00,000 = ‚Çπ2,30,00,000 i.e. ‚Çπ23,00,000 (in thousands).

Actually in the source: cost = ‚Çπ25,000,000 = ‚Çπ250 lakhs. Refund = ‚Çπ2,000,000 = ‚Çπ20 lakhs. Net = ‚Çπ230 lakhs = ‚Çπ2,30,00,000. The options use the format ‚Çπ23,00,000 meaning ‚Çπ23 lakhs (i.e. the figures are in '000s or the question treats the amounts differently). Per ICAI answer: ‚Çπ23,00,000.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: If financial statements are prepared on the assumption that an enterprise will continue operations in the foreseeable future without any intention to materially curtail its scale of operations, which fundamental accounting assumption is being followed?
option_b: Consistency
option_c: Going Concern
option_d: Materiality
explanation_html: The Going Concern assumption states that financial statements are normally prepared on the assumption that an enterprise will continue in operation in the foreseeable future and neither there is an intention, nor there is a need to materially curtail the scale of operations. Financial statements prepared on going concern basis recognise the need for sufficient retention of profit to replace assets consumed in operation.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html:
As per AS 11, how should the following items be reported at the Balance Sheet date?

(i) Foreign currency monetary items (e.g., debtors, creditors, foreign currency loans)
(ii) Non-monetary items carried at historical cost (e.g., PPE, inventory, equity investments) denominated in foreign currency
option_b: (i) Transaction date rate; (ii) Transaction date rate
option_c: (i) Closing rate; (ii) Exchange rate at the date of transaction (historical rate)
option_d: (i) Average rate; (ii) Closing rate
explanation_html:
AS 11 prescribes different rates for different types of items at the balance sheet date:

Monetary items (money held, receivables, payables ‚Äî amounts fixed in money terms): Closing rate. Exchange differences are recognised in P&L.

Non-monetary items at historical cost (PPE, inventory, equity investments): Exchange rate at the date of the transaction (historical rate). These items are not re-translated at the balance sheet date ‚Äî they retain the historical rate used when initially recognised.

Non-monetary items at fair value: Exchange rate when the fair value was determined (usually closing rate).

This distinction is fundamental to AS 11 and a classic examination question.

question_html: At what amount, the machinery should be recognised in the financial statements:
explanation_html:
As per AS 10 (PPE), the cost of an asset acquired on deferred payment terms is the cash price equivalent.

The total deferred payment = ‚Çπ6,30,000 (6 √ó ‚Çπ1,05,000) but includes ‚Çπ30,000 interest. The principal component = ‚Çπ6,00,000.

Total machinery cost = ‚Çπ4,00,000 (upfront) + ‚Çπ6,00,000 (principal of deferred payment) = ‚Çπ10,00,000.

The interest of ‚Çπ30,000 is NOT capitalised ‚Äî it is a financing cost recognised as expense over the payment period.

question_html: Vaibhav Ltd. has 5% Debentures of ₹100 each (total ₹80,00,000). Under the reconstruction scheme, debenture holders surrender existing debentures of ₹100 each and receive 6% Debentures of ₹70 each for every debenture held. What is credited to Capital Reduction Account?
option_b: ₹56,00,000 (value of new debentures issued)
option_c: ₹24,00,000 (difference between old and new debenture value)
option_d: Nil ‚Äî debenture reduction does not create capital reduction credit
explanation_html:
When debenture holders agree to accept new debentures of lower value in settlement of existing debentures, the difference represents a sacrifice by debenture holders:

Old 5% Debentures = ₹80,00,000 (₹100 × 80,000)
New 6% Debentures = ₹56,00,000 (₹70 × 80,000)
Difference = ₹24,00,000 credited to Capital Reduction Account

Journal entry per Illustration 5:
5% Debentures (₹100) A/c Dr. ₹80,00,000
   To 6% Debentures (₹70) A/c Cr. ₹56,00,000
   To Capital Reduction A/c Cr. ₹24,00,000

The ₹24,00,000 represents the sacrifice by debenture holders ‚Äî they gave up ₹24,00,000 of their claim to help the company reconstruct.

question_html: What is the profit on sale of Bonus Shares:
explanation_html:
Under AS 13, profit on sale = Sale proceeds ‚àí Cost of shares sold.

X Ltd. sold 1,000 shares in September 2024 at ‚Çπ110 each.

Sale proceeds = 1,000 √ó ‚Çπ110 = ‚Çπ1,10,000.

Cost per share (after bonus) = ‚Çπ3,03,000 √∑ 4,000 = ‚Çπ75.75.

Cost of 1,000 shares sold = 1,000 √ó ‚Çπ75.75 = ‚Çπ75,750.

Profit on sale = ‚Çπ1,10,000 ‚àí ‚Çπ75,750 = ‚Çπ34,250.

Note: Even though the bonus shares themselves had a Nil notional cost, the cost of ALL shares (original + bonus) is pooled and divided equally. So the cost attributed to each share sold (whether original or bonus) = ‚Çπ75.75.

question_html: AB sells goods to CD on 1st January 20X1 for ₹ 2 lakhs. At the time of sale, there was no reason to doubt collection. CD goes into liquidation on 15th March 20X1. Under AS 9, what is the correct treatment in AB's books for the year ended 31st March 20X1?
option_a: Do not recognise revenue since the customer ultimately went into liquidation
option_b: Recognise revenue of ₹ 2 lakhs on 1st January; write off the receivable as bad debt by 31st March
option_c: Recognise revenue of ₹ 2 lakhs on 31st March, the balance sheet date
option_d: Recognise revenue only to the extent expected to be recovered from liquidation proceeds
explanation_html:
AS 9 requires revenue to be recognised when all conditions are met, provided it is not unreasonable to expect ultimate collection. On 1st January 20X1, when the sale was made, there was no reason to doubt collection ‚Äî so revenue of ₹2 lakhs is correctly recognised on 1st January 20X1.

The subsequent liquidation of CD (on 15th March 20X1) is a separate event. AB should:
1. Recognise revenue on 1st January 20X1 (when performance occurred)
2. Recognise a receivable of ₹2 lakhs
3. Write off the receivable as bad debt (recognise a loss) when CD goes into liquidation

The bad debt loss and the sale are recognised as separate transactions.

question_html: Under AS 9, a contractor wants to include an incentive payment of ₹ 2 crore (for completing construction ahead of schedule) as part of contract revenue. In the past, he has always met similar targets. Can this incentive be recognised as revenue?
option_a: Yes ‚Äî past performance provides sufficient basis for recognition
option_b: No ‚Äî incentive payments can never be included in contract revenue
option_c: Yes, but only to the extent it is probable that the specified performance standards will be met or exceeded for this specific contract, AND the incentive payment can be measured reliably
option_d: Yes ‚Äî as soon as the contract is signed
explanation_html:
Under AS 7 (applicable here as a construction contract), incentive payments are included in contract revenue only when:
(i) It is probable that the specified performance standards will be met or exceeded; and
(ii) The incentive payment can be measured reliably.

Past performance on similar contracts does provide some evidence, but each contract must be assessed individually with respect to its specific challenges, circumstances, and timing. The contractor's past track record alone is not sufficient ‚Äî he must validate assumptions for this specific contract. Only after that assessment, if the conditions are met, can the ₹2 crore incentive be included in contract revenue.

question_html: What is the carrying value of machinery on 31.3.2024 installed in the plant?
explanation_html:
Under AS 10 (Property, Plant and Equipment), the cost of PPE includes all directly attributable costs to bring the asset to working condition, including estimated dismantling costs (present value).

Capitalised cost:

Basic price‚Çπ50,00,000
Delivery & handling‚Çπ10,00,000
Site preparation‚Çπ5,00,000
PV of dismantling costs‚Çπ5,00,000
Total cost‚Çπ70,00,000

Note: Interest charge for deferred credit (‚Çπ1,00,000) and operating losses (‚Çπ4,00,000) are NOT capitalised ‚Äî financing costs post-recognition and post-commissioning losses are expensed.

Depreciation period: Asset was ready for use on 1st July 2023. Depreciation starts from date of readiness = 1st July 2023. Period to 31.3.2024 = 9 months.

Annual depreciation = ‚Çπ70,00,000 √∑ 10 = ‚Çπ7,00,000.

Depreciation for 9 months = ‚Çπ7,00,000 √ó 9/12 = ‚Çπ5,25,000.

Carrying value on 31.3.2024 = ‚Çπ70,00,000 ‚àí ‚Çπ5,25,000 = ‚Çπ64,75,000.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
question_html: As per AS 21, when preparing Consolidated Financial Statements, the financial statements used in consolidation should be drawn up to the same reporting date. If this is not practicable, what is the maximum difference permitted between the reporting dates of the parent and subsidiary?
option_b: 6 months
option_c: 12 months
option_d: No limit ‚Äî adjustments can be made for any difference
explanation_html:
AS 21 states: "When it is impracticable to draw up the financial statements of one or more subsidiaries to such date and, accordingly, those financial statements are drawn up to different reporting dates, adjustments should be made for the effects of significant transactions or other events that occur between those dates and the date of the parent's financial statements. In any case, the difference between reporting dates should not be more than six months."

The consistency principle also requires that the length of reporting periods and any difference in reporting dates should be the same from period to period. Even with the 6-month allowance, significant transactions between the subsidiary's reporting date and the parent's reporting date must be adjusted for in the consolidated financial statements.

question_html: Declaration of dividends for current year is made after providing for
option_b: Depreciation on assets for the current year and arrears of depreciation of past years (if any).
option_c: Depreciation on current year only and by forgoing arrears of depreciation of past years.
option_d: Excluding current year depreciation
explanation_html:
Under the Companies Act 2013 (Section 123), a company cannot declare dividends without providing for current year depreciation and arrears of depreciation (if any) for past years.

The law requires that before any dividend is declared, the company must ensure:

  • Depreciation for the current year has been fully provided.
  • Any arrears of depreciation from past years have also been provided.

This prevents companies from distributing profits that should have been set aside to cover the reduction in asset values. Both past and current depreciation must be fully accounted for before distributing profits to shareholders.

Option (a) is incomplete ‚Äî current year depreciation is also required. Option (c) is incorrect ‚Äî arrears cannot be foregone. Option (d) is incorrect ‚Äî current year depreciation must be provided.

question_html: Pratham Ltd. has the following capital structure: Equity Share Capital = ₹30 lakhs (₹10 each); General Reserve = ₹32.50 lakhs; Securities Premium = ₹6 lakhs; P&L = ₹4.30 lakhs; Revaluation Reserve = ₹6.20 lakhs; Loan Funds = ₹42 lakhs. Buy-back price = ₹30 per share. What is the minimum equity to be maintained under the Debt-Equity Test?
option_b: ₹42 lakhs (equal to loan funds)
explanation_html:
Under the Debt-Equity Ratio Test, post buy-back debt cannot exceed 2 × equity.
Alternatively: Minimum Equity to be maintained = Loan Funds √∑ 2.

Loan Funds = ₹42 lakhs.
Minimum equity = ₹42 √∑ 2 = ₹21 lakhs.

Note: Revaluation Reserve (₹6.20 lakhs) is NOT included in free reserves ‚Äî it represents unrealised gains. Therefore, Shareholders' Funds (for this test) = ₹30 + ₹32.50 + ₹6 + ₹4.30 = ₹72.80 lakhs (excluding Revaluation Reserve).

The maximum buy-back is then computed using simultaneous equations as shown in Illustration 5 of the ICAI chapter, giving maximum = ₹38.85 lakhs (1,29,500 shares).

chapter_id: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
question_html: Please comment regarding consolidation requirements for SEAS Ltd. and ADI Ltd. using the below mentioned options as to which one should be correct.
option_a: ADI Ltd. would use using equity method of accounting for 23% in ASOC Ltd. SEAS Ltd. would consolidate ADI Ltd. and consequently automatically equity account 23% and separately account for the balance 9% as per AS 13.
option_b: ADI Ltd. would account for 23% in ASOC Ltd. as per AS 13. SEAS Ltd. would consolidate ADI Ltd. and consequently automatically account 23% and separately account for the balance 9%.
option_c: ADI Ltd. would account for 23% share in ASOC Ltd using equity method of accounting. SEAS Ltd. would consolidate ADI Ltd. and consequently, automatically account for ASOC Ltd 23% share and separately account for 9% share in ASOC Ltd. using equity method of accounting in consolidated financial statements.
option_d: ADI Ltd. would account for 23% in ASOC Ltd. as per AS 13. SEAS Ltd. would consolidate ADI Ltd. and using equity method of accounting 23% in ASOC Ltd. and separately account for the balance 9% as per AS 13.
explanation_html:
As per AS 23 (Accounting for Investments in Associates in Consolidated Financial Statements):

  • ADI Ltd. holds 23% in ASOC Ltd. ‚Äî significant influence (>=20%) ‚Äî must use equity method in its own consolidated FS.
  • SEAS Ltd. consolidates ADI Ltd. (subsidiary). ADI's equity-accounted 23% stake in ASOC gets included automatically in SEAS's consolidated FS.
  • SEAS's direct 9% in ASOC Ltd.: Group holding = 32%, so ASOC is an associate of the group. SEAS applies equity method for its direct 9% separately in the consolidated FS.

Option (c) correctly states: ADI uses equity method; SEAS consolidates ADI (23% auto-included) and separately equity-accounts 9%.

question_html: Z Ltd. purchased a fixed asset for ₹ 50 lakhs (useful life 5 years, salvage value ₹ 5 lakhs). A government grant of ₹ 10 lakhs was received. Under Method I (grant deducted from asset cost), what is the annual SLM depreciation charged in each year?
option_b: ₹ 7 lakhs (SLM on ₹ 40 lakhs less ₹ 5 lakhs)
option_c: ₹ 8 lakhs (SLM on ₹ 50 lakhs less ₹ 10 lakhs)
option_d: ₹ 2 lakhs (only on grant amount)
explanation_html:
Under Method I (grant deducted from asset cost):
Net cost of asset = ₹50 lakhs – ₹10 lakhs (grant) = ₹40 lakhs.
Salvage value = ₹5 lakhs.
Depreciable amount = ₹40 – ₹5 = ₹35 lakhs.
Annual depreciation (SLM over 5 years) = ₹35 √∑ 5 = ₹7 lakhs per year.

Under this method, the grant effectively reduces the depreciable base, resulting in a lower annual depreciation charge. The grant benefit is thus spread over the asset's useful life through reduced depreciation ‚Äî this is the economic logic of Method I.

question_html: A company facing a damage suit wants to create a provision for the expected damages to be cautious. As per AS 1's principle of prudence, when should such a provision be recognised?
option_a: As soon as the lawsuit is filed, since prudence requires recognising all possible losses
option_b: Only when the case is finally decided against the company in the court
option_c: Only when the probability of losing the suit is more than the probability of not losing it
option_d: Prudence never permits creation of any provision for contingent liabilities
explanation_html: AS 1 clarifies that the exercise of prudence does not permit creation of hidden reserves by understating profits/assets or overstating liabilities/losses. For a damage suit, no provision should be recognised unless the probability of losing the suit is more than the probability of not losing it. This means the recognition threshold is "more likely than not" to lose. Creating a provision merely because a lawsuit has been filed would create hidden reserves and overstate liabilities ‚Äî which is equally prohibited by AS 1. Prudence requires providing for known liabilities ‚Äî not merely possible or speculative ones.

question_html: An enterprise has 100 employees, each entitled to 5 days of paid leave per year (accumulating, non-vesting). Average unused entitlement at year-end = 2 days per employee. Based on past experience, 92 employees will take no more than 5 days in the next year, while 8 employees will take an average of 6.5 days each. How many additional days of pay should be recognised as a liability?
option_b: 16 days (2 days √ó 8 employees)
option_c: 12 days (1.5 days √ó 8 employees)
option_d: 52 days (6.5 days √ó 8 employees)
explanation_html:
For accumulating compensated absences, AS 15 requires recognising the additional amount the enterprise expects to pay as a result of unused entitlement accumulated at the balance sheet date. Since leave is taken on a LIFO basis (current year entitlement first, then carried forward), only employees who will take more than 5 days next year will actually use the carried-forward entitlement.

8 employees are expected to take 6.5 days ‚Äî they will use 5 days from the current year entitlement and 1.5 days from the carry-forward. 92 employees will take ‚â§ 5 days ‚Äî they will NOT use any carry-forward.

Additional liability = 8 √ó 1.5 = 12 days of pay. Option (a) ignores the behavioural pattern; option (b) ignores that each of the 8 employees will only use 1.5 of the 2 carried forward days.

question_html: In an amalgamation in the nature of purchase, certain Statutory Reserves (e.g., Investment Allowance Reserve) of the transferor company that must be maintained under law are taken over. Under AS 14, what is the accounting treatment in the transferee's books?
option_a: The statutory reserve is credited and simultaneously the same amount is debited to General Reserve of the transferee
option_b: The statutory reserve loses its identity and is merged with General Reserve of the transferee
option_c: The statutory reserve is credited and a corresponding debit is made to 'Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve' ‚Äî a separate negative line item in Reserves and Surplus
option_d: The statutory reserve is shown as a deferred liability until its maintenance period expires
explanation_html:
AS 14 makes an exception for statutory reserves in purchase amalgamations: such reserves retain their identity in the transferee's books as long as required by law. The accounting treatment is:

Credit: Statutory Reserve (e.g., Investment Allowance Reserve) ‚Äî shown with its original identity
Debit: Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve ‚Äî this is a separate account showing a negative balance, presented as a separate line item in Reserves and Surplus

The debit CANNOT be set off against the Statutory Reserve ‚Äî both are shown separately. When the statutory maintenance period expires, both the Statutory Reserve and the Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve are reversed simultaneously.

question_html: The composition of the Accounting Standards Board (ASB) of ICAI includes representatives from which of the following bodies?
option_a: ASSOCHAM, CII, FICCI, regulators, academicians, government departments
option_b: RBI, SEBI and IRDAI only
option_c: Only ICAI Council members
option_d: Only Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Corporate Affairs officials
explanation_html:
As per the study material, the composition of the Accounting Standards Board (ASB) includes representatives of:
- Industries
- Associations of industries (namely ASSOCHAM, CII, FICCI)
- Regulators
- Academicians
- Government departments
Although ASB is constituted by the Council of ICAI, it is independent in the formulation of accounting standards. The composition is deliberately broad and consultative to ensure transparency and acceptability.

question_html: As per Section 145(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, the Central Government notified ten Income Computation and Disclosure Standards (ICDSs). These ICDSs are applicable from which Assessment Year, and to whom?
option_a: From A.Y. 2016-17, applicable to all assessees following cash system of accounting
option_b: From A.Y. 2017-18, applicable to all assessees (other than an individual or HUF not required to get accounts audited under Section 44AB) following mercantile system of accounting
option_c: From A.Y. 2017-18, applicable to all companies and LLPs only, following mercantile system of accounting
option_d: From A.Y. 2018-19, applicable to all assessees irrespective of the system of accounting followed
explanation_html: The Central Government, in exercise of powers under Section 145(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, notified ten ICDSs to be followed by all assessees other than an individual or a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) who is not required to get his accounts audited under Section 44AB, following the mercantile system of accounting. These ICDSs are applicable for purposes of computation of income chargeable under the heads "Profits and Gains of Business or Profession" or "Income from Other Sources" from Assessment Year 2017-18. ICDSs do not apply to assessees following the cash system of accounting.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: As per the Framework, Gains and Losses are NOT recognised as separate elements of financial statements. Why?
option_a: Because gains and losses are too uncertain to be measured reliably
option_b: Because the economic characteristics of gains are same as income and those of losses are same as expenses
option_c: Because gains and losses always arise in the ordinary course of business
option_d: Because gains and losses are recognised only on realisation and hence cannot be elements
explanation_html: Gains and losses differ from income and expenses only in the sense that they may or may not arise in the ordinary course of business. Except for the way they arise, economic characteristics of gains are the same as income (increase in economic benefits) and those of losses are the same as expenses (decrease in economic benefits). For this reason, gains and losses are not recognised as separate elements of financial statements. However, they are shown separately in the Statement of Profit and Loss because knowledge of their nature is useful in assessing performance.

question_html:
As per AS 20 an enterprise should present/disclose the following:

(a) the amounts used as the numerators in calculating basic and diluted earnings per share, and a reconciliation of those amounts to the net profit or loss for the period.

(b) the weighted average number of equity shares used as the denominator in calculating basic and diluted earnings per share, and a reconciliation of these denominators to each other.

(c) basic and diluted earnings per share, even if the amounts disclosed are negative (a loss per share).

(d) the nominal value of shares along with the earnings per share figures.
option_b: Statements (a), (b) and (c) are correct
option_c: Statements (b), (c) and (d) are correct
option_d: Statements (a), (b) and (c) are correct
explanation_html:
Under AS 20 (Earnings Per Share), an enterprise should disclose all of the following:

  • (a) Numerator reconciliation: The amounts used as numerators (earnings attributable to equity shareholders) in calculating basic and diluted EPS, with reconciliation to net profit/loss. ‚úì
  • (b) Denominator reconciliation: The weighted average number of equity shares used as denominators for both basic and diluted EPS, with reconciliation between the two. ‚úì
  • (c) EPS even if negative: Basic and diluted EPS must be presented even if the amounts are negative (i.e., a loss per share). ‚úì
  • (d) Nominal value: An enterprise should also disclose the nominal (face) value per share along with EPS figures. ‚úì

All four statements (a), (b), (c), and (d) are correct disclosures required by AS 20. Therefore, the answer is All the statements are correct.

question_html: An oil company has been contaminating land for several years. There is currently no law requiring clean-up. At 31st March, 20X1, it is virtually certain that a new law requiring clean-up of already contaminated land will be enacted shortly after year-end. Should the oil company provide for clean-up costs under AS 29?
option_a: No provision ‚Äî the company has no present legal obligation as at 31st March, 20X1 since the law has not yet been enacted
option_b: No provision ‚Äî the obligation should be recognised only in the year in which the law is actually enacted
option_c: Yes ‚Äî since legislation is virtually certain to be enacted, the causing of the contamination constitutes an obligating event and a provision must be recognised
option_d: Disclose only as a contingent liability since the law is not yet enacted
explanation_html:
AS 29 specifically addresses this situation. When environmental damage is caused, there may be no obligation to remedy it immediately. However, the causing of the damage will become an obligating event when a new law requires the existing damage to be rectified. Where details of a proposed new law have yet to be finalised, an obligation arises only when the legislation is virtually certain to be enacted.

In this case, at 31st March, 20X1, it is virtually certain that the law will be enacted ‚Äî even though not yet formally enacted. Therefore, the contamination is an obligating event, and the company must recognise a provision for clean-up costs. This is confirmed in the ICAI textbook answer to the illustrative problem.

question_html: As per AS 17, which of the following correctly describes the 10% Profit/Loss Test for identifying a reportable segment?
option_a: A segment is reportable if its profit or loss is 10% or more of the net profit or net loss of all segments combined after netting profits and losses
option_b: A segment is reportable if its profit or loss is 10% or more of the combined profit of all profitable segments only
option_c: A segment is reportable if its profit or loss (absolute amount) is 10% or more of the higher (in absolute terms) of: combined profit of all profitable segments OR combined loss of all loss-making segments
option_d: A segment is reportable if its profit or loss is 10% or more of the total enterprise net profit
explanation_html:
The 10% Profit/Loss Test under AS 17 works as follows:
Step 1: Add the profits of all profitable segments.
Step 2: Add the losses (absolute values) of all loss-making segments.
Step 3: Take the higher of the two figures (in absolute amount).
Step 4: A segment is reportable if its profit or loss (absolute) ‚â• 10% of this higher figure.

This test prevents a single large-profit or large-loss segment from distorting the threshold. Option (a) is incorrect because profits and losses are not netted. Option (b) uses only profitable segments. Option (d) uses net enterprise profit which is incorrect.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: As per AS 22, what is the correct definition of Tax Expense?
option_a: Only the current tax payable for the period
option_b: Only the deferred tax charged or credited to the Statement of Profit and Loss
option_c: The aggregate of current tax AND deferred tax charged or credited to the Statement of Profit and Loss for the period
option_d: Advance tax paid plus TDS deducted during the period
explanation_html:
As per AS 22, the key definitions are:

Current Tax: The amount of income tax determined to be payable (recoverable) in respect of taxable income (tax loss) for a period.

Deferred Tax: The tax effect of timing differences.

Tax Expense (Tax Saving): The aggregate of current tax AND deferred tax charged or credited to the Statement of Profit and Loss for the period. Mathematically: Tax Expense = Current Tax ¬± Deferred Tax.

This is important: both current and deferred components form the total tax expense that is reported in P&L, providing a complete picture of the tax effect of all transactions and events during the period.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: In case of conflict between an Accounting Standard and the Framework, which one will prevail?
option_a: The Framework will prevail over the Accounting Standard
option_b: The Accounting Standard will prevail over the Framework
option_c: The one which is more recent will prevail
option_d: The one which is more beneficial to users will prevail
explanation_html: As per the Framework itself, nothing in the Framework overrides any specific Accounting Standard. In case of conflict between an Accounting Standard and the Framework, the requirements of the Accounting Standard will prevail over those of the Framework. The Framework sets out broad underlying concepts while specific ASs deal with particular transactions.

question_html: Gyan Ltd. borrowed ‚Çπ 10 crore for construction of a plant at the rate of 10% per annum (interest paid annually ‚Çπ 1 crore). The construction was being carried on and out of the borrowings, ‚Çπ 4 crore was temporarily placed in a fixed deposit at the rate of 6% per annum (interest earned ‚Çπ 24 lakh). At the year end, how much cost of borrowing Gyan Limited will capitalise?
option_b: Interest paid on ‚Çπ 6 crore as only this amount was utilized i.e. ‚Çπ 60 Lakh.
option_c: Interest paid less income on temporary investment i.e. ‚Çπ 76 lakh
option_d: Nothing will be capitalised.
explanation_html:
As per AS 16 (Borrowing Costs), when borrowed funds are temporarily invested pending their use on a qualifying asset, investment income earned must be deducted from borrowing costs before capitalisation.

Gross borrowing cost = ‚Çπ1,00,00,000 (10% on ‚Çπ10 crore).

Less: Investment income on temporary FD = ‚Çπ24,00,000 (6% on ‚Çπ4 crore).

Net borrowing cost capitalised = ‚Çπ1,00,00,000 ‚Äì ‚Çπ24,00,000 = ‚Çπ76,00,000 i.e. ‚Çπ76 lakh.
