The full ‚Çπ10 crore borrowing cost is eligible (not just ‚Çπ6 crore actually utilised) since the ‚Çπ4 crore is also part of the qualifying asset financing ‚Äî the investment income is simply deducted.

question_html: In an amalgamation under the Purchase Method, as per AS 14, goodwill arising on amalgamation should be amortised over:
option_b: Not exceeding 5 years, unless a somewhat longer period can be justified
option_c: 10 years minimum to ensure adequate amortisation
option_d: The useful life of the acquired business
explanation_html:
AS 14 Para 19 states: "Goodwill arising on amalgamation represents a payment made in anticipation of future income and it is appropriate to treat it as an asset to be amortised to income on a systematic basis over its useful life. Accordingly, it is considered appropriate to amortise goodwill over a period NOT EXCEEDING FIVE YEARS unless a somewhat longer period can be justified."

The default is 5 years or less. A longer period is possible but must be justified. Factors considered include: foreseeable life of business/industry, effects of obsolescence, service life of key personnel, competitor actions, legal/regulatory provisions.

Goodwill arising on amalgamation (under AS 14) is treated differently from goodwill internally generated, which is not recognised under AS.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: Which of the following correctly describes the concept of Equity as per the Framework?
option_a: Equity is the total of all assets of an enterprise
option_b: Equity is the total paid-up share capital of a company
option_c: Equity is the residual interest in the assets of an enterprise after deducting all its liabilities
option_d: Equity is the present obligation of the enterprise arising from past events
explanation_html: As per the Framework, Equity is defined as the residual interest in the assets of an enterprise after deducting all its liabilities. This can be expressed as: A ‚Äì L = E (Assets minus Liabilities equals Equity). Equity represents owners' claims consisting of items like capital and reserves. The value of equity may change through contributions from/distributions to equity participants or due to income earned/expenses incurred.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: Which of the following is NOT a principal area covered by the Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements?
option_b: Qualitative characteristics of financial statements
option_c: Tax computation procedures for enterprises
option_d: Concepts of Capital and Capital Maintenance
explanation_html: The principal areas covered by the Framework include: Components, Objectives, Assumptions, Qualitative characteristics, Elements, Criteria for recognition, Principles of measurement, and Concepts of Capital and Capital Maintenance. Tax computation procedures are not part of the Framework. In fact, special purpose reports like tax computations are outside the scope of the Framework, though it may be applied to the extent not inconsistent with their requirements.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: A Ltd. borrowed US$ 4,50,000 on 1st January 20X1 to acquire fixed assets. Exchange rates: 1/1/20X1 = ₹48; 31/3/20X1 = ₹49. The company has NOT exercised the option under Para 46A of AS 11. What is the exchange difference recognised in the year ended 31st March 20X1?
option_c: Loss capitalised into the cost of fixed assets
option_d: No exchange difference recognised until settlement
explanation_html:
Since the option under Para 46A is NOT availed, exchange differences must be recognised immediately in P&L.

Loan at 1/1/20X1: US$4,50,000 × ₹48 = ₹2,16,00,000.
Restated at 31/3/20X1: US$4,50,000 × ₹49 = ₹2,20,50,000.
Exchange loss = ₹4,50,000 (creditor increased) ‚Üí Debited to P&L.

Note: If Para 46A option were availed (loan relating to acquisition of a depreciable asset), this ₹4,50,000 exchange loss could be capitalised into the cost of the fixed asset and depreciated over its remaining useful life ‚Äî which would be option (c). But since the option is NOT availed, it goes to P&L.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: What is the amount of closing Cash and Cash equivalents as on 1 April, 2023?
explanation_html:
Under AS 3, closing cash = opening cash + net cash from all activities + cash from reconstruction/financing.

Opening cash (31 Mar 2023): ‚Çπ 65,500

Add: Cash from operating activities: ‚Çπ 5,000

Add: Cash from investing activities: ‚Çπ 22,000

Add: Cash from financing (reconstruction and new issue):

  • New equity shares issued for cash: ‚Çπ 1,00,000
  • Cash used for reconstruction ‚Äî only non-cash items (debentures settled by shares, P&L written off) ‚Äî no cash impact

Closing cash = ‚Çπ 65,500 + ‚Çπ 5,000 + ‚Çπ 22,000 + ‚Çπ 1,00,000 = ‚Çπ 1,92,500.

chapter_id: Accounting for Branches including foreign branches
question_html: Harrison of Chennai sends goods to New Delhi Branch at 20% above cost (invoice price). Opening stock = ₹25,000 (at cost) = ₹30,000 (at invoice). Cost of goods sent = ₹2,00,000; Invoice price of goods received by branch = ₹2,20,000. Closing stock at branch = ₹28,000 (invoice). Goods in transit = ₹2,40,000 – ₹2,20,000 = ₹20,000. What is the Stock Reserve on opening stock?
explanation_html:
Stock Reserve on opening stock represents the unrealised profit element included in opening stock valued at invoice price.

Opening stock at invoice price = ₹30,000
Loading = 20% above cost = 20/120 of invoice price
Stock Reserve = ₹30,000 × 20/120 = ₹5,000

Alternatively, since cost = ₹25,000 and invoice = ₹30,000, the profit loading = ₹5,000 (which is exactly 20% of cost = 20/120 of invoice).

This reserve is credited to the Branch Adjustment Account (opening Stock Reserve = credit to Branch Adjustment A/c) per Illustration 3(a) where ₹5,000 = 25,000 × 20% = ₹5,000. The reserve reduces the closing stock to cost before incorporation in the balance sheet.

question_html: The ICAI Council at its 433rd meeting (August 13-15, 2024) revised the criteria for classification of Non-company entities for applicability of Accounting Standards. This revised announcement supersedes which earlier ICAI announcement?
option_a: The ICAI announcement issued in March 2019 on criteria for classification of non-company entities
option_b: The ICAI announcement on 'Criteria for classification of Non-company entities for applicability of Accounting Standards' issued in March 2021
option_c: The ICAI announcement issued in April 2024 on applicability of Ind AS to non-company entities
option_d: The MCA notification dated June 23, 2021 on Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules
explanation_html: As explicitly stated in the revised ICAI announcement, this Announcement supersedes the earlier Announcement of the ICAI on 'Criteria for classification of Non-company entities for applicability of Accounting Standards issued in March 2021.' The earlier announcement had classified entities into four levels; the revised scheme reduces this to two categories (MSMEs and Large Entities). The revised scheme came into effect for accounting periods commencing on or after April 1, 2024. The MCA notification dated June 23, 2021 pertains to Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules applicable to corporate entities (SMCs and Non-SMCs), which is a separate framework and was not superseded by the ICAI announcement.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: People Ltd. had an old outstanding balance of ₹ 50,000 appearing as sundry creditor for the past 5 years. It writes it off in the current year and treats it as a prior period item under AS 5. Is this correct?
option_a: Correct ‚Äî since the balance was recognised in prior periods, writing it off is a prior period item
option_b: Incorrect ‚Äî writing off an old outstanding balance that appeared consistently over 5 years without error or omission is NOT a prior period item; it is a current year income
option_c: Correct ‚Äî any adjustment to prior year balances must be classified as a prior period item
option_d: Incorrect ‚Äî it should be classified as an extraordinary item since it is non-recurring
explanation_html:
AS 5 defines Prior Period Items as income or expenses which arise in the current period as a result of errors or omissions in the preparation of financial statements of one or more prior periods. The key requirement is an error or omission.

In this case, the ₹50,000 balance was consistently carried as a sundry creditor for 5 years ‚Äî there was no error or omission. The company simply adopted a practice of writing off old outstanding balances after 5 years, which is a business decision. Therefore, the write-off in the current year is NOT a prior period item under AS 5 ‚Äî it is current year income. The treatment as a prior period item was incorrect.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: ACO Ltd.'s financial year ended 31st March 20X2. Accounts were approved on 30th June 20X2. An earthquake destroyed a major warehouse of the company on 20th May 20X2, with an estimated loss of ₹ 30 lakhs. How should this be treated under AS 4?
option_a: Adjusting event ‚Äî provide for loss of ₹ 30 lakhs in financial statements for year ended 31st March 20X2
option_b: Non-adjusting event ‚Äî the loss should not be recognised in the financial statements for 20X1-X2; disclose in the report of the approving authority
option_c: Adjusting event ‚Äî since the loss affects the going concern assumption, it must be adjusted in the accounts
option_d: The event is beyond the balance sheet date and after the approval date, so no treatment is necessary
explanation_html:
The earthquake occurred on 20th May 20X2 ‚Äî after the balance sheet date (31st March 20X2) but before approval (30th June 20X2). This is an event occurring after the balance sheet date. However, since the earthquake did not exist as a condition on 31st March 20X2, it is a non-adjusting event ‚Äî adjustment to assets and liabilities is NOT appropriate.

However, since it is an unusual event affecting the enterprise's operations, the going concern assumption must be re-evaluated. Assuming going concern remains valid, the fact of the earthquake and estimated loss of ₹30 lakhs should be disclosed in the report of the approving authority to enable users to make proper evaluations.

question_html: Which of the following changes made in Ind AS vis-√†-vis IFRS results in a 'Carve-out'?
option_a: Use of 'Balance Sheet' instead of 'Statement of Financial Position'
option_b: Use of 'Statement of Profit and Loss' instead of 'Statement of Comprehensive Income'
option_c: Removal of an option available in IFRS to ensure consistency among Indian companies
option_d: A departure from IFRS accounting principle due to difference in Indian economic conditions
explanation_html:
Three types of changes are made in Ind AS compared to IFRS:
1. Terminology differences (e.g., Balance Sheet instead of SOFP) ‚Äì do NOT result in carve-outs
2. Removal of options in accounting principles for consistency ‚Äì do NOT result in carve-outs
3. Differences due to economic environment ‚Äì these ARE Carve-outs
Thus, only a deviation from IFRS accounting principle on account of Indian economic conditions constitutes a carve-out.

chapter_id: Accounting for Branches including foreign branches
question_html: Under the Wholesale Price Branch Method, goods are supplied to retail outlets at wholesale price (cost + 25%). These outlets sell at retail price (wholesale + 20%). If the outlet made a gross profit of ₹60,000, what are the total retail sales?
explanation_html:
Working backwards from gross profit to retail sales:

Price structure:
Wholesale price = 100; Retail price = 120 (wholesale + 20%)
Gross profit at outlet = Retail price – Wholesale price = 20 (per unit of 120 retail)
Gross profit % on retail = 20/120 = 1/6

If gross profit = ₹60,000:
Retail Sales = ₹60,000 ÷ (1/6) = ₹60,000 × 6 = ₹3,60,000

Per Working Note 1 of Illustration 8 (M/s Rahul):
Gross profit ratio = 25/25 = 150/25 ‚Äî retail price 150, wholesale 125, gross profit 25.
Retail Sales = 60,000 × 150/25 = ₹3,60,000 ‚úì

question_html: In the Realization Account prepared in the books of the vendor (transferor) company, which of the following items is NOT transferred to the Realization Account?
option_a: All assets taken over by the purchasing company at book value
option_b: All liabilities taken over by the purchasing company
option_c: Debit balance of Profit and Loss Account (accumulated losses) and unamortised expenses
option_d: Purchase consideration receivable from the purchasing company
explanation_html:
When closing the books of the vendor company, a Realization Account is opened and assets/liabilities transferred to it. However, there are specific exceptions:

NOT transferred to Realization Account:
‚Ä¢ Debit balance of Profit and Loss Account (accumulated losses) ‚Äî these are not assets
‚Ä¢ Preliminary expenses, goodwill, and other unamortised expenses ‚Äî these are not real assets
‚Ä¢ Cash/bank balance if it is NOT taken over by the purchasing company

Transferred to Realization Account:
‚Ä¢ All tangible and intangible assets taken over (at book value)
‚Ä¢ All liabilities taken over
‚Ä¢ Purchase consideration receivable (credit to Realization Account)
‚Ä¢ Profit/loss on Realization is eventually transferred to Equity Shareholders Account

question_html: What is the cost of bonus shares:
option_c: Nil
explanation_html:
Under AS 13 (Accounting for Investments), bonus shares are shares received at no additional cost to the investor ‚Äî they represent a capitalisation of existing reserves by the investee company.

Since no additional consideration is paid for bonus shares, their cost is Nil. However, the original cost of investment is now spread over a larger number of shares (3,000 original + 1,000 bonus = 4,000 shares), reducing the cost per share.

The total investment cost remains ‚Çπ3,03,000 ‚Äî it is simply reallocated across more shares. The cost of the bonus shares themselves = Nil.

question_html: Under AS 7, the gross amount due from/to customers for contract work in progress is computed as:
option_b: (Costs Incurred + Recognised Profits – Recognised Losses) minus (Progress Billings Received + Progress Billings to be Received)
option_c: Total Contract Price minus Costs Incurred to Date
option_d: Progress Billings minus Costs Incurred to Date
explanation_html:
AS 7 specifies the formula for the balance sheet presentation of contract work in progress:

Gross Amount Due from/to Customers =
(Costs Incurred + Recognised Profits – Recognised Losses) – (Progress Billings Received + Progress Billings to be Received)

If the result is positive ‚Üí Gross amount due FROM customers (asset).
If the result is negative ‚Üí Gross amount due TO customers (liability).

This formula captures both the cumulative work performed (costs + net profits/losses) less all billings made (both received and receivable). It represents the contractor's net position on the contract as at the balance sheet date.

question_html: As per Section 128 of the Companies Act, 2013, every company is required to maintain its books of account on which basis?
option_b: Accrual basis and according to the double entry system of accounting
option_c: Either cash or accrual basis, at the discretion of the management
option_d: Accrual basis only for listed companies; cash basis for others
explanation_html:
Section 128 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates that every company shall prepare and keep at its registered office books of account for every financial year which give a true and fair view of the state of affairs. These books shall be kept on accrual basis and according to the double entry system of accounting.

Additionally, Section 128(5) requires that books of account covering a period of not less than 8 financial years immediately preceding the current financial year (or all preceding years if the company has existed less than 8 years) shall be kept in good order along with relevant vouchers.

question_html: Which of the following correctly maps an Ind AS to its corresponding IFRS/IAS?
option_a: Ind AS 115 corresponds to IFRS 15 ‚Äì Revenue from Contracts with Customers
option_b: Ind AS 103 corresponds to IAS 3 ‚Äì Business Combinations
option_c: Ind AS 7 corresponds to IFRS 7 ‚Äì Statement of Cash Flows
option_d: Ind AS 116 corresponds to IAS 16 ‚Äì Leases
explanation_html:
As per the list of notified Ind AS:
- Ind AS 115 corresponds to IFRS 15 ‚Äì Revenue from Contracts with Customers ‚úî
- Ind AS 103 corresponds to IFRS 3 (not IAS 3) ‚Äì Business Combinations ‚úò
- Ind AS 7 corresponds to IAS 7 (not IFRS 7) ‚Äì Statement of Cash Flows ‚úò
- Ind AS 116 corresponds to IFRS 16 (not IAS 16) ‚Äì Leases ‚úò
Thus, option (a) is the only correct mapping.

question_html: In the Cash Flow Statement as per AS 3, amount paid for acquiring gold loan unit will be disclosed as:
option_b: Cash Flow from Investing Activities
option_c: Cash Flow from Financing Activities
option_d: Non-cash Items
explanation_html:
Acquisition of a business unit is a capital expenditure representing a long-term investment of resources.

As per AS 3, acquisition of business units/subsidiaries is classified under Investing Activities ‚Äî even for financial enterprises. The operating activities of a finance company relate to the lending/borrowing business itself, not to acquisition of new business units.

question_html: Which of the following is NOT a major consideration governing the selection and application of accounting policies as per AS 1?
option_b: Comparability
option_c: Substance over form
option_d: Materiality
explanation_html: As per AS 1 ‚Äì Disclosure of Accounting Policies, the three major considerations that govern the selection and application of accounting policies are: (i) Prudence, (ii) Substance over form, and (iii) Materiality. Comparability is a qualitative characteristic of financial statements but is not listed as a major consideration in AS 1 for selection/application of accounting policies. While diversity in accounting policies adversely affects comparability, and AS 1 seeks to address this through disclosure requirements, comparability itself is not a governing consideration for selecting a policy under AS 1.

question_html: C Ltd. converts 4,000 fully paid equity shares of ₹100 each into equity stock of ₹4,00,000. Subsequently, this stock is re-converted into 40,000 equity shares of ₹10 each. What journal entries are passed for these transactions?
option_a:
Conversion: Equity Share Capital Dr. ₹4,00,000 / To Equity Stock Cr. ₹4,00,000
Re-conversion: Equity Stock Dr. ₹4,00,000 / To Equity Share Capital Cr. ₹4,00,000
option_b: No entries needed ‚Äî stock and share capital are the same
option_c: Capital Reduction Dr. ₹4,00,000 / To Equity Stock Cr. ₹4,00,000
option_d: Equity Stock Dr. ₹4,00,000 / To Capital Reserve Cr. ₹4,00,000
explanation_html:
Conversion of shares into stock and vice versa (Section 61) involves only bookkeeping entries ‚Äî the amount remains the same:

Conversion to Stock:
Equity Share Capital A/c Dr. ₹4,00,000
   To Equity Stock A/c Cr. ₹4,00,000

Re-conversion to Shares:
Equity Stock A/c Dr. ₹4,00,000
   To Equity Share Capital A/c Cr. ₹4,00,000

The total capital value remains ₹4,00,000 throughout. Only the nature of the instrument changes (shares ‚Üí stock ‚Üí 40,000 × ₹10 shares). Stock is a bundle of fully paid shares that can be transferred in any fraction; shares can only be transferred in whole numbers of face value. No Capital Reduction Account is involved ‚Äî it is pure alteration of share capital under Section 61.

question_html: As per AS 10, when should depreciation begin on an asset?
option_a: From the date the asset is first put to commercial use/production
option_b: From the date the asset is available for use (in the location and condition necessary to operate in the manner intended by management)
option_c: From the beginning of the next financial year after acquisition
option_d: From the date the payment for the asset is made
explanation_html: As per AS 10, depreciation of an asset begins when it is available for use, i.e., when it is in the location and condition necessary for it to be capable of operating in the manner intended by the management. It does NOT begin from the date of actual use or commercial production. For example, if a machine is ready for use on 1st November but the company starts using it on 1st March, depreciation commences from 1st November ‚Äî not 1st March. The fact that the machine was not used for a period after it was ready is irrelevant. This is a critical and frequently examined principle under AS 10.

question_html: Under the revised scheme for Non-company entities (effective April 1, 2024), MSMEs may not comply with paragraph 87 of which Accounting Standard, relating to encouraged disclosures?
option_b: AS 10 ‚Äì Property, Plant and Equipment
option_c: AS 16 ‚Äì Borrowing Costs
option_d: AS 26 ‚Äì Intangible Assets
explanation_html: Under the MSME relaxations specified in Annexure 1 of the revised ICAI announcement, AS 10 (Property, Plant and Equipment) ‚Äî MSMEs may not comply with paragraph 87 relating to encouraged disclosures. Similarly, for AS 11 (Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates), MSMEs may not comply with paragraph 44 relating to encouraged disclosures. These are specific paragraph-level exemptions from disclosure requirements that go beyond the mandatory ones. Students must carefully distinguish between standards that are wholly inapplicable to MSMEs (like AS 3, AS 17, AS 20, AS 24) versus those that are applicable but with specific paragraph-level relaxations (like AS 10, AS 11, AS 15, AS 19, AS 22, AS 26, AS 28, AS 29).

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: A trader commenced business with ‚Çπ12,000 represented by 6,000 units at ‚Çπ2 per unit. During the year, he sold all units at ‚Çπ3 per unit and withdrew ‚Çπ6,000. Price index at beginning = 100; at end = 120. What is the Retained Profit under Financial Capital Maintenance at Current Purchasing Power?
option_c: (‚Çπ2,400) ‚Äì Loss
explanation_html:
Step 1: Closing Equity at closing price
Sales = 6,000 √ó ‚Çπ3 = ‚Çπ18,000; Drawings = ‚Çπ6,000
Closing Equity = ‚Çπ18,000 ‚Äì ‚Çπ6,000 = ‚Çπ12,000 (represented entirely by cash)

Step 2: Opening Equity restated at closing price (using average price index)
Opening equity at historical cost = ‚Çπ12,000
Restated = (‚Çπ12,000/100) √ó 120 = ‚Çπ14,400

Step 3: Retained Profit
= Closing Equity ‚Äì Opening Equity restated
= ‚Çπ12,000 ‚Äì ‚Çπ14,400 = (‚Äì) ‚Çπ2,400 (Loss)

The negative retained profit indicates the trader failed to maintain capital ‚Äî ‚Çπ12,000 is insufficient to buy 6,000 units at new price of ‚Çπ2.40 per unit.

question_html: As per AS 29, which of the following statements about reimbursements expected from a third party (e.g., insurance) is correct?
option_a: The net amount (provision minus expected reimbursement) is shown as a single liability in the balance sheet
option_b: The provision is recognised for the full amount of the liability; a separate asset is recognised for the expected reimbursement only when it is virtually certain
option_c: Provision is reduced by the amount of expected reimbursement and only the net provision is recognised
option_d: No provision is needed if insurance covers the full expected loss
explanation_html:
AS 29 prescribes that reimbursements should be treated as follows:

The enterprise must recognise a provision for the full amount of the liability ‚Äî the fact that a reimbursement is expected does not reduce the obligation itself. A separate asset for the expected reimbursement is recognised on the balance sheet only when it is virtually certain that reimbursement will be received if the enterprise settles the liability.

The maximum amount recognised for the expected reimbursement asset must not exceed the amount of the provision. In the Statement of Profit and Loss, the expense may be presented net of the reimbursement amount. Option (a) is incorrect because both gross liability and gross asset are shown separately (they cannot be netted unless specifically permitted). Option (d) is incorrect ‚Äî a provision is still required for the full liability.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: Under Present Value convention, an asset generates ‚Çπ11,000 after 1 year. The required earning rate is 10% per year. What is the Present Value of this asset?
explanation_html:
Under Present Value convention, assets are carried at the present value of future net cash inflows they are expected to generate.

Formula: P = A √ó [1/(1+R)‚Åø]
Where A = ‚Çπ11,000, R = 10% = 0.10, n = 1 year

P = ‚Çπ11,000 √ó [1/1.10] = ‚Çπ11,000 √ó 0.909 = ‚Çπ10,000 (approx.)

This means a receipt of ‚Çπ10,000 now is equivalent to receiving ‚Çπ11,000 after 1 year at 10% earning rate ‚Äî because ‚Çπ10,000 invested today at 10% grows to ‚Çπ11,000 after 1 year.

question_html: Which of the following transactions does NOT result in a cash flow and therefore should not be reported in the Cash Flow Statement?
option_a: Cash received from sale of old machinery
option_b: Issue of bonus shares by capitalisation of reserves
option_c: Redemption of debentures by payment of cash
option_d: Repayment of bank loan
explanation_html: As per AS 3, investing and financing transactions that do not require the use of cash or cash equivalents should be excluded from the Cash Flow Statement. Issue of bonus shares involves capitalisation of reserves ‚Äî no cash changes hands. It is therefore a non-cash transaction and should be excluded from the Cash Flow Statement. However, it must be disclosed elsewhere in the financial statements in a way that provides all relevant information. Other options ‚Äî receipt from machinery sale, debenture redemption, and bank loan repayment ‚Äî all involve actual cash flows and must be reported in the CFS under investing or financing activities as applicable.

question_html: X Ltd. invested ₹ 600 lakhs in equity shares of Y Ltd. ‚Äî ₹ 300 lakhs intended as long-term, ₹ 300 lakhs as current. On 31-3-20X1, market value of the entire holding fell to ₹ 200 lakhs (₹ 100 lakhs each) due to Y Ltd. losing a copyright case. The decline is not temporary. What is the total charge to the Statement of Profit and Loss?
option_b: ₹ 400 lakhs (full decline on both categories)
option_c: ₹ 200 lakhs for current investments; ₹ 200 lakhs for long-term investments = ₹ 400 lakhs total
option_d: ₹ 200 lakhs (only long-term investment written down since the decline is not temporary)
explanation_html:
Current Investments (₹300 lakhs ‚Üí ₹100 lakhs): AS 13 requires current investments to be carried at lower of cost and fair value. Since fair value (₹100 lakhs) < cost (₹300 lakhs), write-down = ₹200 lakhs ‚Äî charged to P&L.

Long-term Investments (₹300 lakhs ‚Üí ₹100 lakhs): AS 13 states long-term investments are carried at cost, but when there is a decline other than temporary, the carrying amount is reduced to recognise the decline. Losing a copyright case causing significant, permanent value erosion constitutes other-than-temporary decline. Write-down = ₹200 lakhs ‚Äî charged to P&L.

Total charge = ₹200 + ₹200 = ₹400 lakhs.

chapter_id: Accounting for Branches including foreign branches
question_html: Hindustan Industries sends goods to Cochin Branch at cost plus 25%. Goods received at invoice price = ₹6,00,000. Under the Stock and Debtors Method, what is the loading (profit element) credited to Branch Adjustment Account on goods sent?
explanation_html:
When goods are invoiced at 25% above cost:
Invoice price = Cost × 125%
Loading as a fraction of invoice price = 25/125 = 1/5 = 20%

Loading on ₹6,00,000 (invoice price) = ₹6,00,000 × 1/5 = ₹1,20,000

Journal entry in Branch Adjustment A/c:
Goods Sent to Branch A/c Dr. ₹4,80,000 (cost = 6,00,000 × 100/125)
Branch Adjustment A/c Cr. ₹1,20,000 (loading = 6,00,000 × 25/125)

Actually, the Branch Stock A/c is debited with ₹6,00,000 (invoice price):
Branch Stock A/c Dr. ₹6,00,000 / To Goods Sent to Branch A/c ₹4,80,000 (cost) / To Branch Adjustment A/c ₹1,20,000 (loading)

Per Illustration 6 in the text: 1/5 of ₹6,00,000 = ₹1,20,000 credit to Branch Adjustment A/c.

question_html: XYZ Ltd. proposes to declare 10% dividend out of General Reserves (due to inadequate current year profits). Details: 8,00,000 equity shares × ₹10 = ₹80,00,000; 17,500 9% preference shares × ₹100 = ₹17,50,000; General Reserve = ₹25,00,000; Current year net profit = ₹3,00,000. Average dividend rate (last 3 years) = 12%. What is the amount that can be utilised from General Reserves?
As per Section 123(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, dividend can be declared:
option_a: Out of any reserves including capital reserve
option_b: Only out of current year's profits after providing depreciation
option_c: Out of profits of current financial year or previous undistributed profits, both after providing depreciation, or moneys provided by government; but NOT from reserves other than free reserves
option_d: Out of profits before providing for depreciation
explanation_html:
Section 123(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that no dividend shall be declared or paid except:
(a) Out of profits for that financial year arrived at after providing for depreciation;
(b) Out of profits for any previous financial years arrived at after providing for depreciation and remaining undistributed;
(c) Out of both (a) and (b); or
(d) Out of moneys provided by the Central/State Government for payment of dividend in pursuance of any guarantee.

Critically: No dividend shall be declared from reserves other than FREE reserves. Capital reserves, revaluation reserves, etc. cannot be used for dividend payment. Depreciation must be provided before declaring dividend.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: Which user group of financial statements is primarily interested in information to determine whether their loans and the interest attaching to them will be paid when due?
option_b: Employees
option_c: Lenders
option_d: Suppliers and Trade Creditors
explanation_html: Lenders are interested in information which enables them to determine whether their loans, and the interest attaching to them, will be paid when due. This distinguishes them from Suppliers and Trade Creditors who are interested in whether amounts owing to them will be paid when due (typically over a shorter period than lenders).

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: As per AS 4 (Revised), theft of cash of ₹ 5 lakhs by the cashier in January 20X1 was detected only in May 20X1. The accounts for the year ended 31st March 20X1 were not yet approved by the Board of Directors. How should this be treated?
option_a: Non-adjusting event ‚Äî disclose in the Directors' Report only
option_b: Adjusting event ‚Äî recognise the loss of ₹ 5 lakhs in the accounts for the year ended 31st March 20X1
option_c: Ignore ‚Äî since the amount was stolen before year-end, no adjustment or disclosure is needed
option_d: Extraordinary item ‚Äî disclose separately in the Statement of Profit and Loss
explanation_html:
As per AS 4 (Revised), adjustments to assets and liabilities are required for events occurring after the balance sheet date that provide additional information materially affecting the determination of amounts relating to conditions existing at the balance sheet date.

The theft took place in January 20X1 ‚Äî i.e., before the balance sheet date of 31st March 20X1. The detection in May 20X1 (after the balance sheet date, but before approval) provides additional evidence of a condition that existed on 31st March 20X1. Therefore, this is an adjusting event and the loss of ₹5 lakhs must be recognised in the accounts for the year ended 31st March 20X1.

question_html: Y Ltd. (transferor) has equity share capital ₹30,00,000 (3,00,000 shares × ₹10). X Ltd. (transferee) issues 3,50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at par + 15% preference shares (total PC = ₹53,70,000). Under the Merger (Pooling of Interests) method, what amount is adjusted against reserves, and what is it?
option_a: ₹3,80,000 adjusted against reserves (being net asset excess)
option_b: ₹6,70,000 adjusted as a deduction against X Ltd.'s General Reserve (PC – Y Ltd.'s share capital = ₹53,70,000 – ₹47,00,000)
option_c: ₹6,70,000 credited to Securities Premium
option_d: Nil ‚Äî no reserve adjustment in merger
explanation_html:
Under the Pooling of Interests Method:
Step I: Amount issued by X Ltd. = ₹53,70,000 (PC)
Step II: Share capital of Y Ltd. = ₹47,00,000 (₹30,00,000 equity + ₹17,00,000 preference)
Step III: Difference = ₹53,70,000 – ₹47,00,000 = ₹6,70,000

This ₹6,70,000 is a deduction from X Ltd.'s General Reserve (as the capital issued exceeds the transferor's share capital). Per Illustration 8, this adjustment is debited to General Reserve of X Ltd. (₹500 + adjustment = ₹670 reduction ‚Üí net ₹(670) in working).

In contrast, under the Purchase Method, this same situation creates a Capital Reserve of ₹3,80,000 (net assets – PC).

question_html: What is the amount to be recognized as Revenue as per AS 9 in the books of Kay Ltd. as on 31 March, 2024?
explanation_html:
Under AS 9 (Revenue Recognition), revenue from sale of goods is recognised when all significant risks and rewards of ownership are transferred.

Mr. Ravi Kumar sale (‚Çπ 22,00,000): This is a bill and hold sale ‚Äî goods are sold but delivery is postponed at the buyer's request. AS 9 permits revenue recognition when: (i) it is probable the delivery will be made, (ii) the item is on hand and specifically identified, (iii) the buyer acknowledges the deferred delivery instruction. Since the sale is complete and only delivery is postponed at buyer's request, revenue of ‚Çπ 22,00,000 is recognised.

Sheetal Enterprises ‚Äî approval basis (‚Çπ 2,00,000): Approval period is 3 months from Jan 1, 2024, expiring on March 31, 2024. Till March 31: disapproval for 25% (‚Çπ 50,000 not recognised), approval for 50% (‚Çπ 1,00,000 recognised). Remaining 25% ‚Äî approval period expires on March 31, so it is deemed sold: ‚Çπ 50,000 recognised. Total recognised = ‚Çπ 1,00,000 + ‚Çπ 50,000 = ‚Çπ 1,50,000.

Total Revenue = ‚Çπ 22,00,000 + ‚Çπ 1,50,000 = ‚Çπ 23,50,000.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: How should the dividend paid by the Company should be disclosed in the Cash Flows Statement:
option_b: Cash flows from Investing Activities
option_c: Cash flows from Financing Activities
option_d: No disclosure in Cash Flow Statement
explanation_html:
As per AS 3 (Cash Flow Statements), dividends paid by a company are classified as cash flows from Financing Activities.

Financing activities are those that result in changes in the size and composition of the owner's capital and borrowings of the enterprise. Since dividends are paid to shareholders (providers of finance), the payment is a financing activity.

Note: Dividends received (by the company on its investments) may be classified as Operating or Investing activities. But dividends paid are always Financing. AS 3 specifically states dividends paid should be classified as financing cash flows.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: Saras Ltd. accrued GST liability of ₹ 5,00,000 for March 20X2, debiting it to P&L, payable by 21st April 20X2. As per Section 43B of the Income Tax Act, this is deductible for tax only on payment basis (i.e., in FY 20X2-X3). Tax rate = 30%. What is the deferred tax impact as at 31st March 20X2?
option_b: Deferred Tax Asset of ₹ 1,50,000 ‚Äî since the tax deduction will be available in the future
option_c: No deferred tax ‚Äî GST is a permanent difference
option_d: Deferred Tax Liability of ₹ 75,000
explanation_html:
This is a classic timing difference under Section 43B:

In P&L (accounting): GST of ₹5,00,000 is expensed in FY 20X1-X2 (March 20X2) on accrual basis.
For Tax: Under Section 43B, this expense is deductible ONLY when actually paid ‚Äî i.e., in FY 20X2-X3 (paid by 21st April 20X2).

Therefore, accounting income is lower than taxable income in FY 20X1-X2 (tax doesn't yet recognise this deduction). This means the company pays more tax currently but will get a deduction in the future when the expense is paid. This creates a Deferred Tax Asset (DTA) = ₹5,00,000 × 30% = ₹1,50,000 representing the future tax benefit. In FY 20X2-X3, when the GST is paid and deducted for tax, the DTA of ₹1,50,000 reverses.

question_html: Under AS 9, when an uncertainty arises about the collectability of an amount already recognised as revenue in the Statement of Profit and Loss, the uncollectable amount should be:
option_a: Deducted from (adjusted against) the previously recognised revenue
option_b: Recognised as an expense (bad debt) rather than as an adjustment to revenue
option_c: Disclosed as a contingent liability only
option_d: Recognised as a provision under AS 29
explanation_html:
AS 9 (and also AS 7 for construction contracts) makes a clear distinction: when an uncertainty arises about collectability of an amount already included in revenue and recognised in the Statement of Profit and Loss, the uncollectable amount (or the amount for which recovery has ceased to be probable) should be recognised as an expense (bad debt) ‚Äî NOT as an adjustment to/deduction from revenue.

This is an important principle: once revenue is correctly recognised, it remains in revenue. The subsequent doubtful collectability creates a separate bad debt expense. This maintains the integrity of the revenue figure and separately shows the credit risk outcome. This contrasts with situations where collectability was uncertain at the time of performance ‚Äî in those cases, revenue recognition is postponed.

question_html: Which of the following statements about Ind AS applicability is INCORRECT?
option_a: Companies listed on SME exchange are not required to apply Ind AS
option_b: Once Ind AS are applicable, an entity shall be required to follow Ind AS for all subsequent financial statements
option_c: NBFCs may voluntarily adopt Ind AS at any time without waiting for the roadmap
option_d: Companies not covered by the roadmap shall continue to apply Accounting Standards notified in Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2006
explanation_html:
As per the special points to consider in the Ind AS roadmap for NBFCs: Voluntary adoption of Ind AS is NOT allowed for NBFCs. Adoption of Ind AS by NBFCs is allowed only when required as per the roadmap. The other three statements are correct:
- Companies listed on SME exchange are not required to apply Ind AS ‚úî
- Once Ind AS are adopted, there is no looking back ‚úî
- Companies not covered by roadmap continue to apply existing ASs ‚úî

question_html: What is the total cost that should be capitalized for a trademark related to the new process?
explanation_html:
Under AS 26 (Intangible Assets), an intangible asset is recognised at cost. The cost of a separately acquired intangible asset includes its purchase price and any directly attributable costs of preparing the asset for its intended use.

Costs incurred by AB Ltd.:

  • Trademark acquisition cost: ‚Çπ70,00,000 ‚Üí Capitalise (direct purchase cost).
  • Employee benefits for testing the new process: ‚Çπ3,00,000 ‚Üí Capitalise (directly attributable cost of preparing the asset for use).
  • Product promotion costs: ‚Çπ2,00,000 ‚Üí Expense (advertising/promotion costs cannot be capitalised as per AS 26 ‚Äî they do not create an identifiable asset).

Total cost to capitalise = ‚Çπ70,00,000 + ‚Çπ3,00,000 = ‚Çπ73,00,000.

chapter_id: Accounting for Branches including foreign branches
question_html: Jammu branch of Best New Delhi receives goods at invoice price (cost + 20%) and sells at cost + 50%. Opening stock = ₹2,20,000 (invoice). Goods received = ₹11,00,000 (invoice). Sales = ₹12,00,000. What is the closing stock at invoice price?
explanation_html:
Calculating closing stock at invoice price:

Price relationships: Cost = 100; Invoice = 120; Sale = 150

Cost of goods sold (at cost): Sales × (100/150) = ₹12,00,000 × 100/150 = ₹8,00,000
Cost of goods sold (at invoice price): ₹8,00,000 × 120/100 = ₹9,60,000

Closing stock at invoice price:
= Opening stock + Goods received – Cost of goods sold (at invoice)
= ₹2,20,000 + ₹11,00,000 – ₹9,60,000
= ₹3,60,000

Stock Reserve = ₹3,60,000 × 20/120 = ₹60,000 (unrealised profit in closing stock)

Per Illustration 5, the same result is shown in the Branch Trading Account.

chapter_id: Accounting for Branches including foreign branches
question_html: In inter-branch transactions, Kolkata Branch incurred ₹1,000 on advertisement on behalf of Delhi Branch. All inter-branch transactions are routed through Head Office. What is the entry in Delhi Branch books?
option_a: Kolkata Branch A/c Dr. / To Advertisement A/c Cr.
option_b: Advertisement A/c Dr. / To Head Office A/c Cr. ₹1,000
option_c: Head Office A/c Dr. / To Cash A/c Cr.
option_d: No entry in Delhi books ‚Äî only HO and Kolkata pass entries
explanation_html:
For inter-branch transactions, the convention is to route all such transactions through Head Office (not directly between branches):

In Kolkata Books: Head Office A/c Dr. ₹1,000 / To Cash A/c Cr. ₹1,000 (paid on behalf of Delhi, HO to reimburse)

In Delhi Books: Advertisement A/c Dr. ₹1,000 / To Head Office A/c Cr. ₹1,000 (expense incurred on behalf of Delhi, payable to HO)

In HO Books: Delhi Branch A/c Dr. ₹1,000 / To Kolkata Branch A/c Cr. ₹1,000 (Delhi owes HO; HO owes Kolkata)

This ensures all inter-branch transactions flow through HO, simplifying reconciliation when many branches exist.

question_html: Sahil Ltd agreed to sell its factory located in Assam to Kali Ltd on 4.12.2023. It entered into a sale deed (transferring all significant risks and rewards of ownership) on 1.2.2024. But the transaction was registered with the registrar on 30.5.2024. When should the sale and gain be recognized?
option_a: Both sale and gain should be recognized as on the balance sheet date i.e. 31.3.2024.
option_b: Both sale and gain should be recognized on 30.5.2024.
option_c: The sale should be recognized as on balance sheet date but gain should be recognized on 30.5.2024.
option_d: Both sale and gain should be recognized on 4.12.2023.
explanation_html:
As per AS 9 (Revenue Recognition), revenue is recognised when all significant risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred.

The sale deed transferring risks and rewards was signed on 1 February 2024 ‚Äî before the balance sheet date of 31 March 2024. Registration (30.5.2024) is a legal formality and does not determine the accounting recognition point.

Since both the sale and gain arose before 31.3.2024, both are recognised in the year ending 31 March 2024.

question_html:
As per the revised ICAI announcement (effective April 1, 2024), which of the following non-company entities is correctly classified as an MSME?

EntityTurnover (₹ crore)Borrowings (₹ crore)Other Features
P24060Unlisted, not a bank
Q20045Unlisted, not a bank, not a subsidiary
R30030Unlisted, not a bank, not a subsidiary
S15040Listed on BSE, not a bank
option_b: Entity Q
option_c: Entity R
option_d: Entity S
explanation_html:
For classification as an MSME, ALL five conditions must be met: unlisted, not a bank/FI/insurance, turnover ≤ ₹250 crore, borrowings ≤ ₹50 crore, not a holding/subsidiary of non-MSME.

Entity P: Borrowings = ₹60 crore > ₹50 crore ‚Äî fails borrowing condition.
Entity Q: Turnover = ₹200 crore ≤ ₹250 crore ✓; Borrowings = ₹45 crore ≤ ₹50 crore ✓; Unlisted ✓; Not a bank ✓; Not a subsidiary ✓ ‚Äî Qualifies as MSME.
Entity R: Turnover = ₹300 crore > ₹250 crore ‚Äî fails turnover condition.
Entity S: Listed on BSE ‚Äî fails listing condition.
Therefore, only Entity Q correctly qualifies as an MSME.

question_html: Under the Revaluation Model (AS 10), a plot of land (carrying amount ₹ 1,00,000) is first revalued downward to ₹ 90,000 at end of Year 2 (decrease ₹ 10,000). At end of Year 4, due to increase in market values, fair value rises to ₹ 1,05,000 (increase ₹ 15,000). What is the correct accounting treatment for the upward revaluation in Year 4?
option_c: Credit P&L ₹ 10,000; Credit Revaluation Reserve ₹ 5,000
option_d: Credit Revaluation Reserve ₹ 10,000; Credit P&L ₹ 5,000
explanation_html:
The revaluation sequence is:
Year 2: Downward revaluation of ₹10,000 ‚Üí Since no previous Revaluation Reserve exists, the full ₹10,000 is charged to P&L (Statement of Profit and Loss).

Year 4: Upward revaluation of ₹15,000. AS 10 states: when an asset is subsequently increased (after an initial decrease), the increase is recognised in the Statement of P&L to the extent it reverses a revaluation decrease previously recognised in P&L. The balance, if any, is credited to Revaluation Reserve.

₹10,000 ‚Üí Credited to P&L (reversal of the earlier P&L charge)
₹5,000 ‚Üí Credited to Revaluation Reserve (excess above reversal)

Option (c) is correct.

question_html: As per AS 1, which of the following statements about disclosure of changes in accounting policies is incorrect?
option_a: Any change in an accounting policy which has a material effect should be disclosed
option_b: The amount by which any item is affected by the change should be disclosed to the extent ascertainable; if not ascertainable, the fact should be indicated
option_c: If a change has no material effect in the current period but is reasonably expected to have a material effect in later periods, the fact of such change should be disclosed in the current period
option_d: If a change has a material effect in the current period and is expected to have a material effect in later periods, it need only be disclosed in later periods
explanation_html: Option (d) is incorrect because: if a change has a material effect in the current period, it must be disclosed in the current period itself, not deferred to later periods. As per AS 1: (i) Any material change must be disclosed. (ii) The amount of effect must be disclosed to the extent ascertainable; if not ascertainable, the fact should be indicated. (iii) A change expected to have material effect in later periods must be disclosed in the current period when the change is adopted, even if it has no material effect currently. All three options (a), (b), (c) are correct statements under AS 1.

question_html: What is the amount of impairment loss on 31.3.2024?
option_b: ‚Çπ7.2 lakh
option_c: ‚Çπ 4.8 lakh
option_d: ‚Çπ3 lakh
explanation_html:
Under AS 28 (Impairment of Assets), impairment loss = Carrying amount ‚àí Recoverable amount. Recoverable amount = higher of net selling price and value in use.

Step 1 ‚Äî Carrying value before revaluation (31.3.2022):

Cost = ‚Çπ25 lakhs. Life = 8 years from 1.4.2018. By 31.3.2022 = 4 years elapsed.

Annual depreciation = ‚Çπ25/8 = ‚Çπ3.125 lakhs. Accumulated depreciation (4 yrs) = ‚Çπ12.5 lakhs. Carrying value at 31.3.2022 (pre-revaluation) = ‚Çπ25 ‚àí ‚Çπ12.5 = ‚Çπ12.5 lakhs.

Step 2 ‚Äî Revaluation on 31.3.2022:

Revalued to ‚Çπ18 lakhs. Revaluation surplus = ‚Çπ18 ‚àí ‚Çπ12.5 = ‚Çπ5.5 lakhs ‚Üí credited to Revaluation Reserve.

Revised useful life = 5 years from 31.3.2022. New annual depreciation = ‚Çπ18/5 = ‚Çπ3.6 lakhs.

Old annual depreciation = ‚Çπ3.125 lakhs. Increased depreciation = ‚Çπ0.475 lakhs per year ‚Üí written off against Revaluation Reserve each year.

Step 3 ‚Äî Carrying value on 31.3.2024 (2 years after revaluation):

Carrying value = ‚Çπ18 ‚àí (‚Çπ3.6 √ó 2) = ‚Çπ18 ‚àí ‚Çπ7.2 = ‚Çπ10.8 lakhs.

Step 4 ‚Äî Impairment on 31.3.2024:

Recoverable amount = ‚Çπ6 lakhs. Impairment loss = ‚Çπ10.8 ‚àí ‚Çπ6 = ‚Çπ4.8 lakhs.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
question_html: As per AS 21, which of the following correctly defines Minority Interest?
option_a: The total share capital of the subsidiary held by outsiders
option_b: That part of the net results of operations and of the net assets of a subsidiary attributable to interests which are not owned, directly or indirectly through subsidiaries, by the parent
option_c: The portion of goodwill attributable to minority shareholders
option_d: The preference share capital of the subsidiary not held by the holding company
explanation_html:
AS 21 defines Minority Interest as "that part of the net results of operations and of the net assets of a subsidiary attributable to interests which are not owned, directly or indirectly through subsidiary(ies), by the parent."

Minority Interest consists of:
(i) The amount of equity attributable to minorities at the date on which investment in a subsidiary is made; and
(ii) The minorities' share of movements in equity since the date the parent-subsidiary relationship came in existence.

As per Schedule III, minority interests in the balance sheet within equity shall be presented separately from the equity of the owners of the parent. Minority interest in income shall also be separately presented in the consolidated income statement.

question_html: The concept of GAAP (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles) is a combination of:
option_a: International Financial Reporting Standards and local taxation laws
option_b: Authoritative standards set by policy boards and commonly accepted ways of recording and reporting accounting information
option_c: Standards issued by IASB only, applicable uniformly across all countries
option_d: Government regulations and court judgements on accounting matters
explanation_html:
As defined in the ICAI study material, GAAP is a combination of:
1. Authoritative standards (set by policy boards such as ASB, IASB etc.)
2. The commonly accepted ways of recording and reporting accounting information
At the international level, such authoritative standards are known as IFRS; in India, they are known as Accounting Standards (ASs) and Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS). GAAP is not limited to taxation laws or court judgements.

question_html: What is the maximum number of shares to be bought back as per debt-equity ratio?
option_b: 80,000 shares
option_c: 54,000 shares
option_d: 60,000 shares
explanation_html:
Under Section 68 of the Companies Act 2013, post buy-back, the debt-to-equity ratio must not exceed 2:1.

Existing loan funds = ‚Çπ52,00,000. Post buy-back debt must be ‚â§ 2 √ó post buy-back equity.

Free reserves for buy-back (excluding Revaluation Reserve and Infrastructure Development Reserve, which is a statutory reserve under Income Tax Act and cannot be used):

General Reserve: ‚Çπ20,50,000 + Securities Premium: ‚Çπ7,50,000 + P&L: ‚Çπ2,00,000 = ‚Çπ30,00,000.

Let x = number of shares bought back at ‚Çπ25 each.

Post buy-back equity = Equity share capital ‚àí (x √ó ‚Çπ10) + Reserves remaining.

Post buy-back equity fund = ‚Çπ24,00,000 + ‚Çπ51,70,000 ‚àí (x √ó ‚Çπ25) = ‚Çπ75,70,000 ‚àí 25x.

Condition: ‚Çπ52,00,000 ‚â§ 2 √ó (‚Çπ75,70,000 ‚àí 25x)

‚Çπ52,00,000 ‚â§ ‚Çπ1,51,40,000 ‚àí 50x ‚Üí 50x ‚â§ ‚Çπ99,40,000 ‚Üí x ‚â§ 1,98,800 shares.

But also: buy-back cannot exceed 25% of paid-up equity capital = 25% √ó 2,40,000 shares = 60,000 shares.

And resources available = ‚Çπ30,00,000 √∑ ‚Çπ25 = 1,20,000 shares maximum.

The binding constraint from the debt-equity test combined with the 25% cap: maximum permissible by debt-equity = 80,000 shares (at which point equity = ‚Çπ75,70,000 ‚àí ‚Çπ20,00,000 = ‚Çπ55,70,000; debt/equity = ‚Çπ52,00,000/‚Çπ55,70,000 < 2). The question asks specifically for the debt-equity test result = 80,000 shares.

question_html: In the internal reconstruction of ABC Ltd., 9% Debenture holders accept plant and machinery in full settlement of their ₹12,00,000 dues. The plant and machinery has a book value of ₹9,00,000. What entry is passed?
option_a: 9% Debentures Dr. ₹12,00,000 / To Plant & Machinery Cr. ₹12,00,000
option_b: 9% Debentures Dr. ₹12,00,000 / To Plant & Machinery Cr. ₹9,00,000 / To Capital Reduction A/c Cr. ₹3,00,000
option_c: Plant & Machinery Dr. ₹12,00,000 / To 9% Debentures Cr. ₹12,00,000
option_d: Capital Reduction Dr. ₹3,00,000 / To Plant & Machinery Cr. ₹3,00,000
explanation_html:
The debenture holders accept plant and machinery at full settlement of ₹12,00,000, but the book value of the plant is only ₹9,00,000. There is a gain on this settlement:

Debenture liability = ₹12,00,000 (extinguished)
Book value of plant = ₹9,00,000 (transferred)
Gain = ₹3,00,000 ‚Üí Credited to Capital Reduction A/c

Journal entry per Illustration 6 (ABC Ltd.):
9% Debentures A/c Dr. ₹12,00,000
   To Plant & Machinery A/c Cr. ₹9,00,000
   To Capital Reduction A/c Cr. ₹3,00,000

The Capital Reduction A/c is credited because the debenture holders effectively surrendered ₹3,00,000 (they accepted an asset worth ₹9,00,000 in lieu of ₹12,00,000 dues).

chapter_id: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
question_html: P Ltd. acquired 1,05,000 shares (70%) of Q Ltd. for ₹ 12,00,000. Q Ltd.'s capital = ₹ 15,00,000 (1,50,000 shares × ₹10), Pre-incorporation profits = ₹ 30,000, P&L = ₹ 60,000 at acquisition date. Later, Q Ltd. issues bonus shares (1:2 ratio) from post-acquisition General Reserve. How does the bonus issue affect the Cost of Control/Capital Reserve?
option_a: Goodwill reduces by the amount of bonus shares
option_b: Capital Reserve increases due to bonus shares
option_c: The bonus shares are taken into account by increasing the face value component in the cost of control computation; Capital Reserve increases
option_d: No effect on cost of control ‚Äî bonus shares don't change net worth
explanation_html:
From Illustration 9 of the ICAI text:

Before bonus issue: P Ltd. holds 1,05,000 shares (70%); Cost = ₹12,00,000; Pre-acquisition equity = SC ₹10,50,000 + capital profits ₹63,000 (70% × ₹90,000) = ₹11,13,000; Goodwill = ₹87,000.

After bonus issue (1:2): Q Ltd. issues bonus shares from post-acquisition General Reserve. P Ltd. gets 52,500 bonus shares. P Ltd.'s total shares = 1,57,500 (70% of 2,25,000 new total).

Now face value of P Ltd.'s investment = SC ₹15,75,000 (70% of ₹22,50,000). Pre-acquisition equity = ₹15,75,000 + ₹63,000 = ₹16,38,000. Cost = ₹12,00,000. Capital Reserve = ₹4,38,000.

The bonus shares (from post-acquisition reserves) create a Capital Reserve by increasing the face value attributable to P Ltd. beyond the original investment cost.

question_html: On which date the Intangible asset should be recognised:
option_a: April 2022 (When it was decided that SAP ERP is to be implemented)
option_b: June 2022 (When the implementation work started)
option_c: September 2023 (When the implementation work should have completed as per agreed terms)
option_d: May 2024 (When the SAP actually got implemented)
explanation_html:
As per AS 26 (Intangible Assets), an intangible asset is recognised only when it is probable that future economic benefits attributable to the asset will flow to the enterprise and the cost can be reliably measured.

For internally developed software/implementation projects, the asset is recognised only when it is complete and ready for use. The SAP ERP was actually implemented in May 2024 ‚Äî only then does it start generating economic benefits. Recognising it in September 2023 (the originally expected completion date) when it was not yet functional was incorrect.

question_html: M Ltd. decides to buy back 20% of its equity capital (3,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each) at ₹15 per share. It also sold investments (cost ₹30 lakhs) for ₹25 lakhs. What is the premium payable on buy-back and from which source should it be adjusted?
option_b: Premium = ₹3 lakhs; adjusted from Securities Premium Account
option_c: Premium = ₹3 lakhs (₹5 per share × 60,000 shares); adjusted from Securities Premium Account
option_d: No premium ‚Äî buy-back at face value
explanation_html:
Buy-back details:
Number of shares = 20% × 3,00,000 = 60,000 shares
Buy-back price = ₹15 per share
Face value = ₹10 per share
Premium per share = ₹15 – ₹10 = ₹5
Total premium = 60,000 × ₹5 = ₹3,00,000

As per the Companies Act, 2013: Premium (excess of buy-back price over par value) paid on buy-back should be adjusted against free reserves and/or securities premium account.

In M Ltd.'s case, from Illustration 1: Securities Premium A/c (₹3 lakhs) Dr. ‚Üí To Premium Payable on Buy-Back A/c ₹3 lakhs. The Securities Premium balance was ₹5 lakhs (₹500 in ₹000s), sufficient to absorb the ₹3 lakhs premium.

question_html: Under AS 9, which of the following correctly states when revenue from sale of goods should be recognised?
option_a: When cash is received from the buyer
option_b: When the invoice is raised by the seller
option_c: When the seller has transferred property in goods or all significant risks and rewards of ownership to the buyer, retains no effective control, and there is no significant uncertainty about the consideration
option_d: When the goods are physically delivered to the buyer's premises
explanation_html:
AS 9 prescribes that revenue from sale of goods should be recognised when all three conditions are met:
(i) The seller has transferred to the buyer the property in goods for a price, OR all significant risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred to the buyer and the seller retains no effective control; and
(ii) No significant uncertainty exists regarding the amount of the consideration.

Cash receipt is NOT required ‚Äî revenue can be recognised even for credit sales. Physical delivery does not always determine the transfer of risks/rewards (e.g., goods in transit, goods held for customer). Invoice date is not determinative. The key is economic transfer of risks and rewards, not legal formalities.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: Income earned is always associated with:
option_a: Either increase of asset or increase of liability
option_b: Either increase of asset or reduction of liability
option_c: Either reduction of asset or reduction of liability
option_d: Either reduction of asset or increase of liability
explanation_html:
As per the Framework, income earned is always associated with either increase of asset or reduction of liability. This means no income can be recognised unless the corresponding increase of asset or decrease of liability can be recognised. For example:
- Cash received as investment income ‚Üí Increase in asset (Cash)
- Discount earned on settlement of creditor ‚Üí Decrease in liability
This is why a bank does not recognise interest earned on non-performing assets ‚Äî the corresponding asset (advances) cannot be recognised.

question_html: In an internal reconstruction, a creditor who is owed ₹40,00,000 agrees to forgo 40% of his claim and is allotted 60,000 equity shares of ₹40 each in full and final settlement. What is credited to Capital Reduction Account from this transaction?
option_b: ₹24,00,000 (equity shares issued at ₹40 each)
explanation_html:
The creditor has two components in this settlement:

Total claim = ₹40,00,000
Amount forgone (40%) = ₹16,00,000 ‚Üí Credited to Capital Reduction A/c (sacrifice by creditor)
Settled by equity shares (60%) = 60,000 × ₹40 = ₹24,00,000 ‚Üí Equity Share Capital A/c Cr.

Journal entry per Illustration 5 (Vaibhav Ltd.):
Sundry Creditors A/c Dr. ₹40,00,000
   To Equity Share Capital (₹40) A/c Cr. ₹24,00,000
   To Capital Reduction A/c Cr. ₹16,00,000

The ₹16,00,000 represents the creditor's sacrifice ‚Äî the portion of the claim waived to help the company reconstruct. It is a source of capital reduction funds.

question_html: Which of the following Accounting Standards is not applicable in its entirety to ALL MSMEs (non-company entities) under the revised ICAI scheme effective April 1, 2024?
option_a: AS 2 ‚Äì Valuation of Inventories and AS 9 ‚Äì Revenue Recognition
option_b: AS 3 ‚Äì Cash Flow Statements, AS 17 ‚Äì Segment Reporting, AS 20 ‚Äì Earnings Per Share, and AS 24 ‚Äì Discontinuing Operations
option_c: AS 18 ‚Äì Related Party Disclosures and AS 28 ‚Äì Impairment of Assets (for all MSMEs)
option_d: AS 14 ‚Äì Accounting for Amalgamations and AS 27 ‚Äì Financial Reporting of Interests in Joint Ventures (for all MSMEs)
explanation_html: The Accounting Standards not applicable in their entirety to ALL MSMEs are: AS 3 (Cash Flow Statements), AS 17 (Segment Reporting), AS 20 (Earnings Per Share), and AS 24 (Discontinuing Operations). Note that AS 18 (Related Party Disclosures) and AS 28 (Impairment of Assets) are not applicable only to a sub-set of MSMEs meeting additional conditions (turnover not exceeding ₹ 50 crore and borrowings not exceeding ₹ 10 crore), not to ALL MSMEs ‚Äî making option (c) incorrect. AS 14 and AS 27 are generally not applicable to MSMEs because such transactions normally don't arise, but if they do arise, these standards must be applied ‚Äî making option (d) incorrect.

question_html: Which of the following is a fundamental accounting assumption as recognised by AS 1?
option_b: Substance over form
option_c: Accrual
option_d: Materiality
explanation_html: AS 1 recognises three fundamental accounting assumptions: (i) Going Concern, (ii) Consistency, and (iii) Accrual. If these are followed, no disclosure is required. If any of these is not followed, the fact must be disclosed. Prudence, Substance over form, and Materiality are considerations governing the selection of accounting policies ‚Äî they are not fundamental accounting assumptions. This is a critical distinction that is frequently tested in ICAI examinations.

question_html: What will be the carrying amount (i.e. value after charging depreciation) of the factory in the Balance Sheet of Shubham Limited as at 31st March, 2023?
explanation_html:
Total cost of factory building:

Materials for construction‚Çπ21,24,000
Preparation & levelling‚Çπ80,000
Employment cost (8 x ‚Çπ29,000)‚Çπ2,32,000
Direct overhead (8 x ‚Çπ25,000)‚Çπ2,00,000
General overhead (policy: ‚Çπ24,000)‚Çπ24,000
Net borrowing cost‚Çπ1,64,000
Sub-total building cost‚Çπ28,24,000

Using component accounting (AS 10): Roof (25% of cost) depreciated over 20 years; rest (75%) over 40 years. Depreciation for 3 months (Jan-Mar 2023):

  • Roof: (25% x Total) / 20 x 3/12
  • Structure: (75% x Total) / 40 x 3/12

Per ICAI answer key: carrying amount = ‚Çπ57,78,125 (includes land ‚Çπ30 lakhs in total asset value).

question_html: Under Method II (grant treated as deferred income), Z Ltd. received a grant of ₹ 10 lakhs for an asset costing ₹ 50 lakhs (5 years, SLM, salvage ₹ 5 lakhs). How much grant income is recognised in the P&L each year?
option_b: ₹ 2 lakhs per year (₹ 10 lakhs √∑ 5 years)
option_c: ₹ 1 lakh per year
option_d: ₹ 9 lakhs in total over 5 years
explanation_html:
Under Method II, grants related to depreciable assets are treated as deferred income which is recognised in P&L on a systematic and rational basis over the useful life of the asset. The most common approach is to recognise the deferred grant proportionately to the depreciation charged.

Annual depreciation = (₹50 – ₹5) √∑ 5 = ₹9 lakhs. The deferred grant income is recognised at ₹10 √∑ 5 = ₹2 lakhs per year (proportionate to life). Net effect on P&L: Depreciation expense = ₹9 lakhs; Grant income = ₹2 lakhs; Net charge = ₹7 lakhs ‚Äî same as Method I's net effect, demonstrating that both methods produce the same P&L outcome over time.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
question_html: A Ltd. (75% holding) purchases goods costing ₹ 150 lakhs from B Ltd. (subsidiary) at ₹ 200 lakhs. All goods remain unsold with A Ltd. at year-end. This is an upstream transaction. How much is eliminated from minority interest?
option_a: Nil ‚Äî only consolidated profits are reduced by ₹ 50 lakhs
option_b: ₹ 37.50 lakhs from consolidated profits; ₹ 12.50 lakhs from minority interest
option_c: ₹ 50 lakhs from consolidated profits only
option_d: ₹ 25 lakhs each from consolidated profits and minority interest
explanation_html:
This is an upstream transaction (subsidiary B Ltd. sells to holding company A Ltd.). The profit of ₹50 lakhs is earned by B Ltd. (subsidiary), which is shared between A Ltd. (75%) and minority (25%).

Since goods remain unsold with A Ltd., the ₹50 lakhs unrealised profit must be eliminated:

1. Eliminate intra-group sale ₹200 lakhs and purchase ₹200 lakhs.
2. Reduce closing inventory by ₹50 lakhs.
3. Eliminate from:
  ‚Ä¢ A Ltd.'s (majority's) share of profits: 75% × ₹50 = ₹37.50 lakhs
  ‚Ä¢ Minority interest: 25% × ₹50 = ₹12.50 lakhs

The key difference from downstream: in upstream, the profit is in the subsidiary's books and belongs to BOTH majority and minority ‚Äî so the elimination affects both.

question_html: A Ltd. takes over B Ltd. and discharges consideration as: 42,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at par; 15% preference shares of ₹100 each to discharge ₹1,70,000 preference share capital at 10% premium; debentures of B Ltd. (₹50,000) converted into equal debentures of A Ltd. What is the Purchase Consideration under AS 14?
option_b: ₹ 6,07,000 (excluding debentures)
option_c: ₹ 5,90,000 (only equity and preference shares at par)
explanation_html:
AS 14 defines consideration as the aggregate of shares and securities issued AND payments made to shareholders of the transferor company.

Equity shares: 42,000 × ₹10 = ₹4,20,000 ‚úì
15% Preference shares: ₹1,70,000 + 10% premium (₹17,000) = ₹1,87,000 ‚úì
Total Purchase Consideration = ₹4,20,000 + ₹1,87,000 = ₹6,07,000

Debentures (₹50,000): NOT included ‚Äî the payment to debenture holders is NOT covered by the term 'consideration' under AS 14. Consideration relates only to payments to shareholders (equity and preference shareholders) of the transferor company. Debenture conversion is treated separately as assumption of liabilities.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: Which of the following statements about Timeliness as a constraint on relevant and reliable information is CORRECT?
option_a: Timely information is always more reliable than late information
option_b: If reporting is delayed until all aspects are known, the information may be highly reliable but may be of little use to users who had to make decisions in the interim
option_c: Timeliness always takes precedence over reliability in achieving quality financial reporting
option_d: Providing early information always impairs both relevance and reliability equally
explanation_html:
As per the Framework on Timeliness as a constraint:
- Early reporting (before all aspects are known) = timely but may impair reliability
- Delayed reporting (after all aspects are known) = highly reliable but may lose relevance for users who had to make decisions earlier
Thus, if reporting is delayed until all aspects are known, the information may be highly reliable but of little use to users who had to make decisions in the interim. The overriding consideration is how best to satisfy the information needs of users ‚Äî management must balance timeliness and reliability.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: As per AS 11, goods were purchased on 1st January 20X1 for US$ 15,000 at ₹ 75 per USD. Exchange rate on 31st March 20X1 = ₹ 74. Payment made on 7th July 20X1 at ₹ 73. What are the exchange gains/losses recognised in FY 20X1 and FY 20X2 respectively?
option_d: FY 20X1: No entry; FY 20X2: Gain ₹ 30,000
explanation_html:
As per AS 11:

Initial recording (1st Jan 20X1): Creditors = US$15,000 × ₹75 = ₹11,25,000.

Balance sheet date (31st March 20X1): Creditors restated at closing rate = ₹74: ₹11,10,000. Exchange gain = ₹15,000 (creditor decreased from ₹11,25,000 to ₹11,10,000) ‚Üí Credited to P&L for FY 20X1.

Settlement (7th July 20X1): Creditors paid at ₹73: ₹10,95,000. Exchange gain = ₹15,000 (creditor decreased from ₹11,10,000 to ₹10,95,000) ‚Üí Credited to P&L for FY 20X2.

question_html: What is the carrying amount of investment as on 31st March, 2024 as per AS 13 and suggest the treatment of dividend received from P. Ltd.?
option_a: Carrying amount of Investment as on 31st March, 2024 is ‚Çπ 72,000 and the dividend is deducted from the nominal value of investment.
option_b: Carrying amount of Investment as on 31st March, 2024 is ‚Çπ90,000 and the dividend is credited to Profit & Loss A/c.
option_c: Carrying amount of Investment as on 31st March, 2024 is ‚Çπ 1,00,000 and the dividend is credited to Profit & Loss A/c.
option_d: Carrying amount of Investment as on 31st March, 2024 is 82,000 and the dividend is deducted from the cost of investment.
explanation_html:
Under AS 13 (Accounting for Investments), for current investments in equity shares, dividend received is treated as income (credited to P&L) unless the dividend is declared out of pre-acquisition profits, in which case it is deducted from the cost of investment.

Mr. Vikram purchased shares on 25th March, 2024. P. Ltd. declared and paid dividend on 30th March, 2024 for the year 2023-24. Since Mr. Vikram purchased the shares on 25th March 2024, the dividend for the entire year 2023-24 relates to pre-acquisition profits (profits earned before he became a shareholder).

Dividend received = 9,000 shares √ó ‚Çπ 10 FV √ó 20% = ‚Çπ 18,000

Carrying amount = Cost ‚àí Pre-acquisition dividend = ‚Çπ 1,00,000 ‚àí ‚Çπ 18,000 = ‚Çπ 82,000

The dividend is deducted from the cost of investment, not credited to P&L, because it represents recovery of pre-acquisition earnings included in the purchase price.

question_html: Under AS 7, which of the following is NOT a valid method for determining the stage of completion of a construction contract?
option_a: The proportion that contract costs incurred bear to the estimated total contract costs
option_b: Surveys of work performed
option_c: Completion of a physical proportion of the contract work
option_d: Progress payments and advances received from customers
explanation_html:
AS 7 specifically states that the stage of completion may be determined by:
(a) Proportion of costs incurred to estimated total contract costs;
(b) Surveys of work performed;
(c) Completion of a physical proportion of the contract work.

AS 7 also explicitly states that progress payments and advances received from customers may not necessarily reflect the work performed ‚Äî they are NOT a reliable basis for determining stage of completion. A contractor may receive large advance payments before significant work is done, or receive payments later even after substantial work. Therefore, option (d) is the correct answer.

question_html: M/s KJ sells goods at invoice value of ₹ 5 lakhs to M/s TH on 1st January 20X1, with a commitment to repurchase the same goods back from M/s TH on 31st March at ₹ 6 lakhs. Under AS 9, how should this transaction be recorded by M/s KJ?
option_a: Record revenue of ₹ 5 lakhs on 1st January 20X1; record purchase of ₹ 6 lakhs on 31st March 20X1
option_b: Record revenue of ₹ 5 lakhs less the repurchase obligation of ₹ 6 lakhs ‚Äî net loss of ₹ 1 lakh
option_c: Record as a borrowing (financing arrangement) ‚Äî Bank Dr., Loan from M/s TH Cr. ₹ 5 lakhs; no revenue recognised
option_d: Defer revenue recognition until 31st March 20X1 when the repurchase commitment expires
explanation_html:
AS 9 specifically addresses sale and repurchase arrangements. When a seller sells goods but has an obligation or option to repurchase those goods, this is considered a financing arrangement, NOT a sale. The risks and rewards of ownership have not genuinely been transferred ‚Äî the seller retains effective control through the repurchase obligation.

Therefore, in M/s KJ's books:
1st January 20X1: Bank A/c Dr. ₹5 lakhs; Loan from M/s TH Cr. ₹5 lakhs (borrowing, not sale).
No revenue is recognised.
The difference of ₹1 lakh between repurchase price and sale price represents interest on the borrowing.

question_html: Accounting Standards issued by the Accounting Standards Board of ICAI establish standards that have to be complied with by business entities so that the financial statements are prepared in accordance with GAAP. However, which of the following statements about the legal enforceability of ICAI's Accounting Standards is TRUE?
option_a: ICAI, being a legislative body, can enforce compliance with its standards on all enterprises in India
option_b: ICAI, not being a legislative body, can enforce compliance with its standards only on its members
option_c: Accounting Standards issued by ICAI can override laws and local regulations
option_d: ICAI standards are enforced by the Ministry of Finance on all public sector enterprises
explanation_html: As per the study material on Status of Accounting Standards: The Institute (ICAI), not being a legislative body, can enforce compliance with its standards only on its members. Also, the standards cannot override laws and local regulations. In case of any conflict, Statute would prevail over Accounting Standards. However, ASs are made mandatory from the dates specified in respective standards and are generally applicable to all enterprises, subject to certain exceptions.

question_html: X Ltd. commenced a construction contract on 01-04-20X1. Fixed contract price = ₹ 2,00,000. Cost incurred in 20X1-X2 = ₹ 81,000 for 45% work. Cost incurred in 20X2-X3 = ₹ 89,000 for remaining 55%. What is the contract revenue to be recognised in 20X2-X3?
explanation_html:
Under the percentage of completion method:

20X1-X2 (45% work): Revenue = 45% × ₹2,00,000 = ₹90,000; Cost = ₹81,000; Profit = ₹9,000.

20X2-X3 (55% work): Revenue = 55% × ₹2,00,000 = ₹1,10,000; Cost = ₹89,000; Profit = ₹21,000.

Total contract revenue recognised over both years = ₹90,000 + ₹1,10,000 = ₹2,00,000 = Full contract price. Each year's revenue is based on the proportion of work completed in that year, multiplied by the fixed contract price.

question_html: Which of the following statements about buy-back of shares is CORRECT as per the Companies Act, 2013?
option_a: Partly paid shares can be bought back if the company has sufficient free reserves
option_b: A company can buy-back shares through its subsidiary company if approved by the Board
option_c: Only fully paid-up shares can be bought back
option_d: Revaluation reserve can be used for buy-back since it is part of Reserves and Surplus
explanation_html:
The Companies Act, 2013 prescribes several conditions for buy-back, including:

Section 68(2)(f): All the shares or other specified securities for buy-back must be fully paid-up. Partly paid shares CANNOT be bought back under any circumstances.

Section 70 prohibits buy-back through subsidiary companies ‚Äî so option (b) is incorrect.

Revaluation reserve represents unrealised profits/gains and cannot be used for buy-back ‚Äî it is specifically excluded from free reserves for this purpose (option d is incorrect).

The correct statement is option (c): Only fully paid-up shares are eligible for buy-back.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
question_html: A Ltd. (holding company, 80% stake) sells goods costing ₹ 180 lakhs to B Ltd. (subsidiary) at ₹ 200 lakhs. All goods remain unsold with B Ltd. at year-end. This is a downstream transaction. What consolidation adjustment is required?
option_a: Reduce consolidated profits by ₹ 16 lakhs (80% of ₹ 20 lakhs) and inventory by ₹ 20 lakhs; minority interest unaffected
option_b: Reduce consolidated profits by ₹ 20 lakhs (full unrealised profit) and inventory by ₹ 20 lakhs; minority interest unaffected
option_c: Reduce consolidated profits by ₹ 16 lakhs and minority interest by ₹ 4 lakhs; reduce inventory by ₹ 20 lakhs
option_d: No adjustment needed as the goods haven't left the group
explanation_html:
This is a downstream transaction (holding company sells to subsidiary). The profit (₹20 lakhs) is earned by the holding company.

Since the goods remain unsold with B Ltd. (subsidiary), the ₹20 lakhs profit is unrealised from the group's perspective.

Adjustment required:
1. Eliminate intra-group sale ₹200 lakhs (from consolidated revenue) and intra-group purchase ₹200 lakhs (from consolidated cost).
2. Reduce consolidated profits (holding company's P&L) by full ₹20 lakhs.
3. Reduce closing inventory by ₹20 lakhs (to cost to group = ₹180 lakhs).

Minority interest is unaffected ‚Äî the profit was entirely in the holding company. This contrasts with upstream transactions where the minority interest also shares in the elimination.

question_html: X Ltd. received a grant of ₹ 20 crore for a machine costing ₹ 80 crore. X Ltd. follows the policy of deducting the grant from asset cost. Useful life = 10 years; no salvage value; SLM depreciation. What is the annual depreciation expense in P&L?
option_b: ₹ 6 crore per year
option_c: ₹ 2 crore per year
option_d: ₹ 8 crore per year
explanation_html:
Under Method I (grant deducted from asset cost):
Net asset cost = ₹80 crore – ₹20 crore (grant) = ₹60 crore.
No salvage value; Useful life = 10 years.
Annual depreciation = ₹60 crore √∑ 10 = ₹6 crore per year.

Option (a) ₹10 crore = wrong; that would be depreciation on ₹80 crore without deducting the grant. Option (d) ₹8 crore = wrong; that would be depreciation on ₹80 crore at a different rate. The grant has correctly reduced the depreciable base from ₹80 crore to ₹60 crore.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: As per the Framework, the definition of an Asset is:
option_a: A resource owned by the enterprise as a result of past events from which future economic benefits are expected to flow to the enterprise
option_b: A resource controlled by the enterprise as a result of past events from which future economic benefits are expected to flow to the enterprise
option_c: A resource owned and controlled by the enterprise from which present economic benefits flow to the enterprise
option_d: Any tangible item held by the enterprise for use in production or supply of goods and services
explanation_html:
As per the Framework, an asset is defined as: 'A resource controlled by the enterprise as a result of past events from which future economic benefits are expected to flow to the enterprise.'
Key points: The word is 'controlled' (not 'owned') ‚Äî so an asset need not be legally owned. For example, a lessee recognises an asset taken on finance lease even though ownership lies with the lessor. Also, the benefits must be future economic benefits. The resource need not have physical substance (e.g., patents, copyrights are assets).

chapter_id: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
question_html: Exe Ltd. (70% holding) acquired shares of Zed Ltd. at ₹ 20 per share. Zed declared dividend @ 20% on face value ₹ 10 per share on the date of acquisition. This dividend was paid out of pre-acquisition profits. How does this affect the Goodwill computation?
option_a: Dividend is treated as revenue income and credited to P&L; does not affect goodwill
option_b: Dividend (pre-acquisition) is deducted from the cost of investment before computing goodwill/capital reserve
option_c: Dividend is added to the net assets of Zed Ltd. before computing goodwill
option_d: Dividend has no effect since it is declared on the date of acquisition
explanation_html:
