When a dividend is declared from pre-acquisition profits, it represents a return of part of the investment cost rather than income. AS 13 states that such dividends should be deducted from the cost of investment before computing goodwill.

In Illustration 3 (Exe Ltd./Zed Ltd.): Number of shares purchased = ₹70 lakhs √∑ ₹20 = 3.5 lakh shares. Dividend = 20% × ₹10 × 3.5 lakh = ₹7 lakhs. This ₹7 lakhs is deducted from cost (₹70 – ₹7 = ₹63 lakhs) to arrive at effective cost for goodwill computation. This results in Capital Reserve of ₹33.95 lakhs (as shown in the ICAI illustration).

question_html: Cash balance after buyback
option_b: ‚Çπ 2,200 lakhs
option_c: ‚Çπ 3,250 lakhs
option_d: ‚Çπ 900 lakhs
explanation_html:
Cash balance computation:

Opening cash‚Çπ1,650 lakhs
Add: Sale of investments proceeds‚Çπ3,000 lakhs
Add: Bank loan‚Çπ2,000 lakhs
Less: Preference share redemption (‚Çπ2,500 √ó 110%)(‚Çπ2,750 lakhs)
Less: Equity buy-back (25% of 800 lakh shares √ó ‚Çπ15)(‚Çπ3,000 lakhs)
Closing cash balance‚Çπ900 lakhs

chapter_id: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
question_html: H Ltd. acquired 8,000 shares of S Ltd. (1st July 20X1). S Ltd.'s Profit & Loss on 1st April 20X1 = ₹ 30,000; profit for the year = ₹ 40,000 (accruing evenly). What is the pre-acquisition profit from H Ltd.'s perspective for the 80% stake?
option_d: ₹ 40,000 (full year profit is pre-acquisition)
explanation_html:
H Ltd. acquired shares on 1st July 20X1 (mid-year). Profits must be time-apportioned.

Pre-acquisition period = April to June 20X1 = 3 months (out of 12).
Pre-acquisition profit of S Ltd. = Opening balance ₹30,000 + profit earned up to 1st July = ₹30,000 + (3/12 × ₹40,000) = ₹30,000 + ₹10,000 = ₹40,000 total (of S Ltd.)

Wait ‚Äî Per H Ltd. (acquisition on 1st July, 80% = 8,000/10,000):
Pre-acquisition profits of S = ₹30,000 + ₹10,000 = ₹40,000
H Ltd.'s pre-acquisition share = 80% × ₹40,000 = ₹32,000

But per Illustration 11 in the text, pre-acquisition = 80% × [30,000 + 3/12(40,000-30,000)] = 80% × ₹32,500 = ₹26,000, using only the change in P&L during the year. The interpretation depends on whether full opening balance or only the year's profit is time-split. Per ICAI illustration 11: pre-acquisition = 80% × (30,000 + 3/12 × 10,000) = ₹26,000.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: The Framework recognises four alternative measurement bases for elements of financial statements. Which of the following is NOT one of the four?
option_b: Current Cost
option_c: Realisable (Settlement) Value
option_d: Replacement Cost
explanation_html:
The Framework recognises the following four alternative measurement bases:
1. Historical Cost ‚Äì acquisition price
2. Current Cost ‚Äì amount payable if the same/equivalent asset was acquired currently
3. Realisable (Settlement) Value ‚Äì amount currently realisable on sale
4. Present Value ‚Äì present value of future net cash flows
Replacement Cost is not separately recognised as a measurement basis in the Framework. It is sometimes confused with current cost, but they are not identical concepts in strict accounting terminology.

question_html: Cost of current investment acquired was ‚Çπ 1000 but the fair value was ‚Çπ 800. The Investment was recorded at ‚Çπ 800. Now the fair value of Investment is Rs 1200. At what value should it be recorded and how much gain will be credited to profit and loss account.
option_a: No change is required and it will continue at ‚Çπ 800
option_b: Current investment will be recorded at ‚Çπ 1000 and gain of ‚Çπ 200 will be credited to profit and loss account.
option_c: Current investment will be recorded at ‚Çπ 1200 and gain of ‚Çπ 400 will be credited to profit and loss account.
option_d: Current investment will be recorded at ‚Çπ 1200 but no gain will be credited to profit and loss account.
explanation_html:
Under AS 13 (Accounting for Investments), current investments are carried at the lower of cost and fair value.

When the investment was first recorded: Cost = ‚Çπ1,000, Fair value = ‚Çπ800. Lower of cost/fair value = ‚Çπ800 ‚Üí recorded at ‚Çπ800. A loss of ‚Çπ200 was recognised in P&L at that time.

Now fair value has risen to ‚Çπ1,200.

Under AS 13, the carrying amount of current investments can be increased up to cost (i.e., reversal of previous write-down) when fair value recovers. Any increase above cost cannot be recognised as income (to avoid gain beyond original cost).

Maximum carrying value = Cost = ‚Çπ1,000. The investment is written back up to cost ‚Üí gain recognised in P&L = ‚Çπ1,000 ‚àí ‚Çπ800 = ‚Çπ200.

The investment cannot be carried at ‚Çπ1,200 (above cost) ‚Äî that is not permitted under AS 13 for current investments. Therefore: record at ‚Çπ1,000 and credit gain of ‚Çπ200 to P&L.

question_html: EXOX Ltd. received a sales tax demand of ₹ 2.76 crore which it paid under protest. The company is appealing against additions of ₹ 2.10 crore but NOT appealing against the remaining ₹ 0.66 crore. How should these amounts be treated in the financial statements under AS 29?
option_b: Provide for ₹ 2.10 crore (full appeal amount); disclose ₹ 0.66 crore as contingent liability
option_c: Provide for ₹ 0.66 crore (not appealed = accepted liability); show ₹ 2.76 crore under Loans & Advances; disclose ₹ 2.10 crore as contingent liability
option_d: No provision ‚Äî the entire amount is disputed and can only be recognised after the appeal is decided
explanation_html:
The two components require different treatment:

₹ 0.66 crore (not being appealed): By not appealing against this portion, the company has effectively accepted this as a definite obligation. This represents a present obligation with probable outflow ‚Üí Provision of ₹ 0.66 crore must be created in the accounts.

₹ 2.76 crore paid under protest: The amount paid under protest (the entire ₹ 2.76 crore) should be shown as Loans & Advances (a receivable/deposit, pending final outcome of appeal).

₹ 2.10 crore (being appealed): The outcome is uncertain ‚Äî this is a contingent liability to be disclosed in the notes as per AS 29, not provided for (since the appeal makes the outflow only possible, not probable at this stage).

question_html: At the end of Year 1, how the building should be classified:
option_b: Investments
option_c: Property, Plant and Equipment
option_d: Intangible Asset
explanation_html:
As per AS 2 (Valuation of Inventories), inventories include goods held for sale in the ordinary course of business. Excellence Ltd. is a real estate company ‚Äî it constructs buildings for selling. Since at the end of Year 1 the building was still intended for sale (its NRV was ‚Çπ 40 crore), it must be classified as Inventory, not as PPE.

PPE classification under AS 10 requires the asset to be held for use in production, supply of goods/services, or for administrative purposes. That intention did not exist at the end of Year 1.

question_html: Anu Ltd. redeemed 12% Redeemable Preference Shares of ₹75 crore and bought back 50 lakh equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹50 per share. What is the total amount to be transferred to Capital Redemption Reserve?
option_b: ₹ 5 crore (equity buy-back only)
option_d: ₹ 25 crore (total paid-up value of equity bought back)
explanation_html:
Capital Redemption Reserve must be created equal to the nominal (face) value of:
(i) Preference shares redeemed out of profits/free reserves: ₹75 crore
(ii) Equity shares bought back out of free reserves: 50 lakh × ₹10 = ₹5 crore

Total CRR = ₹75 + ₹5 = ₹80 crore.

Journal entry per Illustration 2: Revenue Reserve Dr. ₹80 crore / To CRR ₹80 crore.

Note: The premium on buy-back (50 lakh × ₹40 = ₹20 crore) is charged to Securities Premium ‚Äî NOT to CRR. The total buy-back price of ₹25 crore (50 lakh × ₹50) is the payment amount, but CRR is created only for the face value (₹5 crore).

question_html: Ind AS 101 corresponds to IFRS 1 (First Time Adoption of Indian Accounting Standards). If a student is asked to identify the Indian AS (old) corresponding to Ind AS 33, the answer would be:
option_a: AS 33 ‚Äì There is no corresponding old AS
option_b: AS 17 ‚Äì Segment Reporting
option_c: AS 20 ‚Äì Earnings per Share
option_d: AS 25 ‚Äì Interim Financial Reporting
explanation_html:
As per the list of Ind AS in the study material:
- Ind AS 33 corresponds to IAS 33 ‚Äì Earnings per Share
- The corresponding Indian AS (old) is AS 20 ‚Äì Earnings per Share
- AS 17 corresponds to Ind AS 108 (IFRS 8 ‚Äì Operating Segments)
- AS 25 corresponds to Ind AS 34 (IAS 34 ‚Äì Interim Financial Reporting)
Thus, the correct old AS corresponding to Ind AS 33 is AS 20.

question_html: A chemical manufacturer installs new chemical handling processes to comply with environmental requirements for the production and storage of dangerous chemicals. Without these processes, it cannot manufacture and sell chemicals. Can these environmental assets be recognised as PPE under AS 10 (Revised)?
option_a: No, because they do not directly increase the future economic benefits of any particular existing PPE item
option_b: Yes, because they enable the enterprise to derive future economic benefits from related assets in excess of what could be derived had those items not been acquired
option_c: No, because safety and environmental assets do not meet the definition of PPE
option_d: Yes, but only to the extent of the directly attributable incremental economic benefits they generate
explanation_html: As per AS 10 (Revised), items of PPE may be acquired for safety or environmental reasons. Although such acquisitions do not directly increase future economic benefits of any particular existing item of PPE, they qualify for recognition as assets because they enable an enterprise to derive future economic benefits from related assets in excess of what could be derived had those items not been acquired. In the example of a chemical manufacturer, without the new chemical handling processes, the company cannot manufacture and sell chemicals ‚Äî thus these processes effectively enable the entire production activity. The resulting carrying amount of such assets and related assets is reviewed for impairment under AS 28.

question_html: As per Accounting Standards, difference between the Gross Investment and the present value of Minimum Lease Payments under finance lease (from the standpoint of the lessor) and Unguaranteed Residual Value accruing to the lessor is recorded as
option_b: Guaranteed Residual Value
option_c: Profit on lease
option_d: Loss on lease
explanation_html:
As per AS 19 (Leases), from the lessor's perspective in a finance lease:

Gross Investment = Total of minimum lease payments + unguaranteed residual value (undiscounted).

The difference between Gross Investment and its present value (discounted amount) = Unearned Finance Income.

This is recognised as income over the lease term using the effective interest rate method ‚Äî it represents the time value component embedded in future lease receivables.

question_html: In assessing whether an Accounting Standard is applicable to a particular situation, the preface to the statements of accounting standards prescribes answering three questions in a specific sequence. Which of the following represents the correct sequential order?
option_a: Does it apply to the financial item? → Does it apply to the enterprise? → Does it apply to the financial statement?
option_b: Does it apply to the enterprise? → Does it apply to the financial statement? → Does it apply to the financial item?
option_c: Does it apply to the financial statement? → Does it apply to the enterprise? → Does it apply to the financial item?
option_d: Does it apply to the enterprise? → Does it apply to the financial item? → Does it apply to the financial statement?
explanation_html:
As per the preface to the statements of accounting standards, the three sequential questions are:
(a) Does it apply to the enterprise concerned? If yes, then
(b) Does it apply to the financial statement concerned? If yes, then
(c) Does it apply to the financial item concerned?
The sequence must be strictly followed in this order. Only if the answer to the first question is affirmative should the second question be considered, and so on. The preface to the statements of accounting standards answers all three questions.

question_html: Which Accounting Standard was withdrawn consequent to the issuance of AS 26 on 'Intangible Assets'?
option_b: AS 8 ‚Äì Accounting for Research and Development
option_c: AS 7 ‚Äì Construction Contracts
option_d: AS 5 ‚Äì Net Profit or Loss for the Period
explanation_html: AS 8 on 'Accounting for Research and Development' was withdrawn consequent to the issuance of AS 26 on 'Intangible Assets', since intangible assets including research and development costs are now comprehensively covered under AS 26. Separately, AS 6 on 'Depreciation Accounting' was withdrawn upon revision of AS 10.

question_html: Under AS 15, Termination Benefits should be recognised as a liability and an expense when:
option_a: The employee submits a resignation or requests voluntary retirement
option_b: Management orally communicates its intent to terminate employees
option_c: The enterprise has a detailed formal plan for termination which is duly approved AND a reliable estimate of the obligation can be made
option_d: A provision for retrenchment is created in the annual budget of the enterprise
explanation_html:
Under AS 15, Termination Benefits are recognised as a liability and an expense only when the enterprise has:
(i) A detailed formal plan for the termination which is duly approved, and
(ii) A reliable estimate can be made of the amount of the obligation.

Merely having management's oral communication or budgeting for termination does not meet the recognition criteria. AS 15 requires more certainty ‚Äî for example, employees must have signed up for the termination scheme before recognition is appropriate. Where there is uncertainty about the number of employees who will accept a voluntary redundancy offer, a contingent liability exists and must be disclosed as per AS 29.

question_html: Accounting Standard 10, Property, Plant and Equipment is applicable to:
option_a: Biological Assets (other than Bearer Plants) related to agricultural activity
option_b: Wasting Assets including Mineral rights, Expenditure on the exploration for and extraction of minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources
option_c: Inventories
option_d: Bearer Plant (except produce on Bearer Plants)
explanation_html:
AS 10 (Property, Plant and Equipment) does NOT apply to certain categories of assets ‚Äî these are specifically excluded from its scope:

  • Biological assets (other than bearer plants) related to agricultural activity ‚Äî excluded from AS 10 scope.
  • Wasting assets including mineral rights, exploration for and extraction of minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources ‚Äî excluded.
  • Inventories ‚Äî covered by AS 2, not AS 10.

AS 10 IS applicable to:

  • Bearer Plants (except produce growing on bearer plants). A bearer plant is a living plant used in the production or supply of agricultural produce, expected to bear produce for more than one period (e.g., tea bushes, grape vines, rubber trees). Bearer plants are treated as PPE under AS 10, though the produce on them is accounted for separately under AS on Agriculture.

Therefore, AS 10 applies to Bearer Plants (except produce on Bearer Plants) ‚Äî option (d).

question_html: Which of the above grants are required to be recognised in the statement of profit and loss on a systematic and rational basis over the useful life of the asset:
option_b: Government Grant of ‚Çπ 30 Lakhs
option_c: Government Grant of ‚Çπ 15 Lakhs with a condition to purchase machinery
option_d: Noe of the above
explanation_html:
Only grants related to specific depreciable assets are systematically recognised in P&L over the asset's useful life.

  • Land (non-depreciable): Recorded at fair value; no P&L amortisation.
  • ‚Çπ30 lakhs (capital/promoter contribution): Credited to Capital Reserve; NOT amortised to P&L.
  • ‚Çπ15 lakhs (tied to machinery): Treated as Deferred Income and recognised in P&L over the useful life of the machinery ‚Äî systematic and rational basis.

question_html: Arka Ltd. purchased machinery for ₹ 3,000 lakhs (SLM, 10% p.a., 10 years). At end of Year 4, it is revalued to ₹ 2,700 lakhs. What is the carrying amount at the end of Year 6?
explanation_html:
Step 1: Book value at end of Year 4 = ₹3,000 – (₹3,000 × 10% × 4) = ₹3,000 – ₹1,200 = ₹1,800 lakhs.
Revaluation to ₹2,700 lakhs; Revaluation surplus = ₹900 lakhs.

Step 2: Remaining useful life = 10 – 4 = 6 years.
Revised annual depreciation = ₹2,700 √∑ 6 = ₹450 lakhs p.a.

Step 3: Carrying amount at end of Year 5 = ₹2,700 – ₹450 = ₹2,250 lakhs.
Carrying amount at end of Year 6 = ₹2,250 – ₹450 = ₹1,800 lakhs.

question_html: In the Surrender of Shares method of internal reconstruction, what happens to the surrendered shares that are NOT re-issued to debenture holders or creditors?
option_a: They are held as treasury shares by the company
option_b: They are cancelled by transferring them to the Reconstruction Account
option_c: They are sold on the stock exchange to raise funds
option_d: They are returned to the original shareholders
explanation_html:
In the Surrender of Shares method:
1. Existing shares are sub-divided into smaller denominations
2. Shareholders surrender some of their shares to the company
3. Surrendered shares are re-issued to debenture holders and creditors in lieu of their claims (reducing these liabilities)
4. Unutilised surrendered shares (not re-issued) are cancelled by transferring them to the Reconstruction Account ‚Äî this represents the sacrifice by shareholders that goes towards writing off accumulated losses and fictitious assets.

As seen in Illustration 7 (Revise Limited): Equity Share Capital (₹100) Dr. / To Share Surrender A/c / To Equity Share Capital (₹10) ‚Äî and Share Surrender A/c Dr. / To Reconstruction A/c (for the balance not re-issued).

chapter_id: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
question_html: P Ltd. acquires 80% of S Ltd. on 31st March 20X1 by paying ₹ 1,000. S Ltd.'s net worth on that date = ₹ 1,000 (Share Capital ₹ 700, Reserves ₹ 300). What is the Goodwill/(Capital Reserve) on consolidation?
option_b: Capital Reserve ₹ 200 (P Ltd. paid less than net worth)
option_c: Goodwill ₹ 200 (cost ₹1,000 exceeds P Ltd.'s 80% share of net worth ₹800)
option_d: Nil ‚Äî no goodwill or capital reserve arises
explanation_html:
Under AS 21, Goodwill = Cost of Investment – Parent's share in equity of subsidiary at date of investment.

Net worth of S Ltd. = ₹700 + ₹300 = ₹1,000.
P Ltd.'s share (80%) = 80% × ₹1,000 = ₹800.
Cost of Investment = ₹1,000.
Goodwill = ₹1,000 – ₹800 = ₹200.

Key insight: Even though total net worth equals the cost paid, P Ltd. acquired only 80% — so only 80% of the net worth is the "intrinsic value" being acquired. The excess paid (₹200) over P Ltd.'s proportionate share represents goodwill. The remaining 20% (₹200) belongs to Minority Interest.

question_html: As per the Debt-Equity Ratio Test under the Companies Act, 2013, what is the maximum debt that can be owed by a company after the buy-back?
option_a: Equal to the total paid-up capital and free reserves (1:1 ratio)
option_b: Not more than twice the total paid-up capital and free reserves after buy-back (2:1)
option_c: Not more than three times the total paid-up capital (3:1)
option_d: Not more than 50% of total assets
explanation_html:
The Debt-Equity Ratio Test under Section 68(2)(e) states: The ratio of the debt owed by the company (both secured and unsecured) after such buy-back should NOT be more than TWICE the total of its paid-up capital and its free reserves.

In ratio form: Debt : Equity (post buy-back) ‚â§ 2:1

Note: Debt includes both long-term and short-term debt. Free reserves include securities premium for this purpose. Capital Redemption Reserve (created on buy-back) is NOT a free reserve and is excluded from this computation. The Central Government may prescribe a higher ratio for specific classes of companies.

question_html: A partnership firm's governing statute does not require compliance with Accounting Standards. When the auditor of such a firm discharges attest functions, the mandatory status of Accounting Standards implies that the auditor must:
option_a: Refuse to sign the audit report if any deviation from Accounting Standards exists
option_b: Examine whether financial statements comply with applicable AS and make adequate disclosures in his report about any deviations
option_c: Prepare revised financial statements in compliance with AS before signing the report
option_d: Ignore the Accounting Standards entirely since the statute does not mandate compliance
explanation_html: Where the statute governing the enterprise does not require compliance with Accounting Standards (e.g., a partnership firm), the mandatory status of an AS implies that members of ICAI, in discharging their attest functions, are required to examine whether financial statements are prepared in compliance with applicable AS. In the event of any deviation, they have the duty to make adequate disclosures in their reports so that users are aware. The responsibility for preparing financial statements and making adequate disclosure rests with management. The auditor's responsibility is to form his opinion and report on such financial statements. The auditor cannot refuse to sign the report merely on grounds of AS deviation, nor is it his duty to revise the financial statements.

question_html: As per AS 17, the 75% Overall Test requires that:
option_a: At least 75% of total enterprise assets must be covered by reportable segments
option_b: At least 75% of total enterprise profit must be covered by reportable segments
option_c: At least 75% of total enterprise revenue (external sales only) must be attributable to reportable segments; additional segments are added if needed even if they do not meet the 10% tests
option_d: At least 75% of total enterprise revenue (external and internal) must be attributable to reportable segments after applying the 10% tests
explanation_html: The 75% Overall Test under AS 17 states: if total external revenue attributable to reportable segments constitutes less than 75% of the total enterprise revenue (external), additional segments must be identified as reportable segments ‚Äî even if they do not meet the 10% thresholds ‚Äî until at least 75% of total enterprise revenue is included in reportable segments. Key points: (i) The 75% test uses external revenue only, not inter-segment. (ii) The 10% revenue test uses both external and internal revenue. This distinction is frequently tested. The purpose of the 75% test is to ensure sufficient coverage of the enterprise in segment disclosures.

question_html: As per AS 29, a Restructuring Provision should include:
option_a: Retraining costs of continuing staff and marketing costs for new product lines
option_b: Investment in new distribution networks after restructuring
option_c: Only the direct expenditures necessarily entailed by the restructuring and not associated with ongoing activities of the enterprise
option_d: All costs expected to be incurred from the date the restructuring plan is announced
explanation_html:
As per AS 29, a restructuring provision should include only the direct expenditures arising from the restructuring, which are those that are both:
(a) Necessarily entailed by the restructuring; and
(b) Not associated with the ongoing activities of the enterprise.

A restructuring provision does NOT include:
‚Ä¢ Retraining or relocating continuing staff
‚Ä¢ Marketing costs
‚Ä¢ Investment in new systems and distribution networks

These relate to the future conduct of the business and are not present obligations for restructuring at the balance sheet date. Also, no provision can be made for a sale of an operation until there is a binding sale agreement. Future operating losses up to the date of restructuring are also excluded from the provision.

question_html: What will be the carrying amount of investment in the separate financial statement of G Ltd. as on 31.3.2024?
explanation_html:
In the separate financial statements of G Ltd., investment in Build Ltd. (an associate) is accounted under AS 13 (Accounting for Investments) ‚Äî at cost less any dividend received that constitutes a return of investment (reduction in cost).

Investment cost on 1.7.2023 = ‚Çπ14,00,000.

Build Ltd. paid dividend of ‚Çπ1,50,000 on 15.7.2023 for the year ending 31.3.2023. G Ltd.'s share = 35% √ó ‚Çπ1,50,000 = ‚Çπ52,500.

This dividend relates to pre-acquisition profits (the year ending 31.3.2023 ‚Äî before G Ltd. acquired the shares on 1.7.2023). Under AS 13, dividend received out of pre-acquisition profits reduces the cost of investment.

Carrying amount = ‚Çπ14,00,000 ‚àí ‚Çπ52,500 = ‚Çπ13,47,500.

Note: Equity method (with share of post-acquisition profit) applies only in Consolidated Financial Statements, not in separate FS.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: The Framework identifies how many broad groups of users of financial statements?
option_b: Six
option_c: Seven
option_d: Eight
explanation_html: As per the Framework, there are seven broad groups of users of financial statements: Investors, Employees, Lenders, Suppliers and other trade creditors, Customers, Governments and their agencies, and Public. All these groups use financial statements to satisfy some of their information needs for making economic decisions.

question_html: What will be the carrying amount of investment in Separate Financial Statements of Sun Limited as on 31.03.2024?
explanation_html:
In separate financial statements, investment in an associate is accounted under AS 13 (Accounting for Investments) ‚Äî at cost less dividend received that is a return of investment (pre-acquisition dividend).

Investment cost = ‚Çπ5,00,000 on 01.07.2023.

Moon Ltd. declared dividend of ‚Çπ80,000 for FY 2022-23 on 15.09.2023. Sun Ltd.'s share = 40% √ó ‚Çπ80,000 = ‚Çπ32,000.

This dividend is for the year ending 31.3.2023 ‚Äî before Sun acquired shares on 01.07.2023. It relates to pre-acquisition profits ‚Üí reduces cost of investment.

Carrying amount in separate FS = ‚Çπ5,00,000 ‚àí ‚Çπ32,000 = ‚Çπ4,68,000.

Note: The dividend declared for FY 2023-24 (‚Çπ90,000) was declared on 15.09.2024 ‚Äî after the balance sheet date of 31.03.2024. It does not affect the 31.3.2024 carrying value.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: Rau Ltd. purchased a plant for US$ 1,00,000 on 1st February 20X1, payable after 3 months. The company entered into a forward contract @ ₹ 49.15 per dollar. Spot rate on 1st Feb = ₹ 48.85. The contract is NOT for trading/speculation. How should the premium be recognised?
option_a: Loss of ₹ 30,000 recognised entirely in the year ended 31st March 20X1
option_b: Loss of ₹ 30,000 recognised entirely in the year following 31st March 20X1
option_c: Loss amortised over 3 months: ₹ 20,000 recognised in FY ended 31st March 20X1; ₹ 10,000 in the following year
option_d: Premium is ignored since the contract is not for speculation
explanation_html:
For a forward exchange contract not intended for trading or speculation (i.e., a hedging contract), AS 11 requires:

Premium/Discount: The difference between forward rate (₹49.15) and spot rate (₹48.85) = ₹0.30 per dollar. Total premium (loss) = ₹0.30 × 1,00,000 = ₹30,000. This should be amortised as expense over the life of the contract (3 months).

Contract period = 3 months (1st Feb to 30th Apr 20X1). Of these, 2 months fall in FY 20X1 (Feb and March) and 1 month in FY 20X2.

FY 20X1: (₹30,000 √∑ 3) × 2 = ₹20,000
FY 20X2: (₹30,000 √∑ 3) × 1 = ₹10,000

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: A piece of information is said to be 'material' if:
option_a: It relates to a large monetary amount in the financial statements
option_b: Its misstatement (omission or erroneous statement) can influence economic decisions of a user taken on the basis of financial information
option_c: It is mandatorily required to be disclosed under law
option_d: It appears in the Balance Sheet rather than the Profit and Loss Account
explanation_html: As per the Framework, a piece of information is said to be material if its misstatement (i.e., omission or erroneous statement) can influence economic decisions of a user taken on the basis of the financial information. Materiality depends on the size AND nature of the item or error, judged in the specific circumstances of its misstatement. Importantly, materiality provides a threshold or cut-off point rather than being a primary qualitative characteristic which the information must have if it is to be useful.

question_html: As per Section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013, accounting standards applicable to companies in India are prescribed by the:
option_b: Central Government on the recommendation of ICAI and in consultation with NFRA
option_c: SEBI after consulting the RBI
option_d: Ministry of Finance directly
explanation_html: As per Section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Central Government may prescribe standards of accounting as recommended by the ICAI (constituted under section 3 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949), in consultation with and after examination of recommendations made by NFRA. Thus, the final authority lies with the Central Government, acting on the recommendation of ICAI and after NFRA review.

question_html: How should the interest on income tax refunds should be disclosed in the Cash Flows Statement:
option_b: Cash flows from Investing Activities
option_c: Cash flows from Financing Activities
option_d: No disclosure in Cash Flow Statement
explanation_html:
As per AS 3 (Cash Flow Statements), interest received is generally classified under Investing Activities for non-financial enterprises.

Interest on income tax refund is essentially interest income received from the government ‚Äî it is classified under Cash flows from Investing Activities since it represents a return on amounts deposited with tax authorities (analogous to interest on deposits/investments).

question_html: As per AS 15, the seven components of Defined Benefit Costs to be recognised in the Statement of Profit and Loss include all of the following EXCEPT:
option_b: Expected return on plan assets and actuarial gains and losses
option_c: Employee's own contribution to the plan
option_d: Past service cost and effect of any curtailments or settlements
explanation_html:
AS 15 identifies seven components of defined benefit costs recognised in P&L:
(a) Current service cost
(b) Interest cost
(c) Expected return on plan assets (and reimbursement rights)
(d) Actuarial gains and losses (recognised immediately)
(e) Past service cost
(f) Effect of curtailments or settlements
(g) Extent to which the negative net defined benefit liability exceeds the economic benefit available

Employee's own contribution to the plan is NOT a component of the employer's defined benefit cost ‚Äî it reduces the employer's obligation or plan assets but is not an employer's expense in P&L. The standard prescribes accounting in the books of the employer, and employee contributions reduce the employer's net defined benefit liability.

question_html: All of the following costs are excluded while computing value of inventories except?
option_b: Allocated fixed production overheads based on normal capacity.
option_c: Abnormal wastage
option_d: Storage costs (which is necessary part of the production process)
explanation_html:
As per AS 2 (Valuation of Inventories), costs excluded from inventory include: selling and distribution costs, abnormal wastage, storage costs (unless necessary in production process), and administrative overheads unrelated to current location/condition.

Allocated fixed production overheads based on normal capacity are included in inventory cost ‚Äî they are part of conversion costs. The phrase "based on normal capacity" is key: overhead per unit is calculated at normal, not actual, capacity utilisation.

question_html: As per AS 3, the Cash Flow Statement is mandatory for which of the following companies under the Companies Act, 2013?
option_b: All companies except One Person Companies, Small Companies, Dormant Companies, and start-up private companies
option_c: Only listed companies and companies with turnover exceeding ₹ 500 crore
option_d: All companies except those with paid-up share capital below ₹ 50 lakhs
explanation_html: Under Section 129 of the Companies Act, 2013, the financial statements with respect to One Person Company, Small Company, Dormant Company, and private company (if such a private company is a start-up) may not include the Cash Flow Statement. The start-up private company exemption was added via Notification dated 13th June, 2017 under Section 462 of the Companies Act, 2013. All other companies are mandatorily required to prepare Cash Flow Statements. For non-corporate entities, AS 3 is mandatory only for Non-SMCs (and Level I entities for non-corporates); it is only encouraged for others.

question_html: What is the maximum number of shares that can be bought back according to the Resources Test?
option_b: 42,500 shares
option_c: 37,500 shares
option_d: 54,375 shares
explanation_html:
The Resources Test limits buy-back to 25% of total paid-up capital and free reserves.

Free Reserves = Revenue Reserve + Securities Premium + Profit & Loss Account = ‚Çπ 23,50,000 + ‚Çπ 2,50,000 + ‚Çπ 2,00,000 = ‚Çπ 28,00,000. (Infrastructure Development Reserve is a statutory reserve ‚Äî not freely available.)

Total paid-up capital and free reserves = ‚Çπ 17,00,000 + ‚Çπ 28,00,000 = ‚Çπ 45,00,000

Maximum buy-back amount = 25% √ó ‚Çπ 45,00,000 = ‚Çπ 11,25,000

Maximum shares = ‚Çπ 11,25,000 √∑ ‚Çπ 30 (buy-back price) = 37,500 shares

question_html: AB Ltd. has received a legal notice from a customer claiming damages of ₹ 5,00,000. The company's lawyers advise that it is NOT probable yet that resources will be required to settle the claim. According to AS 29, the correct accounting treatment is:
option_a: Create a provision of ₹ 5,00,000 since the amount is known
option_b: Disclose as a contingent liability in the notes to financial statements
option_c: No provision, no disclosure since the likelihood is not probable
option_d: Create a provision of ₹ 2,50,000 (50% probability adjustment)
explanation_html:
When an outflow of resources is not probable (i.e., it is possible but not more likely than not), AS 29 requires disclosure as a contingent liability in the notes to the financial statements ‚Äî as long as the possibility of outflow is not remote.

The three-level decision framework under AS 29:
1. Probable outflow ‚Üí Recognise a provision
2. Possible outflow (not probable) ‚Üí Disclose as contingent liability
3. Remote outflow ‚Üí Neither provision nor disclosure

In AB Ltd.'s case, since lawyers advise the claim is 'not probable yet' (but the possibility is not stated as remote), the appropriate treatment is disclosure as a contingent liability. Option (c) would be correct only if the possibility of outflow were remote.

question_html: As per the requirements of AS 3, 'Cash Flow Statements', how the amount for purchase of machinery should be presented:
option_a: ‚Çπ 10 lakhs as 'Cash flows from Investing Activities' and ‚Çπ 30,000 will simply be booked in profit and loss with no presentation if Cash Flow Statement.
option_b: ‚Çπ 10.30 lakhs as 'Cash flows from Investing Activities' as entire amount is spend on purchase of machinery.
option_c: ‚Çπ 10 lakhs as 'Cash flows from Investing Activities' and ‚Çπ 30,000 as 'Cash flows from Financing Activities'.
option_d: ‚Çπ 10.30 lakhs as 'Cash flows from Financing Activities' as the machinery has been purchased on finance.
explanation_html:
As per AS 3 (Cash Flow Statements):

  • The cost of the machinery (‚Çπ10 lakhs) represents an acquisition of PPE ‚Äî classified as Investing Activities (outflow).
  • The interest component (‚Çπ30,000) embedded in the deferred payment instalments represents a financing cost ‚Äî classified as Financing Activities (outflow).

These two components are separated and presented in their respective categories. The principal of the deferred payment (‚Çπ6 lakhs) is part of the ‚Çπ10 lakhs asset cost shown as investing, while the interest (‚Çπ30,000) is financing.

question_html: Under AS 14 (Purchase Method), how are Statutory Reserves of the transferor company (e.g., Investment Allowance Reserve, Export Profit Reserve) treated in the books of the transferee company?
option_a: They are merged with the transferee's General Reserve
option_b: They are completely written off since purchase amalgamation doesn't preserve identity of reserves
option_c: They retain their identity ‚Äî credited to Statutory Reserve; debit to 'Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve' (shown as a negative balance in Reserves and Surplus)
option_d: They are treated as capital reserve of the transferee company
explanation_html:
In a purchase amalgamation, normally the identity of reserves of the transferor is NOT preserved. However, AS 14 makes an exception for statutory reserves (reserves maintained under the requirements of law, e.g., Investment Allowance Reserve, Export Profit Reserve under Income Tax Act).

These must retain their identity. The journal entry is:
Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve A/c Dr. (negative reserve ‚Äî debit balance shown as deduction)
   To Statutory Reserve Cr.

The Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve is shown as a separate negative line item under Reserves and Surplus ‚Äî it cannot be set off against the Statutory Reserve. Once the statutory requirement period ends, both are reversed.

As seen in Illustration 8 (X Ltd.): Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve (300) is shown as a negative ₹300 thousands against Investment Allowance Reserve ₹100 thousands.

question_html: What is the key difference between Internal Reconstruction and External Reconstruction?
option_a: Internal reconstruction requires approval from SEBI; external reconstruction does not
option_b: In internal reconstruction, the existing company is NOT liquidated but its capital/debt structure is changed. In external reconstruction, the existing company is liquidated and a new company is formed with substantially the same shareholders
option_c: Internal reconstruction always involves creation of new shares; external reconstruction never does
option_d: Internal reconstruction is governed by AS 14; external reconstruction is governed by Section 66
explanation_html:
The fundamental distinction:

Internal Reconstruction: The existing company is NOT liquidated. Instead, its capital and debt structure is changed to bring it back to normalcy. The company continues its existence with a reorganized balance sheet. Governed by Sections 61 and 66 of the Companies Act, 2013. Requires Court/Tribunal confirmation.

External Reconstruction: The existing company IS liquidated to form a new company. The existing shareholders become shareholders of the new company. The business of the old company is transferred to the new company. Governed by Section 232 of the Companies Act, 2013. AS 14 classifies this as "Amalgamation in the nature of merger."

External reconstruction requires less time and court interference; internal reconstruction involves more legal procedures.

question_html: Zenith Pharmaceuticals Ltd. paid a penalty of ₹ 75,000 for breach of environmental regulations during the year. The company's total revenue was ₹ 850 crore. The accountant proposes to club this penalty with 'Legal and Professional Charges' in the financial statements since it is insignificant in amount. As per Accounting Standards, this treatment is:
option_a: Correct, because ₹ 75,000 is immaterial relative to ₹ 850 crore revenue and can be clubbed
option_b: Incorrect, because the penalty is a material item due to the information it conveys and must be disclosed separately
option_c: Correct, because materiality is always determined solely by the absolute size of the amount
option_d: Incorrect, because all expenses must always be disclosed as separate line items regardless of materiality
explanation_html: This question tests a critical concept ‚Äî materiality is NOT necessarily a function of size. Even though ₹ 75,000 appears insignificant compared to ₹ 850 crore revenue, it is a material item because of the information it conveys ‚Äî namely, that the company has breached a law. This is specifically illustrated in the ICAI material with the example of a penalty of ₹ 50,000 paid for breach of law. It is not appropriate to club penalties paid with legal charges. If an item is material (based on its information content), it should be shown separately. Option (a) incorrectly assumes materiality is only size-based. Option (d) is too absolute and incorrect.

question_html: As per the Companies Act, 2013, every buy-back must be completed within what time frame from the date of passing the special resolution (or board resolution)?
option_b: 12 months
option_c: 18 months
option_d: 3 months
explanation_html:
As per the Companies Act, 2013, every buy-back shall be completed within twelve months (1 year) from the date of passing the special resolution, or the resolution passed by the Board of Directors.

Additional time-related provisions:
‚Ä¢ No offer of buy-back shall be made within a period of one year from the date of closure of a previous buy-back offer (minimum gap between two buy-backs).
‚Ä¢ After completion of buy-back, the company shall not make further issue of same kind of shares within 6 months (except bonus issue, conversion of warrants/debentures/preference shares, sweat equity, stock options).
‚Ä¢ Return must be filed with ROC (and SEBI for listed companies) within 30 days of completion of buy-back.

question_html: After a scheme of capital reduction is approved by the Court/Tribunal, the words "and Reduced" are required to be added after the company's name in its Balance Sheet. For how long must the reduction in fixed asset values be disclosed in the Balance Sheet?
option_b: For 5 years
option_c: Indefinitely until the asset is disposed of
option_d: Only in the year of reconstruction
explanation_html:
The chapter specifies two important post-reconstruction balance sheet requirements:

(a) After the name of the company, the words "and Reduced" should be added only if the Court so orders.

(b) In case of fixed assets, the amount written off under the scheme of reconstruction must be shown for FIVE YEARS in the Balance Sheet. This disclosure ensures that users of financial statements are aware of the reconstruction and the write-down of asset values for a meaningful period of time, allowing them to understand the adjusted values in context.

This disclosure requirement is demonstrated in the Balance Sheets in the chapter ‚Äî e.g., in A & Co. Ltd.'s Balance Sheet, the PPE note shows "Appreciation under scheme of Reconstruction" and "Disposed of" separately.

question_html: Which of the following Accounting Standards is not applicable in its entirety to Small and Medium-sized Companies (SMCs) under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021?
option_b: AS 20 ‚Äì Earnings Per Share
option_c: AS 17 ‚Äì Segment Reporting
option_d: AS 24 ‚Äì Discontinuing Operations
explanation_html: For Small and Medium-sized Companies (SMCs) under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021, only AS 17 ‚Äì Segment Reporting is not applicable in its entirety. This is in contrast to the MSME (non-company entity) scheme where AS 3, AS 17, AS 20, and AS 24 are all not applicable in their entirety. For SMCs, AS 3 (Cash Flow Statements) is applicable in its entirety; AS 20 (EPS) is applicable but with a relaxation that diluted EPS need not be disclosed; and AS 24 (Discontinuing Operations) is applicable in its entirety. Students often confuse the MSME exemptions with SMC exemptions ‚Äî AS 17 is the only standard completely inapplicable to SMCs.

chapter_id: Accounting for Branches including foreign branches
question_html: In the Debtors method, XP Ltd. sent goods costing ₹50,000 to its Delhi branch. The branch sold the entire goods on credit at ₹62,000. No other transactions occurred. What is shown in the Branch Account?
option_a: Debit: Goods Sent ₹50,000; Credit: Cash Received ₹62,000; Profit ₹12,000
option_b: Debit: Goods Sent ₹50,000; Credit: Closing Debtors ₹62,000; Net Profit ₹12,000
option_c: Debit: Goods Sent ₹62,000; Credit: Profit ₹12,000
option_d: Debit: Goods Sent ₹50,000; Credit: Sales ₹62,000
explanation_html:
In the Debtors Method, the Branch Account in HO books shows:

Debit side:
‚Ä¢ Opening balance (Nil ‚Äî new branch)
‚Ä¢ Goods sent to branch: ₹50,000
‚Ä¢ Net Profit: ₹12,000 (balancing figure)

Credit side:
‚Ä¢ Closing Branch Assets ‚Äî Stock: Nil (all sold), Debtors: ₹62,000

Closing Debtors = ₹62,000 (entire goods sold on credit, no cash collected yet)
Profit = ₹62,000 – ₹50,000 = ₹12,000

The Branch Account is debited with cost of goods sent (₹50,000) and credited with closing assets (₹62,000 debtors). The balancing figure on the debit side = profit ₹12,000, transferred to General P&L A/c.

question_html: After completing a buy-back, a company announces to issue new equity shares. As per Section 68(7) of the Companies Act, 2013, for how long after completing buy-back is the company prohibited from making a fresh issue of the same kind of shares?
option_b: 12 months
option_c: 6 months (except bonus issue, conversion of warrants/debentures/preference shares, sweat equity, or stock options)
option_d: 1 month
explanation_html:
Section 68(7) states: After completing buy-back, the company shall not make further issue of the same kind of shares within a period of SIX MONTHS, except by way of:
‚Ä¢ Bonus issue
‚Ä¢ Discharge of subsisting obligations such as conversion of warrants
‚Ä¢ Stock option scheme
‚Ä¢ Sweat equity
‚Ä¢ Conversion of preference shares or debentures into equity shares

This restriction prevents the company from immediately undoing the buy-back by issuing new shares of the same kind. It ensures the buy-back genuinely reduces the number of outstanding shares for a meaningful period. The 6-month lock-in period applies from the date of completion of buy-back.

question_html: Which of the following Accounting Standards was given the date of applicability of 1st April 2016 (i.e., the most recently made applicable AS among all 27 ASs)?
option_b: AS 28 ‚Äì Impairment of Assets
option_c: AS 10 ‚Äì Property, Plant and Equipment (Revised)
option_d: AS 29 ‚Äì Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
explanation_html:
As per the list of Accounting Standards with their respective dates of applicability:
- AS 10 (Property, Plant and Equipment ‚Äì Revised) has a date of applicability of 01/04/2016, making it the most recently applicable standard
- AS 22 is applicable from 01/04/2006
- AS 28 is applicable from 01/04/2008
- AS 29 is applicable from 01/04/2004
Thus, AS 10 (Revised) with applicability from 1st April 2016 is the correct answer.

question_html: What is the minimum equity Kumar Ltd. needs to maintain after buyback, according to the Debt Equity Ratio Test?
explanation_html:
Debt Equity Ratio Test: Post buy-back debt <= 2 x equity.

Minimum equity = Loan Funds / 2 = ‚Çπ42,00,000 / 2 = ‚Çπ21,00,000.

Note: Revaluation Reserve (‚Çπ6,20,000) is excluded from free reserves for this calculation ‚Äî it represents unrealised gains and is not distributable.

question_html: For corporate entities (companies not following Ind AS), the classification for applicability of Accounting Standards under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021 is into which two categories?
option_b: Listed Companies and Unlisted Companies
option_c: Small and Medium-sized Companies (SMCs) and companies other than SMCs (Non-SMCs)
option_d: Public Companies and Private Companies
explanation_html: For corporate entities (companies not following Ind AS), the Central Government issued the 'Criteria for Classification of Entities and Applicability of Accounting Standards' under which companies are classified into two levels: (i) Small and Medium-sized Companies (SMCs) as defined in the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021, and (ii) companies other than SMCs (Non-SMCs). Non-SMCs must comply with all Accounting Standards in their entirety, while certain exemptions/relaxations have been given to SMCs. The MSME/Large entity classification applies to non-company entities under the ICAI announcement ‚Äî this is a critical distinction students must not confuse.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: The amount of Cash Flow from operating activity is:
explanation_html:
Under AS 3 (Cash Flow Statements), operating activities include cash from trade and operations. For Jay Ltd. on 1st April, 2023:

Operating cash inflows:

  • Interest received on advances to suppliers: ‚Çπ 3,000 (operating activity ‚Äî advances are trade-related)
  • Cash recovered from insolvent debtor: 40% √ó ‚Çπ 40,000 = ‚Çπ 16,000

Operating cash outflows:

  • Taxation paid: ‚Çπ 14,000

Net cash from operating activities = ‚Çπ 3,000 + ‚Çπ 16,000 ‚àí ‚Çπ 14,000 = ‚Çπ 5,000.

question_html: Top & Top Limited set up a factory in a backward area and received ₹ 10 crore (20% of ₹ 50 crore investment) as Central Investment Subsidy ‚Äî a grant given with reference to total capital investment, with no repayment expected and no condition to purchase specific assets. The company wants to credit this to P&L to reduce losses. Is this correct under AS 12?
option_a: Correct ‚Äî the subsidy is a revenue grant and should be credited to P&L
option_b: Incorrect ‚Äî grants of the nature of promoters' contribution must be credited to Capital Reserve, not P&L or deferred income
option_c: Correct ‚Äî the company may choose to credit to either P&L or Capital Reserve
option_d: Incorrect ‚Äî such grants must be deducted from the cost of assets
explanation_html:
AS 12 distinguishes grants by their nature:

Grants in the nature of Promoters' Contribution: Given with reference to total investment in an undertaking or by way of contribution towards its total capital outlay (e.g., Central Investment Subsidy Scheme), with no repayment ordinarily expected. Such grants are treated as Capital Reserve which can be neither distributed as dividend nor considered as deferred income.

The subsidy is neither related to a specific fixed asset (no condition to buy specific asset) nor related to revenue. It is a promoters'-contribution-type grant. Therefore, treating it as revenue in P&L is incorrect. It must be credited to Capital Reserve.

question_html: The ICAI has so far issued 29 Accounting Standards. However, the number of effective Accounting Standards currently in force is:
explanation_html: The ICAI has issued 29 Accounting Standards in total. However, AS 6 on 'Depreciation Accounting' was withdrawn upon revision of AS 10 'Property, Plant and Equipment', and AS 8 on 'Accounting for Research and Development' was withdrawn consequent to the issuance of AS 26 on 'Intangible Assets'. Thus, effectively there are 27 Accounting Standards in force at present.

question_html: What will be the treatment of legal cost and claim for legal action commenced by Mr. Ravi Kumar in the Books of Kay Ltd. as on 31 March, 2024 as per AS 29?
option_b: Create a Provision for ‚Çπ 5,00,000
option_c: Create a Provision for ‚Çπ 45,000 and make a disclosure of contingent liability of ‚Çπ 5,000,000
option_d: Make a disclosure of contingent liability of ‚Çπ 5,45,000
explanation_html:
Under AS 29 (Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets):

  • A provision is recognised when: (i) there is a present obligation as a result of a past event, (ii) it is probable that an outflow of resources will be required, and (iii) a reliable estimate can be made.
  • A contingent liability is disclosed (not recognised) when an outflow is possible but not probable, or the amount cannot be reliably estimated.

Legal cost (‚Çπ 45,000): This is to be incurred irrespective of the outcome ‚Äî it is a certain obligation. A provision of ‚Çπ 45,000 must be created.

Settlement amount (‚Çπ 50,00,000): The lawyers advise "it is not remote yet that resources may be required" ‚Äî meaning it is possible but not probable. This is a contingent liability ‚Äî disclose ‚Çπ 50,00,000 in notes, do not provide for it.

question_html: As per Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013, reduction of share capital can be done in which of the following ways?
option_a: (a) Extinguishing/reducing liability on unpaid amount; (b) Paying off excess paid-up capital; (c) Cancelling paid-up capital lost or unrepresented by available assets
option_b: Only by paying off excess paid-up capital to shareholders
option_c: Only by reducing nominal value of shares
option_d: Only when the company has no reserves available
explanation_html:
Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 permits reduction of share capital in the following THREE ways:

(a) Extinguishing or reducing the liability of shareholders in respect of unpaid amount on shares (e.g., a ₹10 partly-paid share becomes fully paid at ₹7.50 by cancelling the ₹2.50 unpaid liability);

(b) Paying off any paid-up share capital which is in excess of requirements (e.g., returning ₹2 per share to shareholders, reducing ₹10 fully paid to ₹8);

(c) Cancelling any paid-up share capital which is lost or not represented by available assets (most common in loss-making companies ‚Äî writing down capital to match the depleted assets).

Reduction requires a special resolution and confirmation by the Tribunal.

question_html: Under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021, what is the specific relaxation given to SMCs in respect of AS 20 ‚Äì Earnings Per Share?
option_a: SMCs are fully exempt from AS 20 and need not disclose any EPS figure
option_b: SMCs are exempt only from Basic EPS disclosure; diluted EPS must still be disclosed
option_c: SMCs are exempt from disclosing diluted earnings per share (both including and excluding extraordinary items)
option_d: SMCs must disclose both Basic and Diluted EPS but using a simplified computation method
explanation_html: For SMCs under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021, AS 20 (Earnings Per Share) is applicable, but with a specific relaxation: disclosure of diluted earnings per share (both including and excluding extraordinary items) is exempted for SMCs. SMCs are still required to disclose Basic EPS. This relaxation is logical because diluted EPS computations involve complex adjustments for potential dilutive instruments like convertible debentures, ESOPs etc., which are typically not relevant for SMCs. Note: For MSMEs (non-company entities), AS 20 is not applicable in its entirety ‚Äî this is a key distinction between the two frameworks.

question_html: In the Cash Flow Statement as per AS 3, the interest income of ‚Çπ 20 Lacs earned fixed deposits with bank will be disclosed as:
option_b: Cash Flow from Investing Activities
option_c: Cash Flow from Financing Activities
option_d: Non-cash Items
explanation_html:
For a financial enterprise, interest received ‚Äî including on fixed deposits ‚Äî is classified as Operating Activities per AS 3, since investing surplus funds is ancillary to the main finance business.

(For a manufacturing company, FD interest would go to Investing Activities. The classification differs based on the nature of the enterprise.)

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html:
Under Physical Capital Maintenance at Current Costs, using the following data:
Opening: 6,000 units at ‚Çπ2 per unit (Opening Equity = ‚Çπ12,000)
All sold at ‚Çπ3 per unit; Drawings = ‚Çπ6,000
Closing price of product = ‚Çπ2.50 per unit
What is the Retained Profit/(Loss)?
option_b: ‚Çπ3,000 profit
explanation_html:
Physical Capital Maintenance at Current Costs:
Closing Equity at current cost = Cash remaining = ‚Çπ18,000 ‚Äì ‚Çπ6,000 = ‚Çπ12,000

Opening Equity restated at current cost (specific index = 125):
= (‚Çπ12,000/100) √ó 125 = 6,000 units √ó ‚Çπ2.50 = ‚Çπ15,000

Retained Profit = Closing Equity ‚Äì Opening Equity restated
= ‚Çπ12,000 ‚Äì ‚Çπ15,000 = (‚Çπ3,000) Loss

This indicates the trader failed to maintain physical capital. The ‚Çπ12,000 is insufficient to buy 6,000 units at ‚Çπ2.50. Drawings should have been restricted to ‚Çπ3,000 (‚Çπ6,000 ‚Äì ‚Çπ3,000).

question_html: By using the Shares Outstanding Test the number of shares that can be bought back
explanation_html:
Shares Outstanding Test: Buy-back cannot exceed 25% of total paid-up equity capital in a financial year.

Total paid-up equity shares = ‚Çπ12,50,000 / ‚Çπ10 = 1,25,000 shares.

25% of 1,25,000 = 31,250 shares.

question_html: Under AS 14, which of the following is a condition for an amalgamation to qualify as amalgamation in the nature of merger?
option_a: Shareholders holding at least 75% of equity shares of the transferor company become equity shareholders of the transferee company
option_b: Consideration may be paid in equity shares, preference shares, or cash
option_c: Assets and liabilities of the transferor may be revalued to fair values before incorporation
option_d: Shareholders holding not less than 90% of the face value of equity shares of the transferor become equity shareholders of the transferee company
explanation_html:
AS 14 specifies ALL FIVE conditions that must be satisfied for an amalgamation to qualify as a merger:
(i) All assets and liabilities of the transferor become assets and liabilities of the transferee;
(ii) Shareholders holding not less than 90% of the face value of equity shares of the transferor (excluding shares already held by transferee) become equity shareholders of the transferee;
(iii) Consideration is discharged wholly by issue of equity shares (cash only for fractional shares);
(iv) Business of the transferor is intended to be continued;
(v) No adjustment to book values of assets/liabilities except for uniformity of accounting policies.

Options (a), (b), (c) are conditions for purchase, not merger. The 90% threshold and equity-shares-only consideration are critical merger conditions.

question_html: A company has a warranty provision of ₹ 2,400 as at 31st March, 20X1 (from previous question). The required provision as at 31st March, 20X2 (post Oct 20X1 invoice of ₹ 1,35,000) is ₹ 4,850. What is the amount to be debited to the Profit and Loss Account for the year ended 31st March, 20X2?
option_b: ₹ 2,400 (opening provision reversed and new provision created)
option_d: ₹ 7,250 (total of both year provisions)
explanation_html:
The P&L charge for the year = Increase in provision = Closing provision – Opening provision = ₹4,850 – ₹2,400 = ₹2,450.

Note at 31-3-20X2:
‚Ä¢ Invoice 11th Feb 20X0 (₹60,000): Warranty of 2 years expired by 11th Feb 20X2 ‚Äî no provision
‚Ä¢ Invoice 25th Dec 20X0 (₹40,000): Remaining warranty ‚âà 8.8 months < 1 year ‚Üí 2% × ₹40,000 = ₹800
‚Ä¢ Invoice 04th Oct 20X1 (₹1,35,000): Remaining ‚âà 18 months > 1 year ‚Üí 3% × ₹1,35,000 = ₹4,050
Total = ₹800 + ₹4,050 = ₹4,850

The charge to P&L = incremental provision of ₹2,450 (not the full ₹4,850).

question_html: As per AS 12, when a government grant becomes refundable due to non-fulfilment of conditions, it is treated as:
option_a: A change in accounting estimate, recognised prospectively
option_b: A prior period item under AS 5
option_c: An extraordinary item under AS 5
option_d: A contingent liability disclosed in the notes
explanation_html:
AS 12 specifically states: Government grants sometimes become refundable because certain conditions are not fulfilled and are treated as an extraordinary item (AS 5).

The refund is an unusual event that is clearly distinct from ordinary activities ‚Äî it is not a routine transaction. Therefore, it qualifies as an extraordinary item under AS 5 and should be disclosed separately in the Statement of Profit and Loss. The treatment for the refund amount depends on the type of grant:
‚Ä¢ Revenue grant: applied against unamortised deferred credit first; excess to P&L
‚Ä¢ Asset-related grant: increases book value of asset (or reduces deferred income)
‚Ä¢ Promoters' contribution: reduces the Capital Reserve

question_html: Which of the following Accounting Standards is applicable from the earliest date (i.e., oldest applicability date) among the options given?
option_b: AS 1 ‚Äì Disclosure of Accounting Policies
option_c: AS 4 ‚Äì Contingencies and Events Occurring after the Balance Sheet Date (Revised)
option_d: AS 12 ‚Äì Accounting for Government Grants
explanation_html:
As per the list of Accounting Standards with their dates of applicability:
- AS 1 ‚Äì Applicable from 01/04/1993
- AS 2 (Revised) ‚Äì Applicable from 01/04/1999
- AS 4 (Revised) ‚Äì Applicable from 01/04/1998
- AS 12 ‚Äì Applicable from 01/04/1994
Thus, AS 1 (01/04/1993) has the earliest date of applicability among these options. Note that AS 9 (Revenue Recognition) is also applicable from 01/04/1993, but that is not among the given options.

question_html: In the context of AS 21 (Consolidated Financial Statements), AS 23 (Accounting for Investments in Associates in CFS), and AS 25 (Interim Financial Reporting) as applicable to Non-company entities ‚Äî which of the following statements is correct?
option_a: These standards require all non-company entities to mandatorily prepare and present consolidated financial statements and interim financial reports
option_b: These standards do not require a non-company entity to present consolidated financial statements or interim financial report; they are applicable only if the entity is required or elects to prepare and present such statements
option_c: These standards are completely exempt for MSMEs but fully applicable to Large entities regardless of whether they elect to prepare CFS
option_d: AS 21 and AS 23 require consolidated financial statements only from those non-company entities with turnover exceeding ₹ 250 crore
explanation_html: As per the ICAI material, AS 21 (Consolidated Financial Statements), AS 23 (Investments in Associates in CFS), AS 27 (Financial Reporting of Interests in Joint Ventures ‚Äî to the extent of CFS requirements), and AS 25 (Interim Financial Reporting) do not require a non-company entity to present consolidated financial statements and interim financial report, respectively. These standards are applicable only if a non-company entity is required or elects to prepare and present consolidated financial statements or interim financial report. There is no automatic mandatory obligation. This is different from the position for listed companies where regulators like SEBI mandate preparation of CFS and quarterly results. Turnover-based triggers do not determine CFS applicability.

question_html:
Money Ltd. is a non-financial company. Under AS 3, how should the following be classified in its Cash Flow Statement?
(i) Loans given to employees and interest earned thereon
(ii) Loans given to subsidiary companies and interest earned thereon
(iii) Dividends paid to shareholders
option_b: (i) Operating; (ii) Investing; (iii) Financing
option_c: (i) Operating; (ii) Operating; (iii) Financing
option_d: (i) Investing; (ii) Financing; (iii) Operating
explanation_html:
As per AS 3, for a non-financial enterprise:

(i) Loans to employees and interest earned: These are operating cash flows for all enterprises (including non-financial). Employee-related advances are considered part of operating activities.

(ii) Loans to subsidiary companies and interest earned: These are investing cash flows for ALL enterprises (both financial and non-financial). The subsidiary relationship creates a specific rule overriding the general classification.

(iii) Dividends paid: Financing cash outflows for ALL enterprises.

Note: Loans to non-subsidiary entities in ordinary course by non-financial enterprises = Investing; Loans to suppliers = Operating; Advance from customers/interest paid to suppliers = Operating for non-financial enterprises.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: A company changed its method of depreciation from SLM to WDV, resulting in a deficiency (additional depreciation) for past years. The company debited this deficiency to the P&L as an extraordinary expense. Under AS 5, this treatment is:
option_a: Correct ‚Äî change in depreciation method is clearly distinct from ordinary activities
option_b: Incorrect ‚Äî change in depreciation method is a change in accounting estimate, not an extraordinary item; the deficiency should be treated as a normal current year expense
option_c: Correct ‚Äî a change in accounting policy must always be shown as an extraordinary item
option_d: Incorrect ‚Äî the deficiency should be treated as a prior period item
explanation_html:
Under AS 5:

Change in depreciation method = Change in accounting estimate (not extraordinary item, not prior period item).

A change in the method of charging depreciation is NOT an event clearly distinct from the ordinary activities of the enterprise ‚Äî depreciation is a routine expense related to PPE used in operations. Therefore, treating the deficiency as an extraordinary item is incorrect.

The change in depreciation method (an accounting estimate change) affects the current period and future periods prospectively. The deficiency should be recognised as a normal expense in the current period's P&L, classified under the same category as depreciation (ordinary activities). No retrospective restatement of prior periods is required.

question_html: Is the Company required to do any accounting for 1 year warranty provided by it:
option_a: No accounting treatment is required till some warranty claim is actually received by the Company.
option_b: As there exist a present obligation to provide warranty to customers for 1 year, the Company should estimate the amount that it may have to incur considering various factors including past trends and create a provision as per AS 29.
option_c: Accounting for claims will be done on cash basis i.e. expense will be recognised when expense is made.
option_d: As the Company is not charging separately for the warranty provided, there is no need to create any provision.
explanation_html:
As per AS 29 (Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets), a provision should be recognised when:

  • An entity has a present obligation as a result of a past event
  • It is probable that an outflow of resources will be required
  • A reliable estimate can be made

Suman Ltd. has a present obligation (warranty commitment made at point of sale). Even though warranty is free (not charged separately), the company must estimate warranty costs based on past trends and create a provision. The fact that warranty is not separately priced does not exempt the company from creating the provision.

question_html: By using the Resources Test determine the number of shares that can be bought back:
explanation_html:
Resources Test: Buy-back cannot exceed 25% of paid-up capital + free reserves (by value).

Free reserves = Securities Premium ‚Çπ2,50,000 + P&L ‚Çπ1,25,000 + Revenue Reserve ‚Çπ15,00,000 = ‚Çπ18,75,000.

Paid-up equity = ‚Çπ12,50,000. Total = ‚Çπ31,25,000.

25% of ‚Çπ31,25,000 = ‚Çπ7,81,250 (max buy-back value).

At ‚Çπ20/share: ‚Çπ7,81,250 / ‚Çπ20 = 39,062 shares.

question_html: How should the annual maintenance and updation expenses should be accounted for:
option_b: Should be recognised as a separate 'Intangible Asset'
option_c: Should be recognised as expense in Profit and Loss annually.
option_d: No accounting is required
explanation_html:
As per AS 26, subsequent expenditure on an intangible asset is recognised as an expense when incurred unless it can be demonstrated that the expenditure will enable the asset to generate future economic benefits in excess of the originally assessed standard of performance.

Annual maintenance and normal updation are routine costs to maintain the existing performance level ‚Äî they do not enhance the asset beyond its original capability. Therefore, they are recognised as expense in Profit and Loss each year.

question_html: Y Ltd. has 7,50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each. Intrinsic value per share of Y Ltd. = ₹20; intrinsic value per share of X Ltd. (transferee) = ₹30. Under the Intrinsic Value method, X Ltd. issues equity shares to Y Ltd.'s equity shareholders. How many shares of X Ltd. are issued and at what value?
option_a: 7,50,000 shares of X Ltd. at ₹30 each
option_b: 5,00,000 equity shares of X Ltd. at par value ₹10 each (i.e., 20/30 × 7,50,000 shares)
option_c: 11,25,000 shares of X Ltd. at ₹10 each
option_d: 5,00,000 shares at ₹30 each (market value)
explanation_html:
Under the Intrinsic Value/Share Exchange Method:

Exchange ratio = Intrinsic value per share of Y / Intrinsic value per share of X = ₹20/₹30

For every share of Y Ltd., ₹20/₹30 shares of X Ltd. are issued.
Total shares of X Ltd. = 7,50,000 × (20/30) = 5,00,000 equity shares of X Ltd.

AS 14 states: "the entry should be made at par value only." So entries are made at ₹10 (face value) per share, not at intrinsic value ₹30.

PC = 5,00,000 × ₹10 = ₹50,00,000 (recorded at par) per Illustration 3.

This is a classic example where the basis of computation is intrinsic value (for ratio) but recording is at par value.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: Why can the specific management talent or technical skill of an employee NOT be recognised as an asset of an enterprise?
option_a: Because human resources cannot be measured in monetary terms
option_b: Because the enterprise does not have sufficient control over such a resource
option_c: Because future economic benefits from employees are always uncertain
option_d: Because the Companies Act does not permit recognition of intangible assets
explanation_html: As per the Framework, a resource cannot be recognised as an asset if the control is not sufficient. The specific management or technical talent of an employee cannot be recognised as an asset because of insufficient control ‚Äî an employee can leave the organisation. However, when the control over a resource is protected by a legal right (e.g., copyright, patent), the resource can be recognised as an asset. Thus control, not just physical possession, determines asset recognition.

question_html: Accounting Standards cannot override which of the following?
option_a: Guidelines issued by SEBI for listed companies
option_b: Laws and local regulations applicable to the enterprise
option_c: Recommendations made by NFRA to the Central Government
option_d: Internal accounting policies adopted by the management of the enterprise
explanation_html: As explicitly stated in the ICAI study material on applicability of Accounting Standards, Accounting Standards cannot override laws and local regulations. They are nevertheless made mandatory from the dates notified by the MCA and are generally applicable to all enterprises, subject to certain exceptions. The implication of mandatory status of an Accounting Standard depends on whether the statute governing the enterprise concerned requires compliance. If a specific law (like the Banking Regulation Act, Electricity Act, Insurance Act) does not require disclosure of certain matters, financial statements are not treated as failing to give a true and fair view merely for that reason. AS can, however, guide management accounting policies and are typically more detailed than SEBI guidelines or NFRA recommendations on individual accounting treatments.

question_html: Which of the following is a key reason why having multiple different Accounting Standards across the world is considered against the public interest?
option_a: It increases the profits of multinational companies
option_b: It reduces the compliance burden on small companies
option_c: It creates confusion, encourages error, and may facilitate fraud when accounting for the same events produces different reported numbers
option_d: It leads to higher dividend payments to shareholders
explanation_html: As per the study material on the need for convergence towards global standards: Having a multiplicity of types of ASs around the world is against public interest. If accounting for the same events and information produces different reported numbers depending on the system of standards used, then accounting will be increasingly discredited in the eyes of users. It creates confusion, encourages error, and may facilitate fraud. The cure is to have a single set of global standards of the highest quality, set in the interest of public.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: Mohan started a business with ‚Çπ12,00,000 represented by 60,000 units at ‚Çπ20 each. He sold all units at ‚Çπ30 each during the year. What is the maximum amount he can withdraw to maintain Financial Capital at Historical Cost?
explanation_html:
Under Financial Capital Maintenance at Historical Cost:
Opening Equity = 60,000 units √ó ‚Çπ20 = ‚Çπ12,00,000
Closing Equity (after sales) = 60,000 √ó ‚Çπ30 = ‚Çπ18,00,000 (represented by cash)

Capital to be maintained = Opening Equity = ‚Çπ12,00,000
Maximum Drawings = Closing Equity ‚Äì Opening Equity
= ‚Çπ18,00,000 ‚Äì ‚Çπ12,00,000 = ‚Çπ6,00,000

If Mohan withdraws more than ‚Çπ6,00,000, retained profit becomes negative and capital is not maintained at historical cost.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
question_html: With respect to relationship between Companies, it can be said that:
option_a: Star Ltd. is associated of Sun Ltd.
option_b: Moon Ltd. and Star Ltd. both are associates of Sun Ltd.
option_c: Moon Ltd. is an associate of Sun Ltd.
option_d: Sun Ltd. is Parent of both Moon Ltd. and Star Ltd.
explanation_html:
Under AS 23 (Accounting for Investments in Associates in Consolidated Financial Statements), an associate is an enterprise in which the investor has significant influence but not control.

Sun Ltd. and Moon Ltd.: Sun holds 40% in Moon and can exercise significant influence ‚Üí Moon Ltd. is an associate of Sun Ltd.

Sun Ltd. and Star Ltd.: Moon holds 40% in Star. Sun holds Moon as an associate (not a subsidiary). Sun does not directly hold shares in Star, nor does it control Moon. Therefore, Star is an associate of Moon ‚Äî but not an associate of Sun Ltd. (Sun cannot exercise significant influence over Star through its associate Moon).

Sun Ltd. is NOT the parent of Moon or Star ‚Äî 40% does not constitute control (which requires >50% or other control indicators).

Therefore, only option (c) is correct: Moon Ltd. is an associate of Sun Ltd.

question_html: Securities Premium available for Buyback after redemption of Preference Shares
option_b: ‚Çπ 800 lakhs
option_c: Can't utilize securities premium for buyback
option_d: ‚Çπ 350 lakhs
explanation_html:
Securities Premium can be utilised for buy-back of shares under Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013.

For redemption of preference shares, Securities Premium is NOT used (premium on redemption is charged to free reserves or P&L, not Securities Premium in this context).

Since Securities Premium is not consumed in the preference share redemption process, the full ‚Çπ800 lakhs remains available for the equity buy-back.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html:
Under the Consistency assumption, an accounting policy can be changed if:

  • I. The change is required by a statute
  • II. The change is required by an Accounting Standard
  • III. The change leads to more appropriate presentation of financial statements
  • IV. The change will result in a higher reported profit
option_b: I, II and IV only
option_c: I, II and III only
option_d: All of I, II, III and IV
explanation_html:
As per the Framework, under the Consistency assumption, an accounting policy can be changed only if the change is required:
(i) By a statute, or
(ii) By an Accounting Standard, or
(iii) For more appropriate presentation of financial statements
A change in accounting policy merely to report higher profits is NOT a valid reason and would violate the Consistency assumption. Such changes would also be considered creative accounting.

question_html: As per AS 10, the cost of a machinery purchased at ₹ 1,18,000 inclusive of GST of ₹ 18,000, where the GST amount is fully available as input tax credit, is:
option_b: ₹ 1,00,000 (after deducting refundable tax)
explanation_html: As per AS 10, the cost of an item of PPE includes the purchase price including import duties and non-refundable purchase taxes, after deducting trade discounts and rebates. The key word is non-refundable ‚Äî refundable taxes (like GST input tax credit that is available) are deducted from the cost of the asset. Since the GST of ₹18,000 is fully available as input tax credit (i.e., it is refundable through the credit mechanism), it should be excluded from the cost of machinery. Therefore, cost of machinery = ₹1,18,000 – ₹18,000 = ₹1,00,000. Annual depreciation at 10% SLM = ₹10,000 p.a.

question_html: The fair value of plan assets of Zeleous Ltd. was ₹ 1,00,000 on 1st April, 20X1. During the year: benefits paid on 30th Sept = ₹ 19,000; contributions received on 30th Sept = ₹ 49,000. Fair value at 31st March, 20X2 = ₹ 1,50,000. Expected rate of return = 10.25% p.a. (compounding every 6 months = 5%). What is the actual return on plan assets?
explanation_html:
Actual return on plan assets = Closing FV – Opening FV – Contributions + Benefits paid

Closing FV: ₹1,50,000
Less: Opening FV: ₹1,00,000
Less: Contributions received: ₹49,000
= ₹1,49,000

₹1,50,000 – ₹1,49,000 = ₹1,000
Add: Benefits paid: ₹19,000
Actual return = ₹20,000

For comparison, expected return = ₹1,00,000 × 10.25% + ₹30,000 × 5% = ₹10,250 + ₹1,500 = ₹11,750.
Actuarial gain on plan assets = ₹20,000 – ₹11,750 = ₹8,250 (which, combined with ₹600 loss on obligation = net actuarial gain recognised in P&L).

chapter_id: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
question_html: Under AS 21, for preparation of Consolidated Financial Statements, if the parent and subsidiary use different accounting policies for the same type of transaction (e.g., different inventory valuation methods), what should be done?
option_a: Use the subsidiary's accounting policy for the consolidated statements
option_b: Use the parent's accounting policy; adjust the subsidiary's financial statements to align with the parent's policies before consolidation
option_c: Disclose the differences only ‚Äî no adjustment is required
option_d: Average the two accounting policies and apply to both entities
explanation_html:
AS 21 Para 20 states: "Consolidated financial statements shall be prepared using uniform accounting policies for like transactions and other events in similar circumstances."

If a subsidiary uses different accounting policies, appropriate adjustments are made to the subsidiary's financial statements when they are used in preparing consolidated financial statements. For example, if the subsidiary values inventory using weighted average and the parent uses FIFO, the subsidiary's inventory values must be restated to FIFO before consolidation.
