question_html: PQR Ltd. made a loss of ₹ 2,00,000 in FY 20X1. By end of 20X1, the company has reasonable certainty of future taxable income. Tax rate = 40%. Profits in FY 20X2 = ₹ 1,00,000 and FY 20X3 = ₹ 1,20,000 (carry-forward loss set off for tax). What deferred tax is recognised in FY 20X1, and what is the tax saving in FY 20X2?
option_a: FY 20X1: No deferred tax (only losses, not profits); FY 20X2: Current tax ₹40,000
option_b: FY 20X1: Deferred Tax Asset ₹ 80,000; FY 20X2: Current tax Nil; reversal of DTA ₹ 40,000
option_c: FY 20X1: Deferred Tax Asset ₹ 80,000; FY 20X2: DTA reversed ₹ 40,000 (P&L credit)
option_d: FY 20X1: Deferred Tax Liability ₹ 80,000; FY 20X2: DTL reversed ₹ 40,000
explanation_html:
FY 20X1: Loss of ₹2,00,000. Since the company has reasonable certainty of future taxable income, a Deferred Tax Asset (DTA) of ₹2,00,000 × 40% = ₹80,000 is recognised (as a tax effect of the carried-forward loss, which is a timing difference).

FY 20X2: Profit = ₹1,00,000. Since carry-forward loss is set off for tax purposes, taxable income = ₹0. Current tax = Nil. The DTA reversal = ₹1,00,000 × 40% = ₹40,000 (deferred tax income ‚Üí credit to P&L). Remaining DTA after FY 20X2 = ₹40,000.

FY 20X3: Remaining ₹1,00,000 of loss is set off ‚Üí current tax = Nil; DTA reversal = ₹40,000. After FY 20X3, DTA = Nil.

question_html: What is the maximum number of shares that can be buy back as per resource test?
explanation_html:
The resource test under Section 68 of the Companies Act 2013 requires that buy-back must be made only out of free reserves, Securities Premium account, or proceeds of any earlier issue.

Importantly, Revaluation Reserve and Infrastructure Development Reserve (statutory reserve under Income Tax Act) are not free reserves and cannot be used for buy-back.

Free reserves available:

General Reserve‚Çπ20,50,000
Securities Premium‚Çπ7,50,000
P&L Account‚Çπ2,00,000
Total free reserves‚Çπ30,00,000

Maximum buy-back value = ‚Çπ30,00,000.

At buy-back price of ‚Çπ25 per share: Maximum shares = ‚Çπ30,00,000 √∑ ‚Çπ25 = 1,20,000 shares.

But subject to the 25% cap on paid-up capital: 25% √ó 2,40,000 = 60,000 shares.

And 25% cap on total paid-up capital and free reserves: 25% √ó (‚Çπ24,00,000 + ‚Çπ30,00,000) = 25% √ó ‚Çπ54,00,000 = ‚Çπ13,50,000 ‚Üí ‚Çπ13,50,000 √∑ ‚Çπ25 = 54,000 shares.

The binding constraint under the resource test = 54,000 shares.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: Under AS 22, a Deferred Tax Asset arising from carry-forward of losses or unabsorbed depreciation can be recognised only when:
option_a: Reasonable certainty of future taxable income exists
option_b: Virtual certainty supported by convincing evidence that sufficient future taxable income will be available exists
option_c: The company has earned profits in the immediately preceding year
option_d: The carry-forward period under tax law is at least 8 years
explanation_html:
AS 22 distinguishes between two levels of certainty for recognising Deferred Tax Assets:

General timing differences: DTA recognised if there is reasonable certainty of sufficient future taxable income.

Carry-forward losses or unabsorbed depreciation: A much higher bar ‚Äî DTA recognised only to the extent there is virtual certainty supported by convincing evidence that sufficient future taxable income will be available.

Virtual certainty is higher than reasonable certainty ‚Äî it refers to certainty that, for all practical purposes, can be considered certain. It must be supported by concrete evidence (e.g., a profitable binding export order), not merely forecasts or business plans. The carry-forward period (e.g., 8 years) is a tax rule and does not by itself create the virtual certainty required.

question_html: PK Ltd. has identified business segments as its primary reporting format. It has three geographical segments: India (70% of sales), USA (25%), UK (5%). As per AS 17, is PK Ltd. required to disclose secondary segment revenue for UK?
option_a: Yes, because all geographical segments must be disclosed regardless of size
option_b: No, because UK contributes only 5% of enterprise revenue, which is below the 10% threshold for secondary segment disclosure
option_c: Yes, because UK is separately identified in the internal reporting system
option_d: No, because secondary segment disclosures are optional under AS 17
explanation_html: Under AS 17, when the primary format is business segments, secondary geographical segment information is required for each geographical segment whose revenue from sales to external customers is 10% or more of enterprise revenue. India = 70% ≥ 10% (must disclose), USA = 25% ≥ 10% (must disclose), UK = 5% < 10% (NOT required to disclose revenue). PK Ltd. is therefore not required to disclose secondary segment revenue specifically for the UK segment since it does not meet the 10% threshold. However, UK results may be included in an unallocated reconciling item. Other secondary information (assets, capex) must also meet their respective 10% thresholds.

question_html: "Fixed Asset held for sale" will be classified in the Balance Sheet as per Schedule III of the Companies Act as:
option_b: Current Asset
option_c: Non-Current Asset
option_d: Long term Investments
explanation_html:
As per Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013, current assets are those expected to be realised, sold or consumed within the normal operating cycle or within 12 months from the Balance Sheet date.

When a fixed (non-current) asset is classified as "held for sale", the management's intention is to sell it ‚Äî not to use it further in the business. Since it is actively marketed for sale and expected to be sold within 12 months, it no longer meets the criteria for a non-current asset.

Schedule III specifically requires that fixed assets held for sale be presented under Current Assets (generally under "Other Current Assets") in the Balance Sheet. They cannot remain under Non-Current Assets (PPE), as their character has changed from productive use to disposal.

question_html: Microtech Ltd. manufactures batteries for scooters, cars, trucks, and also for invertors and UPS. How many business segments should it have as per AS 17?
option_a: Four segments: one for each product type (scooter, car, truck, and invertor/UPS batteries)
option_b: One segment: all are batteries and the basic product is the same
option_c: Two segments: Automobile batteries (scooters, cars, trucks) and Batteries for Invertors and UPS
option_d: Three segments: Two-wheelers (scooters), Four-wheelers (cars and trucks), and Invertors/UPS
explanation_html: As per AS 17, a business segment is a distinguishable component engaged in providing related products/services subject to risks and returns that are different from other segments. While the basic product (battery) is the same, the risks and returns differ between automobile batteries and invertor/UPS batteries: Automobile batteries ‚Äî affected by government policy, road conditions, quality of automobiles. Invertor/UPS batteries ‚Äî affected by power conditions, standard of living. Since these two types face distinctly different risk/return profiles, Microtech Ltd. should have two business segments. Splitting further into scooter/car/truck would be over-segmentation if their risk/return profiles are similar.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
question_html: Under AS 21, when can a subsidiary be excluded from consolidation?
option_a: When the subsidiary is engaged in a business activity dissimilar from that of the parent
option_b: When the subsidiary is located in a foreign country
option_c: When control is intended to be temporary (subsidiary acquired exclusively for disposal in near future) OR when it operates under severe long-term restrictions significantly impairing fund transfer to parent
option_d: When the subsidiary is a wholly-owned subsidiary of the parent
explanation_html:
AS 21 permits exclusion of a subsidiary from consolidation only in two specific circumstances:

(a) Control is intended to be temporary: The subsidiary is acquired and held exclusively with a view to its subsequent disposal in the near future (generally not more than 12 months from acquisition, unless justified).

(b) Severe long-term restrictions: The subsidiary operates under severe long-term restrictions which significantly impair its ability to transfer funds to the parent.

Dissimilar business activities is specifically NOT a valid reason for exclusion ‚Äî AS 21 states that better information is provided by consolidating such subsidiaries. Foreign location is also not a basis for exclusion. In the Reliance Industries example, despite different industries (telecom, retail, oil), all subsidiaries must be consolidated.

question_html: Wye Ltd. agreed to reimburse liquidation expenses of Zed Ltd. up to ₹10,000. Actual expenses amounted to ₹12,500. In Wye Ltd.'s books, how are these liquidation expenses treated?
option_b: ₹10,000 debited to Goodwill Account (purchasing company's obligation); ₹2,500 is the vendor's expense and does not appear in Wye Ltd.'s books
option_c: ₹12,500 debited to Realization Account
option_d: Ignored entirely since they relate to the vendor company
explanation_html:
When the purchasing company is required to pay liquidation expenses of the vendor company, the amount is debited to Goodwill Account (or Capital Reserve) in the purchasing company's books ‚Äî it is an additional acquisition cost.

In Illustration 5 (Wye Ltd. / Zed Ltd.): Wye Ltd. agreed to reimburse UP TO ₹10,000. Actual expenses = ₹12,500.

In Wye Ltd.'s books: Goodwill A/c Dr. ₹10,000 ‚Üí To Cash ₹10,000 (amount agreed to pay).

The excess ₹2,500 (₹12,500 – ₹10,000) is borne by Zed Ltd. (the vendor) and appears as a debit to Realization Account in Zed's books. It does NOT appear in Wye Ltd.'s books.

chapter_id: Accounting for Branches including foreign branches
question_html: The Bombay Traders invoiced goods to Delhi branch at cost. Credit sales = ₹28,400; Returns from customers = ₹500; Cash received from debtors = ₹28,500; Discount allowed = ₹200; Bad debts = ₹600; Opening debtors = ₹12,600. What is the closing balance of branch debtors?
explanation_html:
Using the Memorandum Branch Debtors Account:

Debit side:
Opening debtors: ₹12,600
Credit sales: ₹28,400
Total: ₹41,000

Credit side:
Cash received: ₹28,500
Returns: ₹500
Discount: ₹200
Bad debts: ₹600
Closing balance (B/F): ₹9,800
Total: ₹39,800 + ₹1,200 remaining = ₹41,000

Check: ₹12,600 + ₹28,400 = ₹41,000 = ₹28,500 + ₹500 + ₹200 + ₹600 + ₹9,800 ‚úì

Closing debtors = ₹9,800 ‚Äî carried forward as closing asset in the Branch Account.

question_html: Under AS 14, goodwill arising on amalgamation should be amortised over:
option_b: Up to 10 years with ICAI approval
option_c: A period not exceeding 5 years unless a longer period can be justified
option_d: The useful life of the transferred business, irrespective of time period
explanation_html:
AS 14 states that goodwill arising on amalgamation should be amortised to income on a systematic basis over its useful life. Due to the nature of goodwill, it is frequently difficult to estimate its useful life. Therefore, AS 14 specifies: "it is considered appropriate to amortise goodwill over a period not exceeding five years unless a somewhat longer period can be justified."

The default is amortisation within 5 years. A longer period is permissible only if justified. Factors for estimating goodwill life include: foreseeable life of business/industry, effects of obsolescence, key personnel service life, competitor actions, and legal/regulatory provisions. Goodwill is treated as an intangible asset to be amortised, not maintained indefinitely.

question_html: As per AS 13, which of the following is the correct definition of a Current Investment?
option_a: An investment that has been held for less than one year from the date of the balance sheet
option_b: An investment that is by its nature readily realisable and is intended to be held for not more than one year from the date on which such investment is made
option_c: An investment in equity shares of listed companies held for trading purposes
option_d: Any investment that can be converted into cash within 3 months from the balance sheet date
explanation_html: As per AS 13, a Current Investment is an investment that is: (i) by its nature readily realisable, and (ii) intended to be held for not more than one year from the date on which such investment is made. The intention to hold for not more than one year is to be judged at the time of purchase of the investment, not at the balance sheet date. This is important ‚Äî even if an investment has been held for 10 months and is still within the one-year period, if the original intention was to hold it long-term, it is classified as a long-term investment. Classification depends on intention at acquisition, not on time elapsed from the balance sheet date.

question_html: An employee Roshan joined XYZ Ltd. with annual emoluments of ₹ 14,90,210. The company gives a lump-sum payment of 25% of last drawn annual salary × completed years (minimum 5 years). Salary grows at 10% p.a. The Defined Benefit Obligation (DBO) at end of service is approximately ₹ 30,00,000. What is the amount of equal annual charge to Profit and Loss Account each year?
option_c: ₹ 3,72,553 (discounted amount in year 1)
explanation_html:
The DBO = Last salary × 25% × 5 years = ₹24,00,000 × 25% × 5 = ₹30,00,000.

This total DBO is spread equally over the 5 years of service: ₹30,00,000 √∑ 5 = ₹6,00,000 per year as the equal apportioned amount of DBO. This represents the undiscounted benefit earned each year. The current service cost (discounted) differs: Year 1 = ₹6,00,000 × 0.735 = ₹4,41,000; Year 5 = ₹6,00,000 × 1 = ₹6,00,000. However, the total annual charge to P&L = ₹6,00,000 (the equal portion of DBO assigned to each year of service, before discounting). This is the straight-line attribution of benefit to service periods.

question_html: Better Ltd.'s stock includes goods worth ₹50,000 purchased from Best Ltd. (the purchasing company) at a profit of 25% on cost. After amalgamation, what adjustment is made in Best Ltd.'s books?
option_a: No adjustment since both companies are now merged
option_b: Capital Reserve Dr. ₹10,000 / To Stock (Inventory) Cr. ₹10,000 (eliminate unrealised profit)
explanation_html:
After amalgamation, goods in the vendor's closing stock purchased from the purchaser (which included the purchaser's profit) must be restated to cost to the group/combined entity. The unrealised profit in that stock must be eliminated.

Profit on cost of 25% means profit as a percentage of selling price = 25/125 = 20%. So profit in ₹50,000 stock = 20% × ₹50,000 = ₹10,000.

Adjustment: Capital Reserve A/c Dr. ₹10,000 / To Current Assets (Stock) A/c Cr. ₹10,000

The debit goes to Capital Reserve (since the inter-company profit was already reflected in the capital reserve arising on amalgamation) ‚Äî as shown in Illustration 6 (Best Ltd. absorbing Better Ltd.).

question_html: Which of the following correctly describes 'Intra-enterprise comparison' in the context of benefits of Accounting Standards?
option_a: Comparison of financial statements of different enterprises for the same accounting period
option_b: Comparison of financial statements of the same enterprise over a number of years
option_c: Comparison of financial statements prepared under Ind AS with those under IFRS
option_d: Comparison between different divisions of an enterprise operating in different countries
explanation_html:
As per the study material on benefits of Accounting Standards:
- Intra-enterprise comparison: Involves comparison of financial statements of the same enterprise over a number of years. This is possible if the enterprise uses the same accounting policies every year in drawing up its financial statements.
- Inter-enterprise comparison: Involves comparison of financial statements of different enterprises for the same accounting period. This requires comparable enterprises to use similar accounting policies.
Both types of comparisons are facilitated by Accounting Standards.

question_html: A profit-sharing plan requires an enterprise to pay 3% of net profit to employees who serve throughout the year. Due to expected staff turnover, total payments are estimated at 2.5% of net profit. What amount should be recognised as expense under AS 15?
option_b: 2.5% of net profit (expected actual payment)
option_c: No provision, since the year has not yet ended when obligation arises
option_d: The difference of 0.5% only (the saving due to turnover)
explanation_html: Under AS 15, for profit-sharing and bonus plans, the enterprise should recognise the expected cost of profit-sharing and bonus payments, not the maximum contractual amount. The enterprise estimates that actual payments will be 2.5% of net profit due to expected staff turnover (employees leaving before year-end will not be entitled to the benefit). Therefore, the enterprise recognises a liability and an expense of 2.5% of net profit. The expected cost reflects the probability-adjusted obligation ‚Äî a key principle of AS 15 that matches costs to the period of service rendered.

question_html: PQ & Associates is a contractor with a contract value of ₹ 40 lakhs. Costs incurred to date = ₹ 3 lakhs. Estimated future costs = ₹ 30 lakhs. Work completed = 10%. Due to uncertainty about regulatory changes, the outcome of the contract cannot be estimated reliably. PQ is certain it will recover costs incurred to date. Under AS 7, what revenue and profit are recognised?
option_b: Revenue = ₹ 3 lakhs (cost recovery basis); Profit = Nil
option_c: Revenue = Nil; Cost = ₹ 3 lakhs; Loss = ₹ 3 lakhs
option_d: Revenue = ₹ 40 lakhs; Profit = ₹ 7 lakhs
explanation_html:
AS 7 specifies that when the outcome of a construction contract cannot be estimated reliably, the percentage completion method should NOT be applied. Instead:

(a) Revenue should be recognised only to the extent of contract costs incurred of which recovery is probable; and
(b) Contract costs should be recognised as an expense in the period incurred.

Since PQ is certain it can recover the costs incurred (₹3 lakhs), revenue = ₹3 lakhs and cost = ₹3 lakhs ‚Üí Profit = Nil.

When the uncertainty ceases to exist, revenue and expenses should thereafter be recognised using the percentage completion method.

question_html: When a company's property (book value ₹4,25,000 + ₹3,25,000 = ₹7,50,000 total freehold) is revalued upward to ₹5,07,500 (gain ₹82,500) under a reconstruction scheme, the journal entry is:
option_a: Capital Reduction A/c Dr. / To Freehold Property A/c
option_b: Freehold Property A/c Dr. ₹82,500 / To Capital Reduction A/c Cr. ₹82,500
option_c: Freehold Property A/c Dr. / To Revaluation Reserve A/c Cr.
option_d: P&L A/c Dr. / To Freehold Property A/c Cr.
explanation_html:
When an asset is appreciated (revalued upward) under a reconstruction scheme, the appreciation is:
‚Ä¢ Debited to the Asset Account (increases the carrying value)
‚Ä¢ Credited to Capital Reduction Account (the appreciation serves as a source to write off losses/overvalued assets)

This is consistent with AS 10 (Revaluation Model) in the context of internal reconstruction. In the chapter's rule: "An appreciation in the value of an asset or reduction in the amount of a liability should be debited to the account concerned and credited to Capital Reduction Account."

Journal entry per Illustration 3 (A & Co. Ltd.):
Freehold Property A/c Dr. ₹82,500
   To Capital Reduction A/c Cr. ₹82,500

question_html: In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognise them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. Which of the following is not an example of such costs:
option_a: Abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour, or other production costs;
option_b: Storage costs, unless the production process requires such storage;
option_c: Raw Material cost
option_d: Selling and distribution costs.
explanation_html:
As per AS 2 (Valuation of Inventories), the following are excluded from inventory cost (recognised as period expenses):

  • Abnormal wastage of materials, labour and overheads
  • Storage costs (unless necessary in the production process)
  • Administrative/selling/distribution costs

Raw material cost is NOT excluded ‚Äî it is a fundamental component of inventory cost (cost of purchase). Raw materials are directly included in the cost of inventories.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: How much is the reporting difference (gain or loss) in case of Trade Receivable:
option_b: Loss of ‚Çπ 34,383 approx
option_c: Gain of ‚Çπ 19,395 approx
option_d: Loss of ‚Çπ 19,395 approx
explanation_html:
Under AS 11, exchange differences on monetary items are recognised in the profit or loss for the period.

Original recorded value of Trade Receivable = ‚Çπ7,00,000.

Restated value on 31.3.2024 = ‚Çπ7,34,383 approx (see Q1a).

Exchange difference = ‚Çπ7,34,383 ‚àí ‚Çπ7,00,000 = ‚Çπ34,383 approx.

Since the USD has appreciated against INR (rate moved from ‚Çπ79.4 to ‚Çπ83.3), Fly Ltd. will receive more INR when the receivable is collected. For a receivable (asset), appreciation of foreign currency = Exchange Gain for the company.

This gain is recognised in the Profit & Loss account for FY 2023-24.

question_html: Under AS 9, dividends from investments in shares should be recognised as revenue:
option_a: When declared by the Board of Directors of the investee company
option_b: When received in cash
option_c: On an accrual basis at the end of each financial year
option_d: When the owner's right to receive payment is established
explanation_html:
AS 9 prescribes different recognition criteria for different types of income from enterprise resources:

Interest: On a time proportion basis (amount outstanding √ó rate).
Royalties: On accrual basis as per the terms of the relevant agreement.
Dividends: When the owner's right to receive payment is established.

For dividends, the right to receive payment is established when the dividend is declared (formally approved by the shareholders/board at the appropriate level, depending on the legal structure). The mere proposal or recommendation of a dividend does NOT establish the right to receive payment. As illustrated in the ICAI material: if dividend was proposed on 10th April but declared on 15th June, the right is established on 15th June.

question_html: The total cost of plant as on march 31, 2024 will be:
explanation_html:
Total cost of plant:

Land‚Çπ50,00,000
Material and direct labour‚Çπ35,00,000
Environmental device (government ordered ‚Äî directly attributable)‚Çπ6,00,000
Capitalised borrowing cost‚Çπ2,00,000
Total‚Çπ93,00,000

Excluded: Head office expenses ‚Çπ10,00,000 (not directly attributable) and Director Finance travel ‚Çπ5,00,000 (not a borrowing cost).

question_html: Z Ltd. has no Foreign Currency Cash Flow during the year. It holds € 1,00,000 deposit in a French bank at the start of the year (rate €1 = ₹ 82). By year-end, interest of € 5,000 is credited, and the closing balance is € 1,05,000 (rate €1 = ₹ 85). The closing balance sheet shows this deposit at ₹ 89,25,000. While preparing the Cash Flow Statement as per AS 3, what adjustment is required?
option_a: Add exchange gain of ₹ 3,00,000 to opening cash balance as a cash inflow from investing activities
option_b: Exchange difference of ₹ 3,00,000 is deducted from net profit in indirect method (non-cash item); separately reconciled in Note to CFS to bridge CFS closing balance with Balance Sheet balance
option_c: Exchange gain of ₹ 3,00,000 is treated as an operating cash inflow since it is credited to P&L
option_d: No adjustment is required; the Cash Flow Statement closing balance will automatically equal the Balance Sheet balance
explanation_html:
The deposit is a cash equivalent (assume) or investing asset. At year-end:
Interest income: €5,000 × ₹85 = ₹4,25,000 (actual cash flow when received)
Exchange gain: €1,00,000 × (₹85 – ₹82) = ₹3,00,000 (non-cash ‚Äî just restatement)

The exchange gain of ₹3,00,000 is not a cash flow ‚Äî it arises merely from restating the balance at closing exchange rate. In the indirect method, this exchange gain (non-cash item) must be deducted from Net Profit to arrive at operating cash flows. The resulting difference between the CFS closing balance (excluding exchange difference) and the Balance Sheet balance (₹89,25,000) is reconciled separately in a note to the CFS by adding the exchange difference of ₹3,00,000 to opening balance.

question_html: As per the Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules, 2014, when a company declares dividend out of accumulated profits transferred to reserves (due to inadequacy of current year profits), what is the maximum amount that can be drawn from such reserves?
option_b: Not exceeding one-tenth (10%) of the sum of paid-up share capital and free reserves
option_c: Not exceeding 15% of the paid-up share capital
option_d: Not exceeding 50% of the previous year's distributable profits
explanation_html:
As per Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules, 2014, when dividend is declared from accumulated reserves (due to inadequacy of current year profits), the following conditions must ALL be met:

Condition I: Rate of dividend ‚â§ average of rates declared in 3 immediately preceding years.
Condition II: Total amount drawn from accumulated reserves ‚â§ 1/10th of (paid-up share capital + free reserves) as per latest audited balance sheet.
Condition III: Amount drawn shall first be used to set off current year losses, before any equity dividend.
Condition IV: Balance of reserves after withdrawal ‚â• 15% of paid-up share capital.

Condition II limits the drawdown to a maximum of 10% of (share capital + free reserves).

question_html: As per The Companies Act, 2013 under Section 68 (2) the buy-back of shares in any financial year must not exceed
option_a: 20% of its total paid-up capital and free reserves
option_b: 25% of its total paid-up capital and free reserves
option_c: 25% of its total paid-up capital
option_d: 20% of its total paid-up capital
explanation_html:
As per Section 68(2) of the Companies Act, 2013:

The buy-back of shares or other specified securities in any financial year shall not exceed 25 percent of the total paid-up capital and free reserves of the company.

Note: There is also a separate limit ‚Äî the buy-back of equity shares in a financial year shall not exceed 25% of the total paid-up equity capital (Shares Outstanding Test). Both limits apply simultaneously and the lower restricts the buy-back.
