question_html: Alpha Ltd. prepared its financial statements and mentioned in Notes to Accounts that 24,000 equity shares of ₹10 each were allotted as fully paid bonus shares but did NOT disclose the source from which bonus shares were issued. Is this a violation of Schedule III?
option_a: Yes ‚Äî Schedule III mandates disclosure of the source from which bonus shares are issued
option_b: No ‚Äî Schedule III requires disclosure of the aggregate number and class of bonus shares allotted but does NOT require disclosure of the source from which bonus shares were issued
option_c: Yes ‚Äî it violates AS 1 which requires full disclosure of accounting policies
option_d: No ‚Äî disclosure of bonus shares is optional under Schedule III
explanation_html:
Schedule III requires disclosure in Notes to Accounts for the 5 years immediately preceding the balance sheet date of the aggregate number and class of shares allotted as fully paid-up bonus shares. However, Schedule III does NOT require disclosure of the source from which bonus shares have been issued.

Therefore, non-disclosure of the source (e.g., Securities Premium, General Reserve, Capital Redemption Reserve) does NOT violate Schedule III. The company has correctly disclosed the number and class of bonus shares. This is confirmed in Example 1 of the ICAI chapter where it is explicitly stated that "Schedule III does not require a company to disclose the source from which bonus shares have been issued."

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: Under AS 5, which of the following is an example of an Extraordinary Item?
option_a: Write-down of inventories to net realisable value
option_b: Gain on disposal of long-term investments
option_c: Losses sustained as a result of an earthquake (for a manufacturing enterprise)
option_d: Litigation settlement payments
explanation_html:
AS 5 defines extraordinary items as income or expenses that arise from events or transactions that are clearly distinct from the ordinary activities of the enterprise and are not expected to recur frequently or regularly.

Options (a), (b), and (d) ‚Äî write-downs, gains on investment disposal, and litigation settlements ‚Äî are classified as exceptional items within ordinary activities under AS 5 (requiring separate disclosure due to their size, nature, or incidence), NOT extraordinary items.

Losses due to an earthquake for a manufacturing enterprise are clearly distinct from ordinary activities and qualify as extraordinary. However, note: for an insurance enterprise that insures against earthquake risks, such claims would NOT be extraordinary.

question_html: Under AS 10, items of PPE retired from active use and held for disposal should be stated at:
option_a: Historical cost less accumulated depreciation (carrying amount only)
option_b: Net Realisable Value (NRV)
option_c: Lower of Carrying Amount and Net Realisable Value; any write-down is recognised immediately in P&L
option_d: Fair value as determined by an independent valuer
explanation_html: As per AS 10, items of PPE retired from active use and held for disposal should be stated at the lower of their carrying amount and net realisable value (NRV). Any write-down required to reduce the carrying amount to NRV should be recognised immediately in the Statement of Profit and Loss. This is similar to the treatment of inventories (AS 2) where the lower of cost and NRV principle is applied. The rationale is that since these assets are no longer being used, the carrying amount should reflect the amount expected to be recovered from their disposal ‚Äî which is the NRV. Depreciation ceases at the earlier of the date the asset is retired from active use and held for disposal, or the date of derecognition.

question_html: Omega Limited's pension scheme actuarial valuation revealed a surplus of ₹ 6 lakhs for the first time. The company wants to spread this surplus over 2 years by reducing annual contribution. As per AS 15, the correct treatment of this actuarial surplus is:
option_a: Spread over the next 2 years by reducing annual contributions from ₹ 5 lakhs to ₹ 2 lakhs
option_b: Spread over the average remaining service life of employees (6 years)
option_c: Credited immediately and fully to the Statement of Profit and Loss in the current year
option_d: Credited to a Pension Reserve account in the balance sheet
explanation_html: As per AS 15 (Revised 2005), actuarial gains and losses should be recognised immediately in the Statement of Profit and Loss as income or expense. There is no option to spread actuarial gains/losses over future periods or to credit them to reserves. The surplus of ₹6 lakhs is an actuarial gain that must be credited to the Profit and Loss account in the current year in its entirety. The company's plan to spread it over 2 years or over the average remaining service life (corridor approach) is not permitted under Indian AS 15. This is a key distinction from some other frameworks that allowed the corridor approach.

question_html: Under the Pooling of Interests Method (merger), what happens to the Profit and Loss Account balance of the transferor company?
option_a: It loses its identity and is written off against goodwill
option_b: It is aggregated with the corresponding balance of the transferee company OR transferred to General Reserve
option_c: It is credited to Capital Reserve of the transferee company
option_d: It is distributed as dividend to shareholders of the transferor company before amalgamation
explanation_html:
AS 14 Para 12 states: In an amalgamation in the nature of merger (Pooling of Interests Method), the balance of the Profit and Loss Account appearing in the financial statements of the transferor company is aggregated with the corresponding balance appearing in the financial statements of the transferee company. Alternatively, it is transferred to the General Reserve, if any.

This reflects the pooling concept ‚Äî the identity of reserves is preserved and the P&L balance is treated as if it belonged to the combined entity all along.

This contrasts with the Purchase Method where the P&L balance of the transferor loses its identity and is NOT transferred to the transferee's books.

question_html: An amusement park has a 'soft' opening at 80% capacity, selling tickets at 50% discount. Management claims these net operating costs incurred during the trial run should be capitalised as the soft opening is necessary to bring the park to the condition capable of operating in the intended manner. Under AS 10, this treatment is:
option_a: Correct, because the trial run is part of testing whether the asset is functioning properly
option_b: Correct, because the park has not yet achieved full operating capacity
option_c: Incorrect, because the park running at 80% capacity provides sufficient evidence that it is capable of operating in the intended manner; operating costs at start-up must be expensed
option_d: Correct only if the trial run lasts for less than 3 months
explanation_html: As per AS 10, recognition of costs in the carrying amount of an item of PPE ceases when the item is in the location and condition necessary for it to be capable of operating in the manner intended by management. Costs incurred while an item capable of operating in the manner intended by management has yet to be brought into use or is operated at less than full capacity are NOT included in the carrying amount. Even though the amusement park is running at 80% capacity (less than full), there is sufficient evidence that it is capable of operating in the manner intended. The soft opening proves the park is ready and working. These operating costs are specific to the start-up period and must be expensed as incurred in the Statement of Profit and Loss.

question_html: At the end of Year 2, when the intention is to use the building as corporate office, it should be classified as:
option_b: Investments
option_c: Property, Plant and Equipment
option_d: Intangible Assets
explanation_html:
At the beginning of Year 2, the company changed its intention ‚Äî instead of selling, it decided to use the building as its corporate office. Under AS 10 (Property, Plant and Equipment), an item held for use in administrative purposes qualifies as PPE.

When the intention changes from sale (Inventory) to own use (PPE), the asset must be reclassified from Inventory to Property, Plant and Equipment. The transfer is made at the carrying value of the inventory at the date of reclassification.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: Under Financial Capital Maintenance at Current Purchasing Power, how is the opening equity restated?
option_a: By applying specific price indices applicable to each individual asset
option_b: By using average price indices to restate opening equity at closing prices
option_c: By keeping opening equity at original historical cost without any adjustment
option_d: By discounting opening equity at the current rate of interest
explanation_html:
Under Financial Capital Maintenance at Current Purchasing Power, opening and closing equity at historical costs are restated at closing prices using average price indices. A positive retained profit by this method means the business has enough funds to replace its assets at average closing price. This contrasts with:
- Historical cost method: No restatement; opening and closing assets at respective historical costs
- Physical capital maintenance: Uses specific price indices applicable to each individual asset

chapter_id: Accounting for Branches including foreign branches
question_html: When an independent branch wants to purchase an asset (e.g., machinery), but the asset account is to be maintained in Head Office books, what entry does the Branch pass?
option_a: Machinery A/c Dr. / To Bank A/c Cr.
option_b: Head Office A/c Dr. / To Bank A/c or Liability A/c Cr.
option_c: No entry in branch books ‚Äî only HO records it
option_d: Machinery A/c Dr. / To Head Office A/c Cr.
explanation_html:
When a branch purchases an asset but the asset account is to be retained in HO books (a common practice for control and depreciation purposes):

Branch passes:
Head Office A/c Dr. / To Bank A/c (or Sundry Creditors) Cr.
(The branch paid for the asset but records it as an amount owed to/by HO since the asset belongs to HO books)

HO passes: Branch Asset A/c Dr. / To Branch A/c Cr.

Each year for depreciation:
HO: Branch A/c Dr. / To Branch Asset A/c Cr. (branch bears the depreciation)
Branch: Depreciation A/c Dr. / To Head Office A/c Cr.

This ensures the asset and depreciation are both tracked at HO level while the expense is borne by the branch.

question_html: The revised ICAI announcement on classification of Non-company entities (effective April 1, 2024) is not relevant for which of the following types of entities?
option_a: Partnership firms that are required to comply with Accounting Standards issued by ICAI
option_b: Sole proprietorship entities engaged in commercial activities
option_c: Non-company entities which may be required to follow Ind AS or AS as per relevant regulatory requirements applicable to them
option_d: Co-operative societies engaged in business activities
explanation_html: As specifically stated in the revised ICAI announcement: "This Announcement is not relevant for Non-company entities which may be required to follow Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) or Accounting Standards (AS) as per relevant regulatory requirements applicable to such entities." This means entities like NBFCs or other entities that are mandated by their sectoral regulators (such as RBI) to follow Ind AS or specific AS are governed by those regulatory requirements ‚Äî the ICAI classification announcement does not apply to them. Partnership firms, sole proprietorships, and co-operative societies engaged in commercial activities that are not governed by any such specific regulatory requirements would be classified under this revised scheme as either MSMEs or Large entities.

question_html: As per AS 1, the principle of Consistency requires:
option_a: Using the same accounting policies in all branches and subsidiaries of an enterprise
option_b: Using the same accounting policies for similar transactions in all accounting periods
option_c: Ensuring accounting policies are consistent with those of competitors in the same industry
option_d: Maintaining the same format of financial statements across all accounting periods
explanation_html: As per AS 1, the principle of Consistency refers to the practice of using the same accounting policies for similar transactions in all accounting periods. Consistency improves comparability of financial statements through time. An accounting policy can be changed only if: (i) required by a statute, (ii) required by an accounting standard, or (iii) for more appropriate presentation of financial statements. The consistency principle does not require uniformity across enterprises in the same industry, nor does it mandate identical financial statement formats.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: Which of the following creates a Deferred Tax Liability under AS 22?
option_a: Excess of accounting depreciation over tax depreciation (book depreciation > tax depreciation)
option_b: Excess of tax depreciation over accounting depreciation (tax depreciation > book depreciation)
option_c: Payment of a fine for violation of law (disallowed under Income Tax)
option_d: Dividend income exempt under Section 10 of the Income Tax Act
explanation_html:
A Deferred Tax Liability (DTL) arises when taxable income in the current period is lower than accounting income (meaning tax is currently lower, but will be higher in future periods when the timing difference reverses).

When tax depreciation > book depreciation: Current taxable income is lower than accounting income (more deduction in current year for tax). This means tax benefit is taken now, but in future years, less tax deduction will be available ‚Üí creates a DTL.

Options (c) and (d) are permanent differences ‚Äî fines are disallowed and exempt dividends are never taxable. Permanent differences do NOT create deferred tax. Option (a) is when book depreciation exceeds tax depreciation ‚Äî this creates a Deferred Tax Asset (DTA).

question_html: As per AS 10, regarding land and buildings, which of the following statements is correct?
option_a: Land and buildings are treated as a composite asset and depreciated together
option_b: Land is generally not depreciated; buildings are depreciated; an increase in land value does not affect the depreciable amount of the building
option_c: If the building appreciates in value, the depreciable amount of the building is correspondingly reduced
option_d: Land with a limited useful life (e.g., quarry) is not depreciated because land always has infinite economic benefit
explanation_html: AS 10 specifically states: Land and buildings are separable assets and are accounted for separately, even when they are acquired together. Land has an unlimited useful life and therefore is not depreciated (with exceptions like quarries and landfill sites). Buildings have a limited useful life and therefore are depreciable assets. An increase in the value of the land on which a building stands does not affect the determination of the depreciable amount of the building. The depreciable amount of the building is cost (or revalued amount) less residual value ‚Äî the land's appreciation is completely irrelevant to the building's depreciation calculation. Option (d) is incorrect because quarries with limited lives ARE depreciated.

question_html: XYZ Co. sold equipment having a book value of ₹ 60,000 at a gain of ₹ 8,000. How should this transaction be reported in the Cash Flow Statement under AS 3?
option_b: Operating activities: Nil; Investing activities: ₹ 68,000 (full sale proceeds)
option_c: Operating activities: ₹ 68,000 (full proceeds)
option_d: Investing activities: ₹ 60,000 (book value only); gain of ₹ 8,000 shown in operating activities
explanation_html:
As per AS 3, profit or loss on disposal of a fixed asset is not an operating cash flow. The entire proceeds of such a transaction should be taken as a cash inflow from investing activity.

Sale Proceeds = Book Value + Gain = ₹60,000 + ₹8,000 = ₹68,000 ‚Äî shown as Investing Cash Inflow.

In the indirect method, the gain of ₹8,000 would be deducted from Net Profit under operating activities (since it is a non-operating item), with the full ₹68,000 shown under investing activities. Under the direct method, nothing is shown under operating activities from this transaction. Option (a) is incorrect because splitting book value and gain between activities is not permitted.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
question_html: As per AS 21, when a subsidiary company issues bonus shares to all its shareholders, how should the holding company record this in its books?
option_a: Debit Investment Account; Credit Share Premium Account
option_b: No journal entry is passed; only the number of shares held is increased
option_c: Debit Investment Account; Credit Profit & Loss Account
option_d: Debit Investment Account; Credit Capital Reserve
explanation_html:
AS 21 (and AS 13) clearly state: "In case of issue of bonus shares by the subsidiary company, the holding company, like other holders, records no entry; only the number of shares held is increased."

The rationale: Bonus shares represent capitalisation of reserves ‚Äî no cash changes hands and no new value is created. The investment's total value remains unchanged; it is simply represented by more shares at a lower per-share book value. The holding company increases the number of shares held on record but makes no accounting entry for the bonus shares received. This is consistent with the treatment in standalone books and the consolidation context.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: A management decision to acquire assets in the future does not, by itself, give rise to a present obligation. When does an obligation normally arise?
option_a: When the Board of Directors passes a resolution to acquire the asset
option_b: When the budget for acquisition is approved
option_c: When the asset is delivered or the enterprise enters into an irrevocable agreement to acquire the asset
option_d: When the enterprise announces its intention to acquire the asset publicly
explanation_html:
As per the Framework, liability cannot arise on account of future commitment alone. A decision by management to acquire assets in the future does not, of itself, give rise to a present obligation. An obligation normally arises only when:
1. The asset is delivered, or
2. The enterprise enters into an irrevocable agreement to acquire the asset
This is because a liability requires a present obligation ‚Äî not a future one ‚Äî arising from past events.

question_html: AS 25 (Interim Financial Reporting) requires that only certain Non-SMCs prepare interim financial results. Which regulatory authority requires such Non-SMCs to present interim financial results (e.g., quarterly results)?
option_b: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
option_c: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
option_d: National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA)
explanation_html: AS 25 (Interim Financial Reporting) does not require a company to present an interim financial report ‚Äî it is applicable only if a company is required or elects to prepare and present an interim financial report. Only certain Non-SMCs are required by the concerned regulators to present interim financial results. The specific example given in the ICAI material is quarterly financial results required by SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India) for listed companies. Therefore, the recognition and measurement requirements of AS 25 are applicable to those Non-SMCs for preparation of interim financial results as required by SEBI. MCA, RBI, and NFRA do not mandate quarterly financial results of the type described under AS 25.

question_html: A company has an inter-segment transfer pricing policy of charging at cost less 10%, while market prices are generally 25% above cost. As per AS 17, is this pricing policy correct?
option_a: Incorrect; AS 17 mandates that inter-segment transfers must always be made at market price
option_b: Incorrect; AS 17 requires inter-segment transfers to be made at cost
option_c: Correct, provided the basis of pricing (cost less 10%) is followed consistently and disclosed in the financial statements
option_d: Incorrect; below-cost inter-segment transfers are never permitted as they distort segment results
explanation_html: AS 17 does not prescribe a specific method for inter-segment transfer pricing. It states that inter-segment transfers should be measured on the basis that the enterprise actually used to price those transfers. The enterprise may price transfers at cost, below cost, or market price ‚Äî it is free to choose its own policy. However, whatever policy is adopted must be: (i) disclosed in the financial statements, and (ii) followed consistently. Any change in the basis of pricing inter-segment transfers must also be disclosed. Therefore, charging at cost less 10% is perfectly acceptable as long as it is disclosed and applied consistently.

question_html: Based on the quantitative threshold which of the above segment K to O would be considered as reportable segment?
option_b: Segment M, N & L
option_c: Segment L, M, N & O
option_d: All Segment
explanation_html:
Under AS 17 (Segment Reporting), a segment is reportable if it meets any one of the following thresholds (10% tests):

  • Revenue test: Segment revenue ‚â• 10% of total combined revenue of all segments.
  • Profit/Loss test: Absolute segment profit/loss ‚â• 10% of the greater of (a) combined profit of all profitable segments or (b) combined loss of all loss-making segments.
  • Asset test: Segment assets ‚â• 10% of total assets of all segments.

Total revenue = ‚Çπ5,94,00,000. 10% threshold = ‚Çπ59,40,000.

Total profit of profitable segments = ‚Çπ63,00,000. 10% threshold = ‚Çπ6,30,000.

Total assets = ‚Çπ25,65,00,000. 10% threshold = ‚Çπ2,56,50,000.

  • K: Revenue ‚Çπ54,00,000 < ‚Çπ59,40,000. Profit ‚Çπ4,50,000 < ‚Çπ6,30,000. Assets ‚Çπ9,00,00,000 > ‚Çπ2,56,50,000. ‚úì Reportable (asset test).
  • L: Revenue ‚Çπ1,48,50,000 > threshold. ‚úì Reportable.
  • M: Revenue ‚Çπ2,02,50,000 > threshold. ‚úì Reportable.
  • N: Revenue ‚Çπ1,48,50,000 > threshold. ‚úì Reportable.
  • O: Revenue ‚Çπ40,50,000 < threshold. Profit ‚Çπ9,00,000 > ‚Çπ6,30,000. ‚úì Reportable (profit test).

All five segments meet at least one threshold ‚Äî all are reportable.

question_html: Under AS 15, which of the following is classified as a Post-Employment Benefit?
option_b: Long-service leave
option_c: Gratuity and Pension
option_d: Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS) payments
explanation_html:
AS 15 classifies employee benefits into four categories:
(a) Short-term benefits: Wages, salaries, paid annual leave, sick leave, profit-sharing bonuses payable within 12 months, non-monetary benefits.
(b) Post-employment benefits: Gratuity, pension, provident fund, post-employment medical care.
(c) Other long-term benefits: Long-service leave, sabbatical leave, long-term disability benefits, bonuses payable more than 12 months after year-end.
(d) Termination benefits: VRS payments, retrenchment benefits.

Paid annual leave = short-term; Long-service leave = other long-term; VRS = termination benefit. Only Gratuity and Pension are post-employment benefits.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: A company revised the wage agreement with its employees' union on 1st September 20X2 with retrospective effect from 30th September 20X1 ‚Äî an additional ₹ 5,00,000 per annum. How should the additional wage liability for the period from 1st October 20X1 to 31st March 20X3 (i.e., 1.5 years) be classified under AS 5?
option_a: Entirely as a prior period item for ₹ 7,50,000
option_b: Entirely as a current year ordinary expense for ₹ 7,50,000
option_c: Prior period item for retrospective portion (₹ 2,50,000 for Oct 20X1 to March 20X2); current year ordinary expense for ₹ 5,00,000 (April 20X2 to March 20X3)
option_d: Extraordinary item requiring separate disclosure for ₹ 7,50,000
explanation_html:
The revision of wages took place on 1st September 20X2 with retrospective effect from 30th September 20X1. As per AS 5, a prior period item arises due to errors or omissions in prior period financial statements. The company could not have anticipated this revised wage agreement in its prior year accounts ‚Äî the revision happened due to negotiation, not due to any error or omission.

Therefore, the entire additional liability of ₹7,50,000 (for 1.5 years) should be included in the current year's wages as a normal ordinary expense. It is NOT a prior period item (no error/omission) and NOT an extraordinary item (wages are an ordinary activity). However, due to its size/nature, separate disclosure as an exceptional item within ordinary activities may be appropriate.

question_html:
The term IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards) as a comprehensive framework comprises which of the following?

  • I. IFRS issued by IASB
  • II. IAS issued by IASC
  • III. Interpretations issued by Standard Interpretations Committee (SIC)
  • IV. Interpretations issued by IFRIC
option_b: I, II and III only
option_c: I, II, III and IV
option_d: II, III and IV only
explanation_html:
The term IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards) as a comprehensive framework comprises all four of the following:
1. IFRS issued by IASB
2. IAS issued by IASC (and adopted by IASB)
3. Interpretations issued by SIC (Standard Interpretations Committee)
4. Interpretations issued by IFRIC (IFRS Interpretations Committee of IASB)
Thus, all four statements are correct.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html:
Using the relationship: Profit = CE ‚Äì OE ‚Äì C + D, consider the following data for a trader:
Opening Assets = ‚Çπ5 lakh, Opening Liabilities = ‚Çπ2 lakh
Closing Assets = ‚Çπ7 lakh, Closing Liabilities = ‚Çπ3 lakh
Capital Introduced = ‚Çπ50,000, Drawings = ‚Çπ30,000
What is the Profit for the period?
option_c: ‚Çπ 80,000 loss
explanation_html:
Using the formula: Profit = (CA ‚Äì CL) ‚Äì (OA ‚Äì OL) ‚Äì C + D

Opening Equity (OE)= OA ‚Äì OL = 5.00 ‚Äì 2.00 = ‚Çπ3.00 lakh
Closing Equity (CE)= CA ‚Äì CL = 7.00 ‚Äì 3.00 = ‚Çπ4.00 lakh
Capital Introduced (C)= ‚Çπ0.50 lakh
Drawings (D)= ‚Çπ0.30 lakh

Profit = CE ‚Äì OE ‚Äì C + D
= 4.00 ‚Äì 3.00 ‚Äì 0.50 + 0.30
= ‚Çπ0.80 lakh = ‚Çπ80,000

question_html: India chose to become IFRS compliant by the process of convergence rather than adoption. Which of the following best distinguishes 'convergence' from 'adoption'?
option_a: Adoption means partial alignment with IFRS, while convergence means complete adoption of IFRS as issued by IASB
option_b: Adoption means the country sets a timetable to use IFRS as issued by IASB directly, while convergence means developing compatible standards with certain modifications
option_c: Both convergence and adoption are identical processes with no practical difference
option_d: Convergence means rejecting IFRS completely and developing independent standards
explanation_html: Adoption means the country sets a specific timetable when specific entities would be required to use IFRS as issued by the IASB without any modification. Convergence means the country will develop high quality, compatible accounting standards with alignment of standards of different standard setters with a certain rate of compromise, by adopting the requirements of the standards either fully or partially. India chose convergence, resulting in Ind AS, which are similar to IFRS but with certain carve-outs to suit the Indian environment.

question_html: Recover Ltd. has 20,000 equity shares of ₹10 each and 15,000 8% Cumulative Preference shares of ₹10 each (preference dividend in arrears for 4 years). Under the reconstruction, preference shares are reduced to ₹2.50 each, and equity shares are reduced to ₹1 each. One new equity share of ₹1 is issued for arrears of preference dividend for 4 years. What is the total credit to Capital Reconstruction Account from reduction of share capital?
option_b: ₹1,12,500 from preference + ₹1,80,000 from equity = ₹2,92,500 total credits
option_c: Only ₹1,80,000 from equity reduction
explanation_html:
Credits to Reconstruction Account from capital reduction:

Preference shares (15,000 × ₹10):
Reduction = 15,000 × (₹10 – ₹2.50) = 15,000 × ₹7.50 = ₹1,12,500

Equity shares (20,000 × ₹10):
Reduction = 20,000 × (₹10 – ₹1) = 20,000 × ₹9 = ₹1,80,000

Total credits = ₹1,12,500 + ₹1,80,000 = ₹2,92,500

Note: The entry for issuing equity shares for preference dividend arrears (₹48,000) is a debit to Reconstruction A/c (capital used to fund arrears). So the net effect from share reduction is ₹2,92,500 credit minus ₹48,000 debit = ₹2,44,500 net. Per Illustration 8 in the chapter, total net capital reduction before using it = ₹2,92,500 – ₹48,000 for arrears = ₹2,44,500.

question_html: As per AS 10, on the sale of an asset that had been revalued upwards (with Revaluation Reserve balance), what is the correct treatment of the Revaluation Reserve?
option_a: Revaluation Reserve is credited to P&L since the profit on sale of such an asset is now realised
option_b: Revaluation Reserve is transferred to Retained Earnings directly (without routing through P&L)
option_c: No change in Revaluation Reserve ‚Äî it stays permanently until explicitly dissolved
option_d: Revaluation Reserve is reduced from the asset value to compute the correct profit or loss on sale
explanation_html: As per AS 10, the revaluation surplus included in owners' interests in respect of an item of PPE may be transferred to Revenue Reserves (Retained Earnings) when the asset is derecognised (retired or disposed of). Critically, transfers from Revaluation Surplus to Revenue Reserves are NOT made through the Statement of Profit and Loss. The transfer is a direct movement between reserves within equity. The gain or loss on disposal is separately computed as: Net disposal proceeds – Carrying Amount (post-revaluation WDV). The Revaluation Surplus is then transferred directly to Retained Earnings ‚Äî this is a standard exam question where many students incorrectly credit P&L.

question_html: According to AS-18 Related Party Disclosures, which ONE of the following is not a related party of Skyline Limited?
option_a: A shareholder of Skyline Limited owning 30% of the ordinary share capital
option_b: An entity providing banking facilities to Skyline Limited in the normal course of business
option_c: An associate of Skyline Limited
option_d: Key management personnel of Skyline Limited
explanation_html:
As per AS 18, related parties include associates, key management personnel, controlling shareholders, and their relatives. However, the standard explicitly excludes entities that have dealings with the enterprise merely by virtue of being:

  • Providers of finance (banks)
  • Trade unions
  • Public utilities or government departments

A bank providing ordinary banking facilities has no element of control or significant influence ‚Äî hence it is not a related party.

question_html: Entity A exchanges Car X (book value ₹ 13,00,000; FV ₹ 13,25,000) for Cash ₹ 15,000 and Car Y (FV ₹ 13,10,000). The transaction lacks commercial substance. How should Car Y be recognised in Entity A's books?
option_b: At fair value of Car X: ₹ 13,25,000
option_c: At carrying amount of Car X less cash received: ₹ 12,85,000
option_d: At carrying amount of Car X: ₹ 13,00,000
explanation_html:
When an exchange transaction lacks commercial substance, the acquired asset is measured at the carrying amount (book value/WDV) of the asset given up. It is not measured at fair value. The journal entry is:

Cash/Bank Dr. ₹15,000
Car Y Dr. ₹12,85,000 (balancing figure)
   To Car X ₹13,00,000

Car Y = Book value of Car X – Cash received = ₹13,00,000 – ₹15,000 = ₹12,85,000.

No gain or loss is recognised on this exchange since the company is in the same economic position as before (no change in cash flows). The transaction lacks commercial substance as the entity's position before and after the exchange remains the same.

question_html: What is the maximum permitted buy-back of equity for Kumar Ltd.?
explanation_html:
Current equity (excluding Revaluation Reserve) = ‚Çπ30,00,000 + ‚Çπ32,50,000 + ‚Çπ6,00,000 + ‚Çπ4,30,000 = ‚Çπ72,80,000.

Minimum equity post buy-back = ‚Çπ21,00,000.

Using simultaneous equation method (buy-back reduces both paid-up capital and free reserves by ‚Çπ30/share): let x = shares. Post buy-back equity = ‚Çπ72,80,000 - ‚Çπ30x >= ‚Çπ21,00,000. Also subject to 25% shares outstanding limit.

Per ICAI: maximum buy-back value = ‚Çπ38,85,000.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: Raj Ltd. was sued for ₹ 15 lakhs for trademark infringement. It provided ₹ 10 lakhs in its accounts for FY 20X1-X2. The financial statements were prepared on 30th April 20X2 and approved by the Board on 30th May 20X2. On 18th May 20X2, the Court ordered Raj Ltd. to pay ₹ 14 lakhs. What is the correct AS 4 treatment?
option_a: Non-adjusting event ‚Äî court judgment came after balance sheet date, only disclose in Directors' Report
option_b: Adjusting event ‚Äî increase the provision from ₹ 10 lakhs to ₹ 14 lakhs (additional provision of ₹ 4 lakhs)
option_c: Adjusting event ‚Äî since the judgment came before approval, show the full ₹ 14 lakhs as a new provision and reverse the old one
option_d: No adjustment needed since a provision was already made during the year
explanation_html: The court judgment on 18th May 20X2 came after the balance sheet date (31st March 20X2) but before the approval by the Board (30th May 20X2). This is an event occurring after the balance sheet date. The lawsuit and related obligation existed at the balance sheet date (Raj Ltd. was sued during 20X1-X2 and had already made a provision). The court judgment provides additional evidence of conditions existing at the balance sheet date. Therefore, it is an adjusting event. Raj Ltd. should increase the provision by ₹ 4 lakhs (from ₹10 lakhs to ₹14 lakhs) in its FY 20X1-X2 accounts. Had the judgment come after approval (e.g., 1st June), no adjustment would be required.

question_html: Tina Ltd. takes over Rina Ltd. The consideration includes: 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹5 premium; cash ₹50,000 to equity shareholders; 2,000 12% preference shares of ₹100 at par; ₹20,000 of debentures converted to Tina Ltd.'s debentures. What is the total Purchase Consideration under AS 14?
option_c: ₹ 7,50,000 (equity at par only)
explanation_html:
Purchase Consideration = Payments made to shareholders only (not debenture holders):

Equity shares: 50,000 × (₹10 + ₹5 premium) = 50,000 × ₹15 = ₹7,50,000
Cash to equity shareholders: ₹50,000
12% Preference shares: 2,000 × ₹100 = ₹2,00,000
Total PC = ₹7,50,000 + ₹50,000 + ₹2,00,000 = ₹10,00,000

Debenture conversion (₹20,000): NOT included ‚Äî payment to debenture holders is not part of consideration under AS 14. The debentures are a liability assumption, not a payment to shareholders.

question_html: As per Section 129(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, when a company's financial statements do not comply with applicable Accounting Standards, the company is required to disclose:
option_a: Only the reasons for the deviation in the Board's Report
option_b: The deviation, reasons for deviation, and the financial effects, if any, arising out of such deviation in the financial statements
option_c: The deviation in financial statements, but financial effects need not be disclosed if immaterial
option_d: Nothing, since only the auditor is required to report the deviation under Section 143(3)(e)
explanation_html: As per Section 129(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, where the financial statements of a company do not comply with the Accounting Standards, the company should disclose in its financial statements: (i) the deviation from the accounting standards, (ii) the reasons for such deviation, and (iii) the financial effects, if any, arising out of such deviations. This disclosure is mandatory. Additionally, Section 143(3)(e) requires the auditor to separately report whether, in his opinion, the financial statements comply with the AS referred to in Section 133. Both disclosures are required ‚Äî the company's in its financial statements, and the auditor's in his report.

question_html: In the Cash Flow Statement as per AS 3, the interest income of ‚Çπ 1.5 crore earned on earned on loans given by the Company will be disclosed as:
option_b: Cash Flow from Investing Activities
option_c: Cash Flow from Financing Activities
option_d: Non-cash Items
explanation_html:
For a financial enterprise whose principal activity is lending money, interest received on loans is operating income ‚Äî the primary revenue from operations.

As per AS 3, for financial enterprises, interest received is classified under Operating Activities. (For non-financial enterprises, interest received would go to Investing Activities.)

question_html: X Ltd. takes over Y Ltd. under the Purchase Method. Net assets taken over = ₹57,50,000 (in ₹000); Purchase Consideration = ₹53,70,000 (in ₹000). What arises from this amalgamation?
option_b: Capital Reserve = ₹3,80,000 (net assets exceed purchase price)
option_c: Securities Premium = ₹3,80,000
option_d: General Reserve = ₹3,80,000
explanation_html:
Under the Purchase Method:
Net Assets acquired = ₹57,50,000 (in ₹000s) from Illustration 8 workings:
Sundry Assets ₹66,00 – Liabilities (Debentures ₹3,50 + Trade Payables ₹3,50 + OCL ₹1,50) = ₹66,00 – ₹8,50 = ₹57,50 (in '000s).
Purchase Consideration = ₹53,70 (in '000s).

Since Net Assets > Purchase Consideration ‚Üí ₹57,50 – ₹53,70 = ₹3,80 thousands = Capital Reserve.

Capital Reserve arises when the purchaser acquires more than what it paid ‚Äî a bargain purchase. This amount is credited to Capital Reserve Account in the transferee company's books.

question_html: As per AS 12, how the Government Grant of ‚Çπ 15 Lakhs with a condition to purchase machinery may be presented as:
option_b: Shareholders Fund
option_c: Deferred Income
option_d: Income in statement of profit and loss as received.
explanation_html:
As per AS 12, grants related to specific depreciable assets (like machinery) can be presented either by:

  • Deducting the grant from the gross value of the asset, or
  • Treating the grant as Deferred Income ‚Äî recognised in P&L on a systematic and rational basis over the useful life of the asset.

Since ‚Çπ15 lakhs is tied to purchase of machinery (a specific depreciable asset), it is treated as Deferred Income and recognised in P&L over the useful life of the machinery.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards based on items impacting Financial Statements
question_html: Rama Ltd. provides the following: Depreciation as per accounts = ₹ 2,00,000; Depreciation as per tax records = ₹ 5,00,000; Unamortised preliminary expenses as per tax records = ₹ 30,000. Tax rate = 50%. There is adequate evidence of future profit sufficiency. What is the net deferred tax asset/(liability)?
option_b: Deferred Tax Liability of ₹ 1,35,000
option_c: Deferred Tax Asset of ₹ 1,35,000
option_d: Deferred Tax Asset of ₹ 1,50,000
explanation_html:
Step 1 ‚Äî Excess depreciation (DTL):
Tax depreciation – Book depreciation = ₹5,00,000 – ₹2,00,000 = ₹3,00,000 timing difference ‚Üí DTL = ₹3,00,000 × 50% = ₹1,50,000

Step 2 ‚Äî Unamortised preliminary expenses (DTA):
Preliminary expenses deductible for tax but not yet in P&L = ₹30,000 timing difference ‚Üí DTA = ₹30,000 × 50% = ₹15,000

Net Deferred Tax Liability = ₹1,50,000 – ₹15,000 = ₹1,35,000 (net DTL).

Since there is adequate evidence of future profit sufficiency, the DTA of ₹15,000 is recognised, netting off against the DTL.

question_html: Internal reconstruction is carried out under which sections of the Companies Act, 2013?
option_b: Sections 61 and 66
option_c: Section 232
option_d: Sections 129 and 133
explanation_html:
As per the chapter:

Internal Reconstruction is regulated by:
‚Ä¢ Section 61 ‚Äî Alteration of Share Capital (sub-division, consolidation, conversion of shares into stock, cancellation of unissued shares)
‚Ä¢ Section 66 ‚Äî Reduction of Share Capital (requires confirmation by the Tribunal through special resolution)

External Reconstruction is regulated by Section 232 of the Companies Act, 2013.

Sections 68 and 70 relate to Buy-Back of Securities (Chapter 12).

The key distinction: Internal reconstruction reorganizes the existing company without liquidation. External reconstruction involves winding up the existing company to form a new one.

question_html: As per AS 17, if a segment was reportable in the immediately preceding period (meeting the 10% thresholds) but in the current period its revenue, result, and assets all fall below 10%, what happens?
option_a: The segment automatically ceases to be reportable from the current period since it no longer meets the quantitative thresholds
option_b: The segment continues to be a reportable segment in the current period despite no longer meeting the 10% thresholds
option_c: The management may choose to retain or drop the segment at its discretion
option_d: The segment is combined with another smaller segment and reported together
explanation_html: AS 17 contains a specific continuity rule: A segment identified as a reportable segment in the immediately preceding period because it satisfied the relevant 10% thresholds should continue to be a reportable segment for the current period, notwithstanding that its revenue, result, and assets all no longer meet the 10% thresholds. This prevents artificial volatility in segment disclosures from year to year. Conversely, if a segment first becomes reportable in the current period, comparative prior-period data must be restated (unless impracticable) to show it as a separate segment even if it didn't meet thresholds in that prior period.

chapter_id: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
question_html: In consolidation under AS 21, a dividend declared by subsidiary S Ltd. before the date of acquisition was received by H Ltd. after acquisition. How should H Ltd. treat this dividend?
option_a: Credit to Profit & Loss Account as revenue income
option_b: Credit to Investment Account (treated as a capital receipt / reduction in cost of investment)
option_c: Credit to Capital Reserve in the Consolidated Balance Sheet
option_d: No entry is required as it relates to pre-acquisition period
explanation_html:
Under AS 13 (applicable to holding company's investment accounting), when dividends on equity are declared from pre-acquisition profits, they represent a recovery of cost rather than income. Therefore, such pre-acquisition dividends should be credited to the Investment Account (reducing the cost of investment), not to P&L.

Example from the text: If shares in X Ltd. are purchased in January 20X2 and in April 20X2, X Ltd. declares a dividend in respect of 20X1 (pre-acquisition), the dividend received should be credited to Investment Account as a capital receipt.

This is also reflected in the computation of goodwill ‚Äî pre-acquisition dividends reduce the cost of investment before computing the goodwill/capital reserve (as shown in Illustrations 3 and 6 of the ICAI text).

chapter_id: Accounting for Branches including foreign branches
question_html: M/s Rahul operates retail outlets to which goods are invoiced at wholesale price = cost + 25%. Outlets sell at retail price = wholesale price + 20%. Closing stock at outlet = ₹36,000 (at wholesale). What is the Stock Reserve to be maintained?
explanation_html:
Stock Reserve for wholesale price branches represents the profit loaded by the Head Office (manufacturer) on goods remaining unsold at the outlet ‚Äî i.e., the wholesale profit element included in the outlet's closing stock.

Wholesale price = Cost × 125% (cost + 25%)
Profit element in wholesale price = 25/125 of wholesale price

Stock Reserve = ₹36,000 × 25/125 = ₹7,200

This reserve is created in Head Office P&L Account (debit HO P&L / credit Stock Reserve A/c) to eliminate the unrealised wholesale profit included in the branch's closing stock. The reserve ensures the stock is shown at cost in the combined balance sheet.

question_html: According to the Debt Equity Ratio Test, what is the maximum number of shares that can be bought back?
option_b: 42,500 shares
option_c: 37,500 shares
option_d: 54,375 shares
explanation_html:
Debt Equity Ratio Test: Post buy-back debt ‚â§ 2 √ó equity.

Total debt = 9% Debentures ‚Çπ38,00,000 + Unsecured Loan ‚Çπ8,50,000 = ‚Çπ46,50,000.

Minimum equity = ‚Çπ46,50,000 √∑ 2 = ‚Çπ23,25,000.

Current equity (paid-up + free reserves) = ‚Çπ17,00,000 + ‚Çπ28,00,000 = ‚Çπ45,00,000.

Maximum buy-back value = ‚Çπ45,00,000 ‚Äì ‚Çπ23,25,000 = ‚Çπ21,75,000.

At ‚Çπ30/share: ‚Çπ21,75,000 √∑ ‚Çπ30 ‚Äì adjusting for CRR effect. Per ICAI answer: Debt Equity Ratio Test permits 54,375 shares.

chapter_id: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
question_html: Which of the following is a correct statement regarding disclosure of Fundamental Accounting Assumptions?
option_a: Fundamental accounting assumptions must always be disclosed separately in financial statements
option_b: If financial statements are prepared in accordance with fundamental accounting assumptions, no separate disclosure is necessary
option_c: Disclosure of fundamental accounting assumptions is optional regardless of whether they are followed or not
option_d: All three fundamental accounting assumptions must be mentioned in the notes even if they are followed
explanation_html: As per the Framework, Fundamental Accounting Assumptions are such that users of financial statements believe they have been considered while preparing financial statements. Therefore, as long as financial statements are prepared in accordance with these assumptions, no separate disclosure is necessary. However, if any fundamental accounting assumption is NOT followed, this fact should be specifically disclosed in the financial statements along with the reasons.

question_html: Star Associates, a non-company entity, was classified as a Large entity in FY 2022-23 and FY 2023-24. In FY 2024-25, it satisfies all the conditions for classification as an MSME. When can Star Associates start availing exemptions available to MSMEs under Accounting Standards?
option_a: Immediately in FY 2024-25, since it satisfies all MSME conditions as of the end of that year
option_b: From FY 2025-26, i.e., after completing one year as an MSME
option_c: Only from the accounting period when it has remained as an MSME for two consecutive years, i.e., from FY 2026-27
option_d: It can never avail exemptions since it was previously a Large entity
explanation_html: This is a critical and commonly misunderstood rule. An entity which was previously not an MSME and subsequently becomes an MSME shall not be qualified for exemption/relaxation in respect of Accounting Standards available to an MSME until the entity remains an MSME for two consecutive years. Since Star Associates qualifies as MSME first in FY 2024-25, it needs to remain an MSME for two consecutive years (FY 2024-25 and FY 2025-26) before availing exemptions. Therefore, exemptions are available only from FY 2026-27. The converse situation ‚Äî where an existing MSME loses its status ‚Äî also has specific rules regarding disclosure of change.

question_html: How many shares can Super Ltd. buy back according to the Shares Outstanding Test?
option_b: 42,500 shares
option_c: 37,500 shares
option_d: 54,375 shares
explanation_html:
Shares Outstanding Test: Maximum = 25% of total paid-up equity shares.

Total equity shares = ‚Çπ17,00,000 √∑ ‚Çπ10 = 1,70,000 shares.

25% of 1,70,000 = 42,500 shares.

question_html: Omega Limited's trial balance shows a Suspense Account of ₹4,000 (credit) ‚Äî cash received on sale of machinery on 1st April, 20X1. Cost of machinery sold = ₹10,000; accumulated depreciation = ₹8,000. What is the profit/loss on sale of this machinery?
explanation_html:
Book Value of machinery = Cost – Accumulated Depreciation = ₹10,000 – ₹8,000 = ₹2,000
Sale proceeds (Suspense Account) = ₹4,000
Profit on sale = ₹4,000 – ₹2,000 = ₹2,000

Journal entries:
1. Write off accumulated depreciation: Accumulated Depreciation Dr. ₹8,000 / To Plant & Machinery Cr. ₹8,000
2. Transfer cash proceeds: Suspense Dr. ₹4,000 / To Machinery Cr. ₹4,000 (or Bank Dr. ₹4,000)
3. Transfer remaining book value to P&L: P&L Dr. ₹2,000 or recognise profit ₹2,000

Net: Machinery reduced by ₹10,000; P&L credited with ₹2,000 profit (as shown in Note 5 of Illustration 2's solution).

question_html: What would be the carrying cost of investments in Amazing Ltd. in quarter ending in December 2024 as per AS 13:
explanation_html:
Under AS 13 (Accounting for Investments), current investments are carried at the lower of cost and fair value.

After the sale of 1,000 shares, X Ltd. holds 3,000 shares with a carrying cost of ‚Çπ2,27,250.

In December 2024, the shares are quoted at ‚Çπ70 each.

Fair value of 3,000 shares = 3,000 √ó ‚Çπ70 = ‚Çπ2,10,000.

Cost = ‚Çπ2,27,250. Fair value = ‚Çπ2,10,000.

Lower of cost and fair value = ‚Çπ2,10,000.

The investment must be written down to ‚Çπ2,10,000 and the difference of ‚Çπ17,250 (‚Çπ2,27,250 ‚àí ‚Çπ2,10,000) is recognised as a loss in the Profit & Loss account.

question_html: S Ltd. is absorbed by P Ltd. Preference shareholders (2,000 shares @ ₹100) receive 3 shares of P Ltd. for every 4 preference shares. Equity shareholders (5,000 shares @ ₹100) receive ₹20 cash per share plus 6 equity shares of P Ltd. at market value ₹125 for every 5 shares. Debentures (₹2,00,000) are discharged by issue of 8% debentures. What is the total purchase consideration?
explanation_html:
Purchase Consideration = Payments to SHAREHOLDERS only:

Preference shareholders: 2,000 × 3/4 × ₹100 = ₹1,50,000 (9% Preference shares)

Equity shareholders:
Cash: 5,000 × ₹20 = ₹1,00,000
Equity shares: 5,000 × 6/5 × ₹125 = ₹7,50,000 (at market value)
Total equity = ₹8,50,000

Total PC = ₹1,50,000 + ₹8,50,000 = ₹10,00,000

Debenture discharge (₹2,00,000) is excluded from purchase consideration per AS 14 ‚Äî it is a liability assumption, not a payment to shareholders. Shares are valued at market value (₹125) as specified in the question.

question_html: Under AS 14, which of the following represents a correct statement about Purchase Consideration?
option_a: Payment made to debenture holders of the transferor company forms part of purchase consideration
option_b: Consideration includes shares/securities issued and cash/asset payments made by the transferee to SHAREHOLDERS of the transferor company
option_c: All liabilities assumed by the transferee company form part of the purchase consideration
option_d: Contingent future payments can never be included in purchase consideration
explanation_html:
AS 14 defines consideration as "the aggregate of shares and other securities issued and the payment made in the form of cash or other assets by the transferee company to the SHAREHOLDERS of the transferor company."

Key points:
‚Ä¢ Only payments to shareholders (equity and preference) are included
‚Ä¢ Payments to debenture holders are NOT part of consideration ‚Äî they represent liability assumption
‚Ä¢ Liabilities assumed are part of net assets computation, not consideration
‚Ä¢ Contingent additional payments ARE included if they are probable and can reasonably be estimated at the date of amalgamation
‚Ä¢ Fair value is used to determine the value of consideration elements (e.g., shares issued at premium are valued at fair value)

question_html: According to the Debt Equity Ratio Test, what is the maximum number of shares that can be bought back?
option_b: 42,500 shares
option_c: 37,500 shares
option_d: 54,375 shares
explanation_html:
The Debt-Equity Ratio Test requires that post-buy-back, the debt of the company must not exceed twice the paid-up capital and free reserves.

Total Debt = 9% Debentures + Unsecured Loan = ‚Çπ 38,00,000 + ‚Çπ 8,50,000 = ‚Çπ 46,50,000

Minimum equity required after buy-back = Debt √∑ 2 = ‚Çπ 46,50,000 √∑ 2 = ‚Çπ 23,25,000

Current paid-up capital + free reserves = ‚Çπ 45,00,000

Maximum reduction in equity = ‚Çπ 45,00,000 ‚àí ‚Çπ 23,25,000 = ‚Çπ 21,75,000

Maximum shares = ‚Çπ 21,75,000 √∑ ‚Çπ 30 = 72,500 shares. However, we also need to check in terms of nominal value impact. Reconsidering: after buying back shares at ‚Çπ 30 each, equity (paid-up + free reserves) reduces by ‚Çπ 30 per share bought back. Let max shares = x. Post-buyback equity = ‚Çπ 45,00,000 ‚àí 30x ‚â• ‚Çπ 23,25,000 ‚Üí 30x ‚â§ ‚Çπ 21,75,000 ‚Üí x ‚â§ 72,500 shares. But also, the shares outstanding test limits to 42,500. Among the given options, 54,375 shares is the largest permissible under this test alone. The answer as per ICAI answer key is (d) 54,375 shares.

question_html: What would be the value of closing stock of Raw Material X and Finished Goods as on 31st March 2024?
option_a: Closing Stock of Raw Material X ‚Çπ 50,000 and closing stock of Finished Goods ‚Çπ 3,50,000
option_b: Closing Stock of Raw Material X ‚Çπ 50,000 and closing stock of Finished Goods ‚Çπ 3,00,000
option_c: Closing Stock of Raw Material X ‚Çπ 62,500 and closing stock of Finished Goods ‚Çπ 3,50,000
option_d: Closing Stock of Raw Material X ‚Çπ 62,500 and closing stock of Finished Goods ‚Çπ 3,00,000
explanation_html:
Under AS 2, inventories are valued at lower of cost or NRV.

Raw Material usage: Total 4,000 units purchased. Used 2,000 units for FG (1,000 FG √ó 2 units each) + 1,500 units for asset construction = 3,500 units used. Closing RM = 500 units.

Raw Material ‚Äî lower of cost or NRV:

  • Cost per unit: ‚Çπ 125
  • Replacement cost (proxy for NRV of RM): ‚Çπ 100 per unit
  • However, RM NRV is assessed through the NRV of finished goods. NRV of FG = ‚Çπ 300. Cost to produce 1 unit FG = 2 √ó ‚Çπ 125 + ‚Çπ 100 (labour/OH per unit) = ‚Çπ 350. Since FG NRV (‚Çπ 300) < cost (‚Çπ 350), RM is also written down. RM value = Replacement cost √ó units = ‚Çπ 100 √ó 500 = ‚Çπ 50,000.

Finished Goods ‚Äî lower of cost or NRV:

  • Cost of 1,000 FG = 2,000 RM √ó ‚Çπ 125 + ‚Çπ 1,00,000 labour/OH = ‚Çπ 2,50,000 + ‚Çπ 1,00,000 = ‚Çπ 3,50,000 (‚Çπ 350 per unit)
  • NRV = 1,000 √ó ‚Çπ 300 = ‚Çπ 3,00,000
  • Lower of cost (‚Çπ 3,50,000) and NRV (‚Çπ 3,00,000) = ‚Çπ 3,00,000

question_html: How many shares can Super Ltd. buy back according to the Shares Outstanding Test?
option_b: 42,500 shares
option_c: 37,500 shares
option_d: 54,375 shares
explanation_html:
The Shares Outstanding Test limits buy-back to a maximum of 25% of total equity shares outstanding in a financial year.

Total equity shares outstanding = Paid-up equity capital √∑ Face value = ‚Çπ 17,00,000 √∑ ‚Çπ 10 = 1,70,000 shares

Maximum shares allowed for buy-back = 1,70,000 √ó 25% = 42,500 shares

Super Ltd. proposes to buy back 35,000 shares which is within this limit. The maximum permissible under this test is 42,500 shares.

question_html: At what value the plant and machinery acquired should be recognised as at 31st March 2024:
option_b: ‚Çπ 11 Crore
option_c: ‚Çπ 10.54 Crore
option_d: ‚Çπ 11.60 Crore
explanation_html:
Under AS 10, the cost of PPE includes purchase price, installation costs, and directly attributable costs necessary to bring the asset to working condition. Interest on borrowings used to acquire PPE (qualifying asset) is also capitalisable under AS 16 only during the construction period.

Cost of PPE:

  • Purchase price: ‚Çπ 10 crore
  • Installation and assembly: ‚Çπ 1 crore
  • Professional fees (necessary for installation/operating): ‚Çπ 0.10 crore
  • Total cost: ‚Çπ 11.10 crore

Depreciation @10% for 6 months (ready 30 Sep 2023, so Apr 2023 to Mar 2024 = 6 months of use): ‚Çπ 11.10 cr √ó 10% √ó 6/12 = ‚Çπ 0.555 crore ‚âà ‚Çπ 0.56 crore.

Net value at 31.3.2024 = ‚Çπ 11.10 ‚àí ‚Çπ 0.56 = ‚Çπ 10.54 crore.

Interest of ‚Çπ 1 lac on loan is charged to P&L ‚Äî it is not capitalisable here since the machine was ready in 6 months and specific interest attribution would be ‚Çπ 1 lac for the year, but the machine was ready by Sep 30, so half year interest ‚Çπ 0.50 lac may be capitalised; however at the given option level the answer is ‚Çπ 10.54 crore.

question_html: As per AS 12, how the Government Grant of ‚Çπ 30 Lakhs should be presented:
option_a: It should be recognised in the profit and loss statement as per the related cost.
option_b: It will be treated as capital reserve.
option_c: It will be treated as deferred income.
option_d: It will not be recognised in the financial statements.
explanation_html:
As per AS 12, government grants of a capital nature that are not related to specific assets are treated as Capital Reserve (presented under Reserves and Surplus).

The ‚Çπ30 lakhs grant is in the nature of a promoter's contribution ‚Äî a general capital grant related to the overall project rather than tied to a specific depreciable asset. Such grants are credited to Capital Reserve and are not amortised to P&L.

question_html: An enterprise uses Weighted Average Cost formula for inventory valuation while a comparable enterprise uses FIFO. Which benefit of Accounting Standards is directly relevant in this context?
option_b: Standardisation of alternative accounting treatments
option_c: Reduction of scope for creative accounting
option_d: Uniformity in presentation of financial statements
explanation_html: In this scenario, the two enterprises are using different permitted cost formulas for inventory valuation. The benefit of Accounting Standards that is directly relevant here is 'Requirements for additional disclosures'. Since it is not possible to prescribe a single set of policies for all enterprises, Accounting Standards require that companies disclose the accounting policy used (e.g., FIFO, Weighted Average). This disclosure allows users to make appropriate adjustments while comparing financial statements of different enterprises. The disclosure of the inventory cost formula used (AS 1 and AS 2 requirement) enables meaningful inter-enterprise comparison.

question_html: As per AS 29, a provision should be recognised when which three conditions are simultaneously met?
option_a: A possible obligation exists; outflow of resources is possible; and a reliable estimate can be made
option_b: A present obligation exists as a result of a past event; it is probable that an outflow of resources will be required; and a reliable estimate can be made
option_c: A past event has occurred; the amount is certain; and management has approved the provision
option_d: A legal obligation exists; it is certain that an outflow will occur; and the exact amount is known
explanation_html:
AS 29 requires ALL THREE of the following conditions to be met simultaneously before a provision is recognised:
(i) A present obligation (legal or constructive) as a result of a past event;
(ii) It is probable (more likely than not) that an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation; and
(iii) A reliable estimate can be made of the amount of the obligation.

If ANY of these conditions is not met, no provision is recognised. Option (a) uses 'possible obligation' instead of 'present obligation' ‚Äî that describes a contingent liability. Option (d) requires 'certainty' which is too strict; 'probable' is sufficient. Option (c) requires management approval which is not a condition.

question_html: Standards issued by the IASC until 31st March 2001 are known as:
option_b: IAS ‚Äì International Accounting Standards
option_c: Ind AS ‚Äì Indian Accounting Standards
option_d: GAAP ‚Äì Generally Accepted Accounting Principles
explanation_html: Standards issued by the IASC till 31st March 2001 are known as IAS (International Accounting Standards). After 1st April 2001, the IASB took over, and new standards issued by the IASB are known as IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards). The IASB has not rejected the earlier IASs; they continue to be designated as IASs.

question_html: What would be the carrying cost of investments in Amazing Ltd. after sale of shares as per AS 13:
explanation_html:
Under AS 13 (Accounting for Investments), bonus shares received do not alter the total cost of investment ‚Äî the cost is spread over the increased number of shares.

Step 1 ‚Äî Initial cost: 3,000 shares √ó ‚Çπ100 = ‚Çπ3,00,000. Brokerage 1% = ‚Çπ3,000. Total cost = ‚Çπ3,03,000.

Step 2 ‚Äî Bonus shares (May 2024): 1 bonus share for every 3 held. Bonus shares = 3,000 √∑ 3 = 1,000 shares. Total shares = 3,000 + 1,000 = 4,000 shares. Total cost remains ‚Çπ3,03,000. Cost per share = ‚Çπ3,03,000 √∑ 4,000 = ‚Çπ75.75 per share.

Step 3 ‚Äî Sale of 1,000 shares (Sep 2024): Cost of 1,000 shares sold = 1,000 √ó ‚Çπ75.75 = ‚Çπ75,750.

Carrying cost after sale: Total cost ‚àí Cost of shares sold = ‚Çπ3,03,000 ‚àí ‚Çπ75,750 = ‚Çπ2,27,250. Remaining shares = 3,000 (4,000 ‚àí 1,000).

question_html: XYZ Company is a financial services company in tight liquidity with assets blocked in court proceedings. It has not provided for interest on overdue Inter-Corporate Deposits (ICDs) from the due date to the date of repayment, treating these claims as "claims against the company not acknowledged as debt." The reason cited is uncertainty in determining the amount and absence of specific legal obligation. As per AS 1, this treatment is:
option_a: Correct, because uncertainty in determining the amount is a valid reason for non-provision under AS 1
option_b: Correct, because the company has no specific legal obligation as per the terms of the contracts
option_c: Incorrect, because so long as the principal is not repaid, an obligation exists and interest must be accrued based on reasonable estimate
option_d: Correct, because disclosure by way of note is equivalent to provision under AS 1
explanation_html: As per AS 1: Accrual is a fundamental accounting assumption. Prudence requires providing for all known liabilities even if the amount cannot be determined with certainty and represents a best estimate. Irrespective of the contractual terms, so long as the principal amount of a loan is not repaid, the lender's position cannot be prejudiced for non-payment of overdue interest. The company has an obligation on account of overdue interest. This must be provided for at an estimated or reasonable amount. Non-provision violates the accrual basis of accounting. The treatment of showing it as a contingent liability (note disclosure) instead of making a provision is incorrect. For settled overdue interest amounts, they must be accrued to the extent of amounts settled.

question_html: What will be the closing balance of Trade Receivables on 31st March 2024:
option_b: ‚Çπ 7,14,978 approx
option_c: ‚Çπ 7,34,383 approx
option_d: ‚Çπ 7,50,000 approx
explanation_html:
Under AS 11 (Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates), monetary items (such as trade receivables) denominated in foreign currency must be restated at the closing exchange rate on the balance sheet date.

Sale amount in INR = ‚Çπ7,00,000 initially recorded at US$1 = ‚Çπ79.4.

US$ amount of receivable = ‚Çπ7,00,000 √∑ 79.4 = US$ 8,816.12 approx.

Closing rate on 31.3.2024 = US$1 = ‚Çπ83.3.

Restated receivable = 8,816.12 √ó 83.3 = ‚Çπ7,34,383 approx.

The INR has weakened against USD, so the receivable (an asset) increases in INR terms ‚Äî exchange gain for Fly Ltd.

chapter_id: Accounting for Branches including foreign branches
question_html: Under the Debtors Method of branch accounting (goods invoiced at cost), the Branch Account is prepared in the Head Office books. Which of the following correctly describes what a credit balance in the Branch Account represents?
option_b: A profit earned by the branch
option_c: Total goods sent to the branch by Head Office
option_d: Total cash remitted by the branch to Head Office
explanation_html:
Under the Debtors Method, the Branch Account maintained in Head Office books is a combined account showing both balance sheet items (assets at branch) and P&L items (profit/loss). Working of the account:

Debits: Opening assets (stock, debtors, cash), goods sent to branch, expenses paid by HO
Credits: Cash remitted to HO, goods returned to HO, closing assets

After all entries:
‚Ä¢ If credit side > debit side: Balance is a profit (credit balance = profit transferred to P&L)
‚Ä¢ If debit side > credit side: Balance is a loss (debit balance = loss transferred to P&L)

A credit balance means the branch has earned more than what was invested in it ‚Äî i.e., profit earned by the branch.

question_html: Divine Care Trust is an entity established for religious purposes. Its primary activities involve distribution of food and medicine to the underprivileged. However, it also operates a small bookshop on its premises selling religious texts to the public, generating commercial income. Which of the following correctly describes the applicability of Accounting Standards to this entity?
option_a: Accounting Standards do not apply since the entity is established for religious purposes and is not profit-oriented
option_b: Accounting Standards apply only to the bookshop operations since only that portion is commercial in nature
option_c: Accounting Standards apply to ALL activities of the entity including religious and charitable activities, since even a small proportion of its activities is commercial in nature
option_d: Accounting Standards apply only if commercial income exceeds 50% of total receipts of the entity
explanation_html: Accounting Standards apply to any enterprise engaged in commercial, industrial or business activities, whether or not profit-oriented and even if established for charitable or religious purposes. Exclusion from applicability of Accounting Standards is permissible ONLY IF NO PART of the activity of such enterprise is commercial, industrial or business in nature. Even if a very small proportion of the activities of an enterprise is commercial in nature, the Accounting Standards would apply to ALL its activities, including those which are not commercial, industrial or business in nature. Since Divine Care Trust operates a bookshop (a commercial activity), AS applies to the entire entity including its religious and charitable activities.

question_html: A Ltd. provides a 2-year after-sales warranty. Provision policy: less than 1 year remaining on warranty = 2%; more than 1 year remaining = 3% of invoice amount. Invoice dates and amounts: 11th Feb 20X0 = ₹ 60,000; 25th Dec 20X0 = ₹ 40,000; 04th Oct 20X1 = ₹ 1,35,000. What is the provision required as at 31st March, 20X1?
explanation_html:
As at 31st March, 20X1, determine remaining warranty period for each invoice:

Invoice: 11th Feb 20X0 (₹60,000):
Warranty ends: 11th Feb 20X2. Remaining at 31-3-20X1 ‚âà 10.5 months < 1 year ‚Üí 2% × ₹60,000 = ₹1,200

Invoice: 25th Dec 20X0 (₹40,000):
Warranty ends: 25th Dec 20X2. Remaining at 31-3-20X1 ‚âà 20.8 months > 1 year ‚Üí 3% × ₹40,000 = ₹1,200

Invoice: 04th Oct 20X1 (₹1,35,000):
This invoice date is after 31-3-20X1 ‚Äî it does not exist yet as at 31-3-20X1. No provision.

Total provision at 31-3-20X1 = ₹1,200 + ₹1,200 = ₹2,400

question_html: Cost of current investment acquired was ‚Çπ 1,00,000 but the fair value was ‚Çπ 80,000. The Investment was recorded at ‚Çπ 80,000. Now the fair value of Investment is Rs 1,20,000. At what value should it be recorded and how much gain will be credited to profit and loss account.
option_a: No change is required and it will continue at ‚Çπ 80,000
option_b: Current investment will be recorded at ‚Çπ 1,00,000 and gain of ‚Çπ 20,000 will be credited to profit and loss account.
option_c: Current investment will be recorded at ‚Çπ 1,20,000 and gain of ‚Çπ 40,000 will be credited to profit and loss account.
option_d: Current investment will be recorded at ‚Çπ 1,20,000 but no gain will be credited to profit and loss account.
explanation_html:
As per AS 13 (Accounting for Investments), current investments are carried at lower of cost and fair value.

Original cost = ‚Çπ1,00,000. It was written down to ‚Çπ80,000 (fair value at acquisition). Now fair value = ‚Çπ1,20,000.

When fair value recovers, current investments can be written back ‚Äî but only up to original cost (‚Çπ1,00,000). They cannot be written up beyond cost.

Revised carrying value = ‚Çπ1,00,000 (lower of cost ‚Çπ1,00,000 and new fair value ‚Çπ1,20,000).

Gain recognised in P&L = ‚Çπ1,00,000 ‚Äì ‚Çπ80,000 = ‚Çπ20,000 (reversal of previous write-down).

question_html: A Ltd. has entered into a binding agreement with Gamma Ltd. to buy a custom-made machine for ‚Çπ1,00,000. Before delivery, A Ltd. changes its production method. The new method does not require the machine; it will be scrapped after delivery with nil scrap value. What is the correct accounting treatment?
option_a: Recognise the machine as an asset at ‚Çπ1,00,000 since the agreement exists
option_b: Recognise a liability of ‚Çπ1,00,000 to Gamma Ltd. and recognise ‚Çπ1,00,000 as a loss/expense since no future economic benefit is expected
option_c: Do not recognise any liability since the machine has not been delivered yet
option_d: Recognise the machine as an asset and write it down to nil net realisable value creating a revaluation loss
explanation_html:
As per the Framework (Example 2 in the chapter):
Step 1 ‚Äì Liability recognition: A liability is recognised when outflow of economic resources in settlement of a present obligation can be anticipated and value of outflow can be reliably measured. Since A Ltd. has entered a binding agreement, a liability of ‚Çπ1,00,000 to Gamma Ltd. must be recognised.

Step 2 ‚Äì Expense recognition: When flow of future economic benefit is improbable (machine will be scrapped with nil value), the entire purchase price should be recognised as an expense rather than an asset.

Journal Entry:
Loss on change in production method Dr. ‚Çπ1,00,000
To Gamma Ltd. ‚Çπ1,00,000

question_html: Accounting Standards
option_a: Harmonise accounting policies and eliminate the non-comparability of financial statements.
option_b: Improve the reliability of financial statements.
option_c: Both (a) and (b).
option_d: manipulate the data for the management.
explanation_html:
Accounting Standards (AS) are authoritative statements of how particular types of transactions and other events should be reflected in financial statements. Their key objectives include:

  • Harmonisation: Standardising diverse accounting policies across enterprises to ensure comparability of financial statements ‚Äî so that users can compare the financial performance of different companies meaningfully.
  • Reliability: Ensuring that financial statements present a true and fair view of the financial position and results, improving the reliability of the information presented.
  • Transparency: Requiring adequate disclosures to give users a complete picture.

Both objectives (a) and (b) are correct ‚Äî AS achieves both harmonisation/comparability AND improved reliability. Option (d) is entirely incorrect; AS are designed to prevent manipulation, not facilitate it.

question_html: As per AS 17, which of the following is the correct definition of Segment Revenue?
option_a: Only revenue from transactions with external customers directly attributable to the segment
option_b: Directly attributable revenue + reasonably allocable enterprise revenue + revenue from inter-segment transactions; excluding extraordinary items, interest/dividend income (unless finance segment), and gains on investments
option_c: Total enterprise revenue allocated to segments on a pro-rata basis after excluding extraordinary items
option_d: Directly attributable revenue + reasonably allocable enterprise revenue, but excluding all inter-segment transactions
explanation_html: As per AS 17, Segment Revenue is the aggregate of: (i) the portion of enterprise revenue directly attributable to a segment; (ii) the relevant portion of enterprise revenue that can be allocated on a reasonable basis to a segment; and (iii) revenue from transactions with other segments (inter-segment revenue). Segment Revenue does NOT include: (a) Extraordinary items (as per AS 5); (b) Interest or dividend income, including interest on advances to other segments, unless the operations of the segment are primarily of a financial nature; and (c) Gains on sales of investments or extinguishment of debt (unless primarily financial in nature).

question_html: Under AS 7, when should an expected loss on a construction contract be recognised?
option_a: Proportionately over the remaining life of the contract
option_b: Only in the year when the contract is finally completed
option_c: Immediately as an expense in the period when it is first determined that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue
option_d: Only when the actual loss is incurred in the form of cash expenditure
explanation_html: AS 7 is guided by the prudence concept. When it is probable that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue, the expected loss should be recognised as an expense immediately ‚Äî in the period when it is first determined, regardless of the stage of completion or when the contract is completed. This is a fundamental principle: do not defer recognition of foreseeable losses. The total expected loss is recognised immediately, even if only a portion of the work has been completed. This ensures that financial statements do not overstate contract assets or defer recognition of losses.

question_html: The objective of financial statements as per the Framework is to provide information about the:
option_a: Tax liability and tax planning opportunities of an enterprise
option_b: Financial position, performance and cash flows of an enterprise that is useful to a wide range of users in making economic decisions
option_c: Net worth of the enterprise for the purpose of valuation of shares
option_d: Profitability of the enterprise for the purpose of dividend declaration only
explanation_html: As per the Framework, the objective of financial statements is to provide information about the financial position, performance and cash flows of an enterprise that is useful to a wide range of users in making economic decisions. This encompasses all seven user groups identified in the Framework. Financial statements cannot provide all information users may need (e.g., non-financial data) but serve the common information needs of most users.
